anesthesia-machine-check.caption: A four-step pre-use check of the anaesthesia machine: emergency oxygen, leak test, scavenging, monitors and alarms.
anesthesia-machine-check.body:
In short: The anaesthesia machine delivers oxygen, gases and vapour to a patient who cannot breathe for themselves, so it is checked before every list. This card turns the check into four ordered steps so none is skipped.

What the card shows

Four teal tick-boxes run down the left of this graphic, joined by a dotted line to show that they are a sequence. They read: emergency oxygen (flow, suction, breathing system), leak test at 30 cmH₂O (no leak, vaporizers off), scavenging flow (unobstructed path, canister check) and monitors and alarms (capnography, pulse oximeter, pressure).

What each block is protecting

The check exists because a fault is far better found before induction than in the middle of a case. Emergency oxygen confirms you can ventilate the patient if anything fails. The leak test shows the circuit holds pressure. Scavenging keeps waste anaesthetic gases out of the theatre air. Monitors and alarms must be on, responding, and set to sensible limits.

Why it is a sequence and not a list

Under pressure, people skip steps they feel they have done before. Making it four numbered, ordered blocks means you always start with the thing that keeps the patient alive. The same logic sits behind the WHO anaesthesia safety check in the Sign In phase. As a student, you will usually watch the anaesthetist or technologist perform this, so learn the order well enough to notice when something is skipped, and always follow your hospital's own machine checklist.

How the machine works, in plain terms

An anaesthesia machine takes oxygen (and sometimes air or nitrous oxide) from the wall supply or cylinders, controls the flow, adds a measured amount of anaesthetic vapour from a vaporizer, and delivers the mixture through a breathing circuit to the patient. A ventilator or the reservoir bag pushes the gas in, and the used gas passes through a carbon dioxide absorber and out to the scavenging system.

Because every one of these parts can fail, the check proves the essentials: there is a backup supply of oxygen, the circuit holds pressure, waste gas leaves safely and the monitors will warn the team if something goes wrong.

What the technologist and student can do

Anaesthetists carry responsibility for the machine check, but theatre technologists often help by making sure the room is ready: oxygen cylinders full and in place, suction working, the circuit and filters the right type and size, the absorber not exhausted, and spare airway equipment within reach. Learn what a full check looks like so you can notice when the machine in front of you has not been checked.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming the machine was checked by the previous shift without confirming.
  • Skipping the emergency oxygen step because the wall supply seems fine.
  • Leaving a vaporizer switched on during the leak test.
  • Ignoring a small leak or a stuck valve because the list is running late.

Check yourself

Why is a separate emergency oxygen supply checked first?

Because if the main supply or machine fails, the backup is what keeps the patient oxygenated.

What does the leak test show?

That the breathing circuit holds pressure, so gas is not escaping before it reaches the patient.

Why do monitors and alarms matter before induction?

They are the team's early warning; alarms must be on, audible and set to sensible limits.

Quick revision points

  • Check order: emergency oxygen, leak test, scavenging, monitors and alarms.
  • A fault found before induction is far safer than one found mid-case.
  • Leak test is done with vaporizers off.
  • Scavenging protects the team from waste anaesthetic gas.
  • Always follow the hospital's own machine checklist.

ot-fun-quiz.caption: A quick quiz: which sterilisation indicator is the gold standard, and why the others are not enough on their own.
ot-fun-quiz.body:
In short: Sterilisation is checked three ways, and only one of them tests whether living organisms were really killed. This quiz card helps you remember which.

What the card shows

A bright quiz layout fills this graphic, with a heading that reads "OT Fun Quiz" and a question: which indicator is the gold standard for sterilisation? Four rounded options are drawn with icons: mechanical printout with a printer icon, chemical integrator with a test-tube icon, biological spore test with a petri dish icon, and all equal. A banner at the bottom says "Comment your answer, we'll share the answer".

The answer

The gold standard is the biological indicator, the spore test. It uses highly resistant bacterial spores, so if those die, you can trust that the process has killed everything else. The mechanical printout shows that the machine reached the right temperature, pressure and time, and the chemical integrator changes colour in response to those same conditions. Both are useful but neither proves that living organisms were killed.

Why "all equal" is a trap

Each indicator tells you something different, so they work as a team, but only the biological one tests the real result. That is why a hospital runs mechanical, chemical and biological checks together.

Try it yourself

Cover the answer and explain in your own words why spores are used. Then check the Sterilization Indicators and Autoclave cards for the full picture. Quiz formats like this are good for spaced practice, so come back in a few days and see whether you still remember it.

The three kinds of indicator

Mechanical indicators are the machine's own gauges and printouts of temperature, pressure and time. Chemical indicators are strips, tapes or integrators that change colour when exposed to the right conditions. Biological indicators contain living bacterial spores and are the only check that proves the process killed them.

Spores are used because they are far harder to kill than ordinary bacteria. If the spores die, everything easier to kill has died too.

How a biological test is run

A vial of spores is placed in the load, put through the cycle, then incubated alongside an unprocessed control vial. If the processed vial shows no growth and the control does, the cycle worked. Hospitals usually run biological tests on a regular schedule and with loads such as implants, following their own policy.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating a printout that looks right as proof of sterility.
  • Choosing 'all are equal' because each indicator seems useful.
  • Reading a colour change on a tape as evidence that the whole pack is sterile.
  • Releasing implants before the biological result, where local policy requires waiting.

Check yourself

Which indicator is the gold standard?

The biological indicator, the spore test.

Why can a chemical indicator not replace it?

It shows exposure to conditions, not that organisms were killed.

What does a failed spore test mean for the load?

Quarantine and re-process it, and investigate the machine.

Quick revision points

  • Biological indicator = spore test = gold standard.
  • Mechanical and chemical indicators support, not replace, it.
  • Spores are chosen because they resist killing.
  • Run all three together.
  • A failed result means quarantine the load.

positioning-injuries-prevention.caption: How lithotomy, lateral and prone positions can injure an anaesthetised patient, and the padding and checks that prevent it.
positioning-injuries-prevention.body:
In short: An anaesthetised patient cannot feel pressure or pain, so the team has to protect nerves, skin and joints for them. This card lists the main risks of three common positions and how to prevent them.

What the card shows

Four teal panels with shield icons stack on the right of this graphic, with me on the left holding my chin in thought. Lithotomy: common peroneal nerve risk, compartment syndrome and padding the knees. Lateral decubitus: brachial plexus, eye and ear pressure and an axillary roll. Prone: eye and face pressure, ventilation and chest rolls. General prevention: pad bony prominences, avoid hyperextension and check circulation.

What can go wrong

The anaesthetised patient cannot say "that hurts". Pressure on a nerve, stretching a joint too far or restricting blood flow can cause numbness, weakness or tissue damage that lasts long after surgery. In lithotomy, pressure on the outside of the knee can injure the common peroneal nerve, and long cases raise the risk of compartment syndrome in the legs. In the lateral position, the arm and shoulder need support, and the dependent eye and ear must be free of pressure. In the prone position, the face, eyes and chest need protection and the airway needs close watching.

How we prevent it

Pad every bony point, keep joints in a natural range, avoid stretching limbs beyond about 90 degrees, check pulses and skin before and after, and reposition if the case runs very long. Document the position and the padding used. The Safe Patient Positioning in Theatre blog post covers it in more depth.

Why positioning injuries happen

Under anaesthesia, muscles relax and protective reflexes switch off. A limb can be stretched beyond its normal range, a nerve can be squeezed against a hard edge, and skin over bone can be starved of blood flow by constant pressure. Longer operations raise the risk, because pressure and stretch last for hours.

Most injuries are neuropraxia, a temporary nerve injury, but some leave lasting weakness or numbness, pressure sores or, in the legs, compartment syndrome, where swelling inside a tight muscle compartment cuts off blood supply.

Position by position

Lithotomy: legs are raised and supported; avoid pressure on the outside of the knee (common peroneal nerve), lift and lower the legs together and slowly, and keep operating times in mind. Lateral: protect the dependent shoulder and arm, place an axillary roll as per local practice, keep the neck neutral and make sure the ear and eye do not rest on anything. Prone: the head and face must not press on eyes or nose, the chest and pelvis need support so the abdomen hangs free, and the arms must not be over-stretched.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Moving a patient into position without enough hands, causing shear or stretch.
  • Forgetting to pad bony points such as heels, sacrum, elbows and fibular head.
  • Leaving arms hanging or stretched beyond a comfortable range.
  • Not rechecking the position after the table is tilted or the patient is moved.

Check yourself

Which nerve is at risk from pressure on the outside of the knee in lithotomy?

The common peroneal nerve.

Why must the dependent eye and ear be free of pressure in the lateral position?

Pressure can damage the eye or skin, and the patient cannot report it.

What do we record after positioning?

The position used, the padding and supports, and any checks made.

Quick revision points

  • Pad every bony prominence.
  • Avoid stretching joints beyond a natural range.
  • Lift and lower legs together, slowly, in lithotomy.
  • Protect eyes and face in the prone position.
  • Recheck circulation and skin before and after the case.

carpal-bones-wrist.caption: The eight carpal bones in two rows, with a mnemonic and a note on why the scaphoid matters clinically.
carpal-bones-wrist.body:
In short: The wrist contains eight small bones arranged in two rows. Learning their order is a classic anatomy hurdle, and this card makes it easier.

What the card shows

A drawing of the hand and wrist sits in the centre of this graphic, with coloured dots on each of the eight carpal bones and labelled leader lines: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate, plus the radius and ulna at the forearm end. A colour key sits underneath. A note at the bottom explains that the eight bones are arranged in two rows, the proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform) and the distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate).

The two rows

The proximal row sits next to the radius and ulna, and the distal row sits next to the metacarpals of the hand. Together they let the wrist bend, extend and rotate.

A classic mnemonic

Many students use "Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle", which follows the order scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate, going from the thumb side across the proximal row and then across the distal row, again from the thumb side. The scaphoid is the one worth special attention, because it is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, often after a fall on an outstretched hand. A fracture there can be missed on the first X-ray and heal poorly.

Why the wrist has so many small bones

A single big bone would make the wrist stiff. Eight small carpal bones, linked by ligaments, glide over each other so that the hand can bend, straighten, tilt sideways and rotate. The proximal row connects to the forearm bones, and the distal row connects to the long bones of the palm (metacarpals).

The scaphoid bridges the two rows, which makes it vulnerable to injury when the wrist is forced backwards, for example in a fall on an outstretched hand.

Why theatre students meet this anatomy

Wrist fractures, scaphoid fractures and carpal tunnel surgery are common in orthopaedic and hand lists. Knowing the carpal bones helps you follow the surgeon's language, understand X-rays and anticipate small fragment and screw sets. Carpal tunnel release, a frequent day case, involves dividing the ligament that forms the roof of the tunnel through which the median nerve and tendons pass.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Confusing the order of the two rows or the direction of the sequence.
  • Mixing up trapezium and trapezoid, which are next to each other.
  • Forgetting the pisiform sits on top of the triquetrum and is the one you can feel at the base of the palm.
  • Thinking a normal first X-ray rules out a scaphoid fracture.

Check yourself

Name the proximal row from the thumb side.

Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.

Which carpal bone is most often fractured?

The scaphoid.

What is the mnemonic?

Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle.

Quick revision points

  • Eight carpal bones in two rows of four.
  • Proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.
  • Distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
  • Scaphoid fractures can be missed and heal poorly.
  • Pisiform is the small pea-shaped bone you can feel.

bones-and-nicknames.caption: Thirteen bones with everyday nicknames and their anatomical names, on the skeleton.
bones-and-nicknames.body:
In short: Nicknames give you a handle on bone names before the formal terms stick. This card pairs thirteen everyday names with the correct anatomical terms.

What the card shows

A full skeleton fills the left of this graphic with thirteen coloured labels that pair each nickname with its proper name: brain box (cranium), upper jaw (maxilla), jaw bone (mandible), cheek bone (zygomatic), beauty bone (clavicle), shoulder blade (scapula), breast bone (sternum), funny bone (humerus), finger and toe bones (phalanges), back bone (the vertebral column), tail bone (coccyx), knee cap (patella) and heel bone (calcaneus).

Why nicknames work

Medical Latin is hard to hold in your head at first. A nickname gives the bone a handle: you know where it is and what it looks like before you know its formal name, and then the two get linked.

One honest nuance

The "funny bone" is not really a funny bone. The tingling jolt comes from the ulnar nerve passing behind the inner side of the lower humerus at the elbow. Knowing that makes the nickname easier to remember. Try covering the right-hand names and saying each one, then cover the nicknames and go the other way. If a label trips you up, put it on a sticky note on your mirror. This is the main skeleton version, and the other two Bones cards use different layouts of the same idea.

From nickname to anatomy

Anatomical names come from Latin and Greek, and many describe something ordinary. Clavicle means 'little key', scapula is simply the Latin word for the shoulder blade, patella means 'little plate' and coccyx comes from the word for a cuckoo, because of its beak-like shape. Seeing the story behind a name turns it from a random word into a picture.

Use the nickname to find the bone on a skeleton or on your own body, and then say the formal name aloud.

Why it matters in a hospital

Doctors, radiographers and surgeons use the formal names. A request for a 'mandible' or 'clavicle' X-ray, or a patient with a 'fractured calcaneus', must be understood instantly. Patients, on the other hand, use the nicknames, so you need both: the formal language for the team and the simple language to explain things to a patient.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Learning only the nickname and missing the formal name in an exam.
  • Mixing up maxilla (upper jaw) and mandible (lower jaw).
  • Treating the 'funny bone' as a bone rather than the ulnar nerve at the elbow.
  • Memorising a flat list instead of linking each name to a position on the body.

Check yourself

What is the anatomical name for the collarbone?

Clavicle.

Which bone is the knee cap?

The patella.

What is the heel bone called?

The calcaneus.

Quick revision points

  • Pair each nickname with its formal name.
  • Learn them by body region.
  • Maxilla = upper jaw; mandible = lower jaw.
  • Funny bone tingling comes from the ulnar nerve.
  • Say the name while touching the bone on yourself.

cranial-nerves-mnemonic.caption: All twelve cranial nerves in order, with two mnemonics: one for the names and one for sensory, motor or both.
cranial-nerves-mnemonic.body:
In short: There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves, and exams love them. This card gives the order and two mnemonics so you can remember both the names and what each one does.

What the card shows

A tidy numbered list of all twelve cranial nerves runs down the left of this graphic, with the full mnemonic sentence in a banner above: "Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet AH". The list reads I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory and XII hypoglossal.

Decoding the sentence

Each word gives the first letter of a nerve: Oh for olfactory, Oh for optic, Oh for oculomotor, To for trochlear, Touch for trigeminal, And for abducens, Feel for facial, Very for vestibulocochlear, Good for glossopharyngeal, Velvet for vagus, and AH for accessory and hypoglossal.

A second mnemonic for function

For sensory, motor or both, many students use "Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More". It reads S, S, M, M, B, M, B, S, B, B, M, M, meaning sensory, sensory, motor, motor, both, motor, both, sensory, both, both, motor, motor. Learn the order first, then the function, then the clinical tests. The vagus nerve matters in theatre because stimulation of it can slow the heart, which is why the airway and traction on organs are handled with care.

What cranial nerves are

Cranial nerves leave the brain and brainstem directly rather than from the spinal cord, and they serve the head, neck and some of the chest and abdomen. Some are purely sensory (smell, vision, hearing), some purely motor (eye muscles, tongue), and some carry both.

A quick function map: I smell, II see, III, IV and VI move the eye, V feels the face and chews, VII moves the face and tastes, VIII hears and balances, IX and X swallow and regulate organs, XI shrugs and turns the head, XII moves the tongue.

Where this matters in theatre and recovery

The vagus nerve (X) slows the heart, so airway manipulation or traction on organs can trigger a slow pulse. The facial nerve (VII) can be injured in surgery near the parotid gland, and the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus is a risk in thyroid surgery. Monitoring these nerves is part of some operations, which is why surgeons talk about identifying and protecting them.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Mixing up the order of III, IV and VI (all supply eye movement).
  • Forgetting that the vagus nerve is number X and has widespread effects.
  • Learning the names and forgetting the functions.
  • Using a mnemonic without checking it against the full list.

Check yourself

Which cranial nerve is the vagus?

The tenth, X.

Which nerves control eye movement?

Oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and abducens (VI).

Which nerve is purely sensory for vision?

The optic nerve (II).

Quick revision points

  • Twelve pairs, numbered I to XII.
  • Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet AH.
  • Vagus (X) can slow the heart.
  • III, IV, VI move the eye.
  • Learn order, then function, then clinical tests.

patient-file-soap-notes-made-simple.caption: How to write clear clinical notes using SOAP: Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan.
patient-file-soap-notes-made-simple.body:
In short: SOAP is a simple structure that keeps clinical notes clear and consistent, so the next person can understand a patient's story in seconds.

What the card shows

Four rounded boxes sit in a two-by-two grid in the lower part of this graphic, with me above them shrugging with both palms up. S equals Subjective, which is what the patient says. O equals Objective, which is vitals and examination. A equals Assessment, which is what you think. P equals Plan, which is what to do.

What each letter means

Subjective is the patient's own words about symptoms, such as "my wound hurts when I cough". Objective is what you can see or measure: temperature, pulse, the look of the wound. Assessment is your clinical interpretation, such as "early wound infection suspected". Plan is the action, such as "swab, start antibiotics, review tomorrow".

An example in four lines

S: Pain at the incision, worse on movement. O: Temp 38.1, wound red and warm, no discharge. A: Possible surgical site infection. P: Inform the doctor, take a swab, continue monitoring.

Why it works

SOAP separates what you were told from what you found and from what you concluded, so the next person can follow your thinking. It also keeps notes short. Avoid putting opinions in the Objective section, and avoid vague words like "okay". Always sign and time the entry, and keep patient confidentiality. Your hospital may use a variation, such as SOAPIE, so use whichever format your unit has adopted.

Why structure matters

A note that mixes what the patient said, what you measured and what you think is hard to use. SOAP gives each type of information a place, which also helps you think in order: listen, examine, interpret, act.

The structure is used in many forms across healthcare, and variations such as SOAPIE add Intervention and Evaluation. What stays the same is the separation of facts from opinions.

In a surgical setting

After an operation, a SOAP note might record that the patient says the wound is painful (S), that the temperature, pulse and wound appearance are as measured (O), that you or the doctor think it may be early infection (A), and what was done (P). Even students who do not write a formal note benefit from thinking this way when giving a handover.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Putting opinions in the Objective section.
  • Using vague words like 'fine' or 'okay' instead of measurements.
  • Forgetting to sign, date and time the entry.
  • Writing plans that nobody can act on.

Check yourself

Which part contains vital signs?

Objective.

Where do you record the patient's own words?

Subjective.

What goes in Plan?

The actions to be taken and follow-up.

Quick revision points

  • S = what the patient says; O = what you see and measure.
  • A = interpretation; P = actions.
  • Keep opinions out of Objective.
  • Sign, date and time every entry.
  • Use your unit's accepted format.

first-aid-kit-what-should-be-inside.caption: The essential contents of a basic first aid kit and how to keep it ready.
first-aid-kit-what-should-be-inside.body:
In short: A first aid kit only helps if it is complete, in date and easy to find. This card lists the six basics and explains what each is for.

What the card shows

A white rounded box lists six essential items with an icon beside each: gloves, gauze and bandages, adhesive tape, scissors, antiseptic wipes and a documentation card.

What each item is for

Gloves protect you and the casualty from infection. Gauze and bandages control bleeding and cover wounds. Adhesive tape holds dressings in place. Scissors cut clothing and tape without delay. Antiseptic wipes clean the skin around a wound. The documentation card is the one most people forget: it is where you record who was hurt, what happened, what you did, the time and who you handed over to.

Build it, then keep it alive

A first aid kit is only useful if it is complete and in date. Pick a regular day each month to check the contents, replace anything used or expired, and make sure everyone knows where the kit is kept. Keep one at home, one at your workplace and a small one in your bag or vehicle. Depending on your setting, you may also add a pocket mask for CPR, a thermometer, a triangular bandage, a small torch, and any personal medicines for yourself. Remember that a kit helps, but training is what makes you confident. Consider a basic first aid course, and call for emergency help when the situation is serious.

Why each item is there

Gloves keep you and the casualty safe from infection. Gauze and bandages control bleeding and protect wounds. Tape holds dressings in place. Scissors cut clothing and tape quickly. Antiseptic wipes clean the skin around a wound, but should not be used to scrub deep wounds. The documentation card or notebook means the facts survive the stress: names, time, what happened and what was done.

Additional items often recommended include a face shield or pocket mask for CPR, a triangular bandage, a thermometer and a torch.

Using a kit well

Knowing what is in the box and where it is matters as much as having it. First aid courses give you the skills; the kit gives you the tools. For serious injuries, bleeding that will not stop, breathing problems or unconsciousness, call for emergency help straight away while you give first aid.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Never checking expiry dates.
  • Leaving the kit locked or in an unknown place.
  • Using it once and not restocking.
  • Skipping the written record after an incident.

Check yourself

Why is a documentation card included?

To record who was hurt, what happened, what you did and who took over.

How often should a kit be checked?

Regularly, for example monthly, and after any use.

What protects you from infection while helping?

Gloves, and a face shield for CPR.

Quick revision points

  • Gloves, dressings, tape, scissors, wipes, record card.
  • Check contents and expiry monthly.
  • Know where the kit is kept.
  • Add a CPR face shield if you can.
  • Call emergency help for serious injuries.

anaemia-simple-overview.caption: Anaemia in plain language: what it is, common signs, common causes and prevention.
anaemia-simple-overview.body:
In short: Anaemia means the blood carries less oxygen than it should because of too few red cells or too little haemoglobin. It is common and often preventable.

What the card shows

This one is a plain-language card. A small note at the bottom says "general education only".

What anaemia means

Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. When it drops, tissues get less oxygen, so you feel tired, look pale, get dizzy and become short of breath on effort. The graphic keeps the causes simple, but blood loss and nutritional shortage are the two you will meet most often in practice.

Why theatre students should care

Anaemia matters before surgery because a patient who starts low has less reserve if they lose blood. That is why haemoglobin is checked in preoperative work-up and why blood may be cross-matched. Iron-rich foods such as beans, green leafy vegetables, eggs and meat help prevent the nutritional type, but a person with symptoms needs a proper check, not just advice from a poster. Think of this card as the first page of a bigger topic, and see the Types of Anemia card for the four common kinds.

What is happening in the body

Haemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it to tissues. When there is not enough, the heart has to work harder and tissues may be starved of oxygen. This is why people feel tired, look pale and become breathless or dizzy when they exert themselves.

Causes fall into three groups: losing blood (heavy periods, injuries, bleeding in the gut), not making enough red cells (lack of iron, vitamin B12 or folate, bone marrow disease) and destroying them too fast (haemolysis, as in sickle cell disease or malaria).

Why it matters before surgery

A patient with low haemoglobin has little reserve if they bleed. Surgeons and anaesthetists check haemoglobin before planned operations, treat the cause where there is time, and keep blood available for major cases. If a patient looks pale, is breathless on walking or feels faint, they should be reported rather than rushed to theatre.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming tiredness is always just 'stress'.
  • Treating anaemia with iron tablets without finding the cause.
  • Ignoring the possibility of hidden blood loss.
  • Skipping the haemoglobin check before elective surgery.

Check yourself

What does haemoglobin do?

It carries oxygen in red blood cells.

Name two common causes of anaemia.

Blood loss and nutritional deficiency, such as iron.

Why is it relevant to surgery?

Low reserves make blood loss more dangerous.

Quick revision points

  • Anaemia = low haemoglobin or red cells.
  • Signs: tiredness, pallor, dizziness, breathlessness.
  • Causes: blood loss, poor nutrition, destruction of cells.
  • Find and treat the cause.
  • Check haemoglobin before elective surgery.

hypertension-simple-overview.caption: What high blood pressure is, why it is called silent, and how it affects surgery.
hypertension-simple-overview.body:
In short: Hypertension often causes no symptoms, yet it raises the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney problems. This card gives the plain-language basics.

What the card shows

A white rounded card with large, easy-to-read text sits on the left of this graphic while What it is: the force of blood pushing against artery walls is high. Normal: below 120/80 mmHg. Common silent signs: headache, dizziness, and often no signs at all. Risk factors: salt, obesity, stress and family history. General pillars: low-salt diet, exercise, regular checks and taking medication as advised.

Why it is called silent

Most people with high blood pressure feel perfectly well, so the only way to know is to measure it. A single high reading does not make a diagnosis, because blood pressure rises with pain, stress and a full bladder. Doctors confirm it with repeated readings.

Why it matters in theatre

Hypertension raises the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney problems, and uncontrolled blood pressure can complicate anaesthesia and bleeding. Patients are usually asked to continue their blood pressure medicines on the morning of surgery unless told otherwise, so the preoperative check always includes the medicine list. Between visits, the best habits are the pillars on the card: less salt, more movement, healthier weight, and never stopping medicine without advice. Treat this card as a first overview for general education.

What the numbers mean

Blood pressure is written as two numbers, for example 120/80 mmHg. The first is the pressure when the heart contracts (systolic) and the second is the pressure between beats (diastolic). A diagnosis of hypertension usually needs repeated readings above the agreed threshold on different occasions, with correct technique and a rested patient; the exact thresholds follow national guidelines.

Over time, high pressure damages the walls of the arteries and strains the heart, which is why it is a leading risk factor for stroke and heart attack.

Why it matters for theatre

Blood pressure responds to pain, anxiety, full bladders and anaesthetic drugs, so readings before surgery help the anaesthetist plan. Long-term hypertension is often treated with daily tablets, and the team will tell the patient exactly which ones to take on the morning of surgery. Patients who stop their medicine on their own can arrive with dangerously high pressure.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Taking one high reading as a diagnosis.
  • Using the wrong cuff size, which gives false readings.
  • Taking blood pressure just after the patient has walked or while talking.
  • Telling patients to stop their medicines without advice from the team.

Check yourself

Why is hypertension called silent?

Most people feel well, so only measurement reveals it.

What does the top number measure?

Systolic pressure, when the heart contracts.

Name two lifestyle measures that help.

Less salt and regular physical activity.

Quick revision points

  • Normal is around 120/80 mmHg or lower.
  • Diagnosis needs repeated readings.
  • Risk: stroke, heart disease, kidney damage.
  • Cuff size and technique matter.
  • Never stop medicine without advice.

diabetes-mellitus-simple-overview.caption: Diabetes in plain language: types, signs, risks and why blood sugar matters in surgery.
diabetes-mellitus-simple-overview.body:
In short: Diabetes mellitus means the body cannot keep blood sugar in a healthy range. This card gives a simple overview and what it means for surgery.

What the card shows

This is another plain-language card: What it is: high blood sugar. Types: Type 1 and Type 2. Common signs: thirst, frequent urination and fatigue. Risk factors: family history and lifestyle. General management pillars: diet, exercise, medication adherence and follow-up.

The simple picture

Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into cells. In Type 1 the body makes little or none, and in Type 2 the body does not respond to it well enough. Either way sugar builds up in the blood and causes the classic signs of thirst, passing urine often and tiredness.

Why it matters in theatre

Diabetes affects wound healing and infection risk, and blood sugar can swing during fasting and anaesthesia, so the team usually checks glucose before and during surgery and may adjust medicines and insulin on the day. Patients should tell the team exactly what they take. Low blood sugar can be as dangerous as high blood sugar, so signs like sweating, shakiness or confusion need quick attention.

Keep it simple

The management pillars on the card apply to almost every chronic condition: food, movement, medicine taken as prescribed, and regular check-ups. This card is a first overview for general education only, not a substitute for clinical guidance.

How the two main types differ

Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas that lets sugar move from the blood into cells. In type 1 diabetes the body makes little or no insulin, usually starting younger and needing insulin treatment. In type 2 diabetes the body does not respond properly to insulin and may not make enough, and it is linked to age, weight, inactivity and family history. There is also diabetes in pregnancy, which needs its own care.

High sugar over years damages blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys, and slows wound healing.

Why surgery needs a plan

Fasting, stress and anaesthesia change blood sugar, and diabetic medicines can cause low blood sugar if the patient is not eating. The team usually checks glucose before and during an operation and gives clear instructions on which tablets or insulin doses to take. Hypoglycaemia (low sugar) shows as sweating, shaking, hunger or confusion and needs quick treatment; hyperglycaemia can raise infection risk.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming a patient who is not eating needs no sugar check.
  • Missing signs of low blood sugar in an anaesthetised or sedated patient.
  • Telling patients to take or skip tablets without the doctor's instruction.
  • Ignoring foot and skin problems in diabetic patients.

Check yourself

What does insulin do?

It moves sugar from blood into cells.

Name signs of low blood sugar.

Sweating, shaking, hunger, confusion.

Why might diabetic wounds heal slowly?

High sugar affects circulation and immune function.

Quick revision points

  • Type 1: little or no insulin; type 2: poor response.
  • Classic signs: thirst, frequent urination, tiredness.
  • Check glucose before and during surgery.
  • Low sugar can be as dangerous as high sugar.
  • Follow the team's medicine instructions.

wound-assessment-what-to-document.caption: What to look at and record when assessing a wound, using clear and measurable language.
wound-assessment-what-to-document.body:
In short: Good wound notes let the next person see exactly how a wound is changing. This card gives the headings to record every time.

What the card shows

A wound cross-section drawing sits at the top right of this graphic, held up by me, with the layers labelled epidermis, dermis and subcutis, plus the measurements length by width by depth and notes on exudate amount and colour and the surrounding tissue. Below, a Documentation Checklist lists site location, size (length, width and depth), type (clean, dirty or infected), exudate (amount and colour), pain level on a 0 to 10 scale and surrounding skin (colour, swelling and erythema). A small note adds: use clear, objective, measurable terms, record the date and time and photograph if policy allows.

Why use a checklist

Wound notes are often vague, such as "looks better", which tells the next nurse nothing. Fixed headings force you to record the same things each time, so changes can be tracked.

Objective language

Write "2 by 1 cm, 0.5 cm deep, moderate yellow exudate, no odour, surrounding skin pink and warm" rather than "small wound with some discharge". Describe what you see and measure, not what you assume. Use a ruler or disposable measuring guide, and measure the same way each time.

Why it matters

Good records show whether a wound is healing, stuck or infected, guide the choice of dressing and protect the care team legally. Photographs should only be taken with consent and under hospital policy. See the Stages of Wound Healing card for what the changes mean.

What each heading tells you

Site and size show where the wound is and whether it is shrinking or growing. Type (clean, contaminated or infected) guides the dressing and antibiotics. Exudate (the fluid from a wound) tells you about healing: small amounts of clear or straw-coloured fluid are normal, while thick, green or foul-smelling fluid suggests infection. Pain and the surrounding skin show whether inflammation is spreading.

Measuring in the same way each time, with the same reference point, makes comparisons reliable.

Writing it so others can use it

Use numbers and plain descriptions: '3 cm by 2 cm, 0.5 cm deep, moderate yellow exudate, no odour, surrounding skin red for 1 cm'. Add the date, time and your signature. Photographs help only when policy and consent allow, and must not identify the patient outside the record.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Writing 'looks better' without any measurement.
  • Measuring in a different way each time.
  • Missing the surrounding skin and exudate details.
  • Taking photographs without consent or policy.

Check yourself

Name three things you should record about exudate.

Amount, colour and odour.

Why use a ruler?

To measure length, width and depth consistently.

What is a sign of spreading infection?

Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain or pus.

Quick revision points

  • Record site, size, type, exudate, pain and surrounding skin.
  • Use objective, measurable terms.
  • Measure the same way each time.
  • Date, time and sign every entry.
  • Photographs need consent and policy.

medical-legal-ethics-3-key-areas.caption: Confidentiality, informed consent and defamation: three legal and ethical pillars for health students.
medical-legal-ethics-3-key-areas.body:
In short: These three ideas protect patients and professionals alike. This card sets them out in simple language.

What the card shows

A single white panel with three green boxes sits on the right of this graphic, with me on the left resting my chin on one hand and pointing with the other. The boxes are confidentiality (breach of privacy; conversations are strictly confidential), informed consent (risks, benefits and autonomy) and defamation (false words, slander and libel). A small credit says it comes from page 190 of the POTT guide.

Confidentiality

Everything you see, hear or read about a patient stays with the care team. That includes the operating list, the chart and what the patient says before they are asleep. Talking about a patient in the cafeteria or posting about them online is a breach, even if you never use their name.

Informed consent

A patient has the right to know the risks, benefits and alternatives of a procedure, and to accept or refuse it freely. Autonomy means the decision is theirs. Consent must be given before the procedure, by someone able to understand, and recorded properly.

Defamation

Spoken false statements that damage a person's reputation are slander, and written ones are libel. In records and conversation, stick to facts and objective wording. Laws and rules differ by country and by hospital, so learn the ones that apply to your own practice, and when you are unsure, ask your supervisor before you act.

Why they matter

Confidentiality builds trust: patients tell the truth only if they believe it will stay private. Informed consent respects the patient's right to decide what happens to their body. Defamation law protects people from false statements that damage their reputation.

In practice they show up in everyday situations: who you talk to about a case, what you post on social media, what a patient has been told before signing, and how you write in a record.

Applying them in theatre

Do not discuss patients in public places or online, even without names. Check that the consent form is signed and the patient has been given information before the procedure; if it is missing or the patient seems confused, raise it with the team. In writing and speech, stick to facts and avoid labelling a person or colleague unfairly. Laws differ by country, so learn the Kenyan rules and your hospital's policy.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Talking about patients at lunch or on WhatsApp.
  • Assuming a signed form means the patient understood.
  • Writing opinions about patients in the record.
  • Sharing photographs from theatre.

Check yourself

What is the difference between slander and libel?

Slander is spoken; libel is written.

Who decides whether to accept treatment?

The patient, when able to understand, under the principle of autonomy.

Is confidentiality broken if you share without a name?

It can be, if the person could still be identified.

Quick revision points

  • Confidentiality: protect patient information.
  • Informed consent: risks, benefits, alternatives, free choice.
  • Defamation: false words that harm reputation.
  • Stick to facts in records.
  • Learn local law and hospital policy.

types-of-shock-4-main-types.caption: The four main types of shock: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive and obstructive.
types-of-shock-4-main-types.body:
In short: Shock means tissues are not getting enough blood flow. Naming the type guides treatment, which is why this four-way split is so useful.

What the card shows

Four cards in a two-by-two grid show the main types, each with an icon, and 1 Hypovolaemic: low blood volume from blood loss or dehydration. 2 Cardiogenic: heart pump failure, such as a myocardial infarction. 3 Distributive: widespread vasodilation, as in septic, anaphylactic and neurogenic shock. 4 Obstructive: a physical blockage, such as pulmonary embolism, tamponade or tension pneumothorax.

What shock really means

Shock is not fear or surprise. It is a state in which the body's tissues are not getting enough blood flow and oxygen. The four types are four different ways this can happen: not enough blood, a weak pump, widened vessels or a blockage in the circuit.

Recognising it

Typical signs are a fast pulse, low blood pressure, cold clammy skin, fast breathing, confusion and poor urine output, though the details differ by type. In septic or anaphylactic shock the skin may be warm at first.

Why it matters in theatre

Surgery involves blood loss, drugs that dilate vessels and, rarely, allergic reactions, so recognising shock early lets the team act: stop the bleeding, give fluids or blood, give drugs that support the heart or reverse the cause. The treatment depends on the type, which is why naming it correctly matters. Call for help straight away.

Think of the body as a circuit

For blood to reach the tissues you need enough fluid (volume), a working pump (the heart), vessels of the right width and a clear path. Hypovolaemic shock is a volume problem, such as bleeding or dehydration. Cardiogenic shock is a pump problem, such as a heart attack. Distributive shock is a vessel problem, where vessels widen too much, as in sepsis, anaphylaxis or neurogenic shock. Obstructive shock is a path problem, such as a pulmonary embolism, tamponade or tension pneumothorax.

Each needs different treatment, so the first job is to recognise shock and get help.

What the theatre team does

In theatre, the usual suspects are bleeding, drug reactions and sepsis. Keep an eye on pulse, blood pressure, breathing, skin and urine output, and report changes early. Know where suction, blood, intravenous fluids and emergency drugs are kept, and be ready to assist the anaesthetist and surgeon as directed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Waiting for blood pressure to fall before worrying.
  • Treating all shock with fluids, which can harm cardiogenic shock.
  • Missing anaphylaxis because the cause is a drug or latex.
  • Leaving a patient alone with unexplained fast pulse and cold skin.

Check yourself

Which type is caused by a heart attack?

Cardiogenic shock.

Name a cause of distributive shock.

Sepsis, anaphylaxis or neurogenic shock.

What is common to all types of shock?

Inadequate blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues.

Quick revision points

  • Four types: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive, obstructive.
  • Volume, pump, vessels, blockage.
  • Early signs: fast pulse, cool skin, fast breathing.
  • Call for help early.
  • Treatment depends on the cause.

specimen-handling.caption: How to label, contain, document and transport surgical specimens so nothing is lost or mislabelled.
specimen-handling.body:
In short: A specimen is the evidence behind a diagnosis. This card gives the four steps that keep it safe.

What the card shows

Four teal panels with shield icons stack on the right of this graphic, with me on the left holding both hands out. Labelling: patient name, MRN, site, date and time. Container: an appropriate fixative, leak-proof and not overfilled. Documentation: a requisition form, a double check and verbal confirmation. Transport: immediate to the lab, in a biohazard bag, with the cold chain where needed.

The four panels in order

You label to say whose specimen it is and where it came from, you choose the right container so the tissue stays preserved and safe, you document so the lab knows what to test and you transport quickly so the sample does not spoil.

Fixative and fresh

Tissue for histology is commonly put in formalin, which fixes it and prevents decay, while some tests need a fresh sample, with no fixative, sent at once or kept cold. If you are not sure which, ask the surgeon before the sample leaves the table. A container that is too small, or overfilled, can leak or give poor fixation.

Why it matters

A specimen is the evidence for a diagnosis. If it is unlabelled, mixed up or lost, the patient may need another procedure. Two-person checks and spoken confirmation catch most errors. See the Specimen Handling Guide in the Inside the Operating Theatre series for the student version.

What happens to a specimen

Tissue removed in surgery is sent to the pathology laboratory, where it is examined by eye, processed and studied under a microscope. The result may confirm a diagnosis such as cancer, so any mistake in labelling or transport can lead to the wrong treatment or a repeat operation.

Fixatives such as formalin preserve tissue; some tests need fresh tissue or special media, so ask the surgeon what the specimen needs before it leaves the room.

The chain of custody

Every handover should be traceable: who took it from the field, who labelled it, who put it in the register, who carried it and who received it. Reading the label aloud and having a second person check it catches most errors. Treat specimens as infectious: wear gloves, avoid spills and clean up promptly.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Labelling after the patient has left or from memory.
  • Using the wrong container or too little fixative.
  • Leaving specimens unattended or in a pocket.
  • Failing to record the specimen in the register.

Check yourself

Why label at the table?

So the correct patient and site are recorded while the surgeon confirms what it is.

What does formalin do?

It preserves and fixes tissue.

What should you do if unsure how to send a specimen?

Ask the surgeon before it leaves the room.

Quick revision points

  • Label, container, document, transport.
  • Read the label aloud and double check.
  • Ask if the specimen is fixed or fresh.
  • Use a biohazard bag and handle as infectious.
  • Record in the register.

hormones-nicknames.caption: Eighteen key hormones paired with memorable one-line nicknames, with notes on what each really does.
hormones-nicknames.body:
In short: Hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate growth, mood, metabolism and reproduction. Nicknames help you remember their jobs.

What the card shows

A rounded card with a DNA and pill border lists the hormones in two columns, each paired with a short nickname. On the left: melatonin (helps regulate sleep), oxytocin (bonding and connection), dopamine (motivation and pleasure), serotonin (mood and happiness), endorphins (natural pain relief), adrenaline (fight or flight, stress response and energy) and cortisol (stress hormone). On the right: thyroxine T4 (controls metabolism), leptin (signals fullness), ghrelin (stimulates hunger), testosterone (male hormone and drive), oestrogen (female reproductive hormone), progesterone (pregnancy keeper) and hCG (pregnancy detector, the hormone in pregnancy tests). The title says it covers eighteen key hormones.

Why nicknames help

Hormones have abstract names, so a one-line nickname gives you something concrete: ghrelin says "hungry", leptin says "full", cortisol says "stress".

A small accuracy note

Some items on this list, such as dopamine, serotonin and endorphins, are mainly neurotransmitters or neuropeptides that also act as chemical messengers, so you will see them in both hormone and neuroscience lessons. Treat the nicknames as memory hooks, not complete definitions. Each hormone has more functions than its nickname. Once the hooks are fixed, add where it is made (for example thyroxine in the thyroid, cortisol in the adrenal cortex) and what happens when there is too much or too little.

What hormones are

Hormones are made by glands such as the thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, ovaries and testes, and released into the blood to act on distant organs. Because they travel in the blood, their effects are slower but longer-lasting than nerve signals.

Each hormone works within feedback loops: when levels rise, the body reduces production; when they fall, it makes more. Disease can arise from too much or too little, for example an overactive or underactive thyroid.

Adding depth to a nickname

Start with the nickname, then add three facts: where it is made, what it does and what happens when it is out of balance. For example, cortisol is made in the adrenal cortex, helps the body respond to stress and regulates blood sugar, and too much or too little causes serious illness. Stress hormones also matter in theatre because pain, fear and surgery all trigger adrenaline and cortisol release.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating nicknames as complete definitions.
  • Mixing up leptin (fullness) and ghrelin (hunger).
  • Forgetting some items are neurotransmitters.
  • Learning the list without learning where each hormone is made.

Check yourself

Which hormone signals fullness?

Leptin.

Where is cortisol made?

In the adrenal cortex.

What does hCG detect?

Pregnancy; it is the hormone in pregnancy tests.

Quick revision points

  • Hormones are chemical messengers in the blood.
  • Nicknames are memory hooks, not full definitions.
  • Add source, action and imbalance for each.
  • Leptin = full; ghrelin = hungry.
  • Stress hormones rise during surgery.

retained-items-prevention.caption: How surgical teams prevent sponges, instruments and needles from being left inside a patient.
retained-items-prevention.body:
In short: A retained surgical item is one of the most preventable harms in surgery. This card shows the risks, the checks and what to do if the count is wrong.

What the card shows

Four teal panels with shields stack on the right of this graphic, with me on the left turning my palm up. Risk Factors: emergency surgery, high BMI and multiple teams. Prevention: count three times, use a standardised count board and use only radio-opaque sponges. Technology Use: RFID-tagged sponges and X-ray when in doubt. If Suspected: inform the surgeon immediately, take an intra-operative X-ray and document the incident.

What counts as a retained item

A retained surgical item is a sponge, instrument, needle or other object left inside the patient after the operation. It is one of the "never events", meaning something that should never happen if the proper checks are done.

Why risk factors matter

Emergencies, large patients and handovers between teams all raise the chance of a miscount, because things happen fast and attention is divided. That is why extra care is built in for those cases.

Prevention and response

Counting at the start, before closure and at the end, using one whiteboard and saying the numbers aloud, keeps everyone aligned. Radio-opaque sponges show up on X-ray, and RFID tags let a wand detect them. If the count is wrong, stop, search, tell the surgeon and image the patient before closing. Never ignore a discrepancy, and document it. This card pairs with the Surgical Count Sheet card in the Inside the Operating Theatre series.

Why it still happens

Retained items are usually found after emergency operations, operations with unexpected changes in the plan, or when staff change during the case. Counts can be rushed, mis-recorded or skipped when everyone is busy with bleeding. A sponge that is soaked in blood can look like tissue.

The effects can be serious: infection, pain, bowel obstruction or abscess, often needing another operation.

Layers of protection

A standard count at the start, before closure and at the end, spoken aloud and written on a board, is the main defence. Radio-opaque sponges show on X-ray. Some hospitals add technology such as barcoded or RFID-tagged sponges. If the count is incorrect, stop, search the field, floor, bins and drapes, tell the surgeon and take an X-ray if needed. Never close with an unexplained discrepancy.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Accepting 'it must be in the bin' without looking.
  • Failing to count items added mid-case.
  • Skipping the count in a hurry or after a staff change.
  • Not documenting an incorrect count and the action taken.

Check yourself

When are counts done?

Before incision, before closure and at the end, and when staff change.

Why use radio-opaque sponges?

They show on X-ray if one is left.

What do you do if the count is wrong?

Stop, search, inform the surgeon and image if needed, then document.

Quick revision points

  • Count aloud, with two people, and record it.
  • Count again when staff change.
  • Use radio-opaque sponges.
  • Never close with an unexplained discrepancy.
  • Document all actions.

medical-records-importance-of-documentat.caption: Why accurate records matter for communication, safety, continuity of care and legal protection.
medical-records-importance-of-documentat.body:
In short: A patient record is the memory of the care team. This card explains five reasons documentation matters and what a good record looks like.

What the card shows

A rounded teal frame sits on the right of this graphic, with me turned side-on pointing at it. Inside, five reasons are listed: it communicates with other health personnel, reduces malpractice risk, ensures appropriate reimbursement, maintains the continuum of care and offers legal protection. Below, a list of record types follows: patient information sheet, medical history, discharge summary, lab tests and mental status exam.

What each reason means

Communication: the next shift, the next ward and the next doctor all rely on what you wrote. Malpractice risk: a clear, honest record shows that the care was reasonable. Reimbursement: insurers pay for what is documented. Continuum of care: the patient's story continues from one team to another without gaps. Legal protection: a record made at the time is the best evidence of what really happened.

The types of record

The patient information sheet captures identity and contacts, the medical history captures past conditions and medicines, the discharge summary captures what happened and what to do next, lab tests carry results and the mental status exam notes cognition and mood.

A habit to build

Write clearly, write at the time or immediately after, sign and date everything and never alter a record to hide a mistake. If you have to correct something, draw a single line through it and initial it. The Perioperative Documentation card in the Inside the Operating Theatre series goes deeper.

A record is a safety tool

Many patients are cared for by several teams over days or years. The record lets each team know what was done, what the patient said, what was found and what is planned. It supports decisions, medicine safety and handover.

It is also used in audits, insurance, teaching and legal reviews, which is why it must be accurate, complete and readable.

What a good entry looks like

Timely (written at or soon after the event), factual, clear, signed and dated, with the writer's name and role. Avoid unclear abbreviations and never alter or erase an entry; correct it with a single line and your initials. If you are a student, record under supervision and follow your institution's rules.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Writing notes hours later from memory.
  • Using unclear abbreviations.
  • Using correction fluid or overwriting.
  • Documenting an action that was not done.

Check yourself

Why is a timely entry important?

It is more accurate and reliable.

How should an error be corrected?

With a single line through it, initialled and dated.

Name two reasons documentation matters.

Communication and legal protection.

Quick revision points

  • Record promptly, clearly and honestly.
  • Sign, date and time entries.
  • Never overwrite or hide errors.
  • Records support continuity of care.
  • Respect confidentiality.

surgical-terms-suffixes.caption: Seven suffixes that unlock hundreds of surgical procedure names.
surgical-terms-suffixes.body:
In short: Operation names look scary until you know the endings. Learn seven suffixes and you can decode most of them.

What the card shows

Seven rounded bars with icons run down the right of this graphic, with me thinking on the left with my chin in my hand. -tomy means cut into or incision, as in tracheotomy. -ectomy means cut out or removal, as in appendectomy. -ostomy means creating an opening, as in colostomy. -plasty means reshape or repair, as in rhinoplasty. -pexy means fixation, as in gastropexy. -rrhaphy means suturing, as in herniorrhaphy. -centesis means puncture or aspiration, as in amniocentesis.

How to decode a term

Break the word into the organ and the suffix. Appendix plus -ectomy is removal of the appendix. Colon plus -ostomy is an opening made in the colon. Once you know the seven suffixes, hundreds of operation names become readable.

Watch the near-twins

Tracheotomy is the incision, and tracheostomy is the opening that stays. -ostomy creates an opening, and -otomy simply cuts. Missing one letter can change the meaning, so read carefully.

Practice

Pick any operation on your list and say what it means in plain English before the surgeon says it. Add prefixes next: cholecyst- for gallbladder, hyster- for uterus, nephr- for kidney, gastr- for stomach. With a prefix and a suffix you can build and decode almost any procedure, and you will also write consent and count sheets more accurately.

The suffix tells you the action

-tomy: cut into (laparotomy). -ectomy: cut out (appendicectomy). -ostomy: create an opening (colostomy). -plasty: reshape or repair (rhinoplasty). -pexy: fix in place (orchidopexy). -rrhaphy: stitch (herniorrhaphy). -centesis: puncture to remove fluid (paracentesis).

The front of the word names the organ: nephr- (kidney), hyster- (uterus), cholecyst- (gallbladder), gastr- (stomach), col- (colon), arthr- (joint), cardi- (heart).

Putting it to work

Read a theatre list and decode each procedure: 'laparoscopic cholecystectomy' is keyhole removal of the gallbladder; 'tracheostomy' is the creation of a lasting opening in the windpipe; 'hysterectomy' is removal of the uterus. This helps you predict instruments, drapes and position, and spot errors such as a list that says '-otomy' where '-ectomy' was meant.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Mixing up -otomy and -ostomy.
  • Confusing -ectomy with -ectasis or -ectomy-like words.
  • Forgetting that the front of the word names the organ.
  • Spelling errors that change meaning on records.

Check yourself

What does -ectomy mean?

Removal.

What is the difference between tracheotomy and tracheostomy?

Tracheotomy is the incision; tracheostomy is the opening that stays.

What does -plasty mean?

Repair or reshape.

Quick revision points

  • -tomy cut; -ectomy remove; -ostomy opening.
  • -plasty repair; -pexy fix; -rrhaphy suture; -centesis puncture.
  • Front of the word names the organ.
  • Decode every list item.
  • Spell carefully on forms.

types-of-fractures-accurate-guide.caption: Six common fracture patterns, what causes them and what first aid they need.
types-of-fractures-accurate-guide.body:
In short: The pattern of a break tells you how the injury happened and helps decide how it is treated. This card lists six common types.

What the card shows

Six cards in a two-by-three grid each have a small bone drawing: 1 Transverse, a straight break perpendicular to the shaft. 2 Oblique, a diagonal, slanted break. 3 Spiral, caused by a twisting force. 4 Comminuted, with multiple fragments where the bone is shattered into several pieces. 5 Greenstick, an incomplete break where one side bends, common in children because their bones bend and partly crack. 6 Compound, or open, where the bone breaks through the skin and the risk of infection is higher. A bottom tip says to seek immediate medical attention for all fractures and not to try to realign the bone.

What the pattern tells you

The shape of the break hints at how the injury happened: a straight blow gives a transverse fracture, twisting gives a spiral and a crush gives comminution. This helps the surgeon choose the treatment.

Open fractures are urgent

A compound fracture exposes the bone to germs, so it needs prompt cleaning, antibiotics, stabilisation and often surgery.

First aid

Keep the person still, support the limb in the position found, control bleeding with a clean dressing, cover any wound and get help. Do not push the bone back or move the person unless they are in danger. Today's term for compound is open fracture, and you will hear both.

How fractures are described

Doctors describe a fracture by its line (transverse, oblique, spiral), its fragments (simple or comminuted), whether the skin is broken (open or closed) and whether the bone ends have moved (displaced or not). A greenstick fracture is an incomplete break seen in children because their bones are more flexible.

X-rays show the pattern. The pattern affects treatment: a stable transverse break may need only a cast, while a displaced or comminuted break may need plates, screws, nails or an external fixator.

Open fractures and first aid

An open (compound) fracture exposes bone to the outside, so infection and bleeding are the main dangers and it is treated as an emergency: control bleeding with a clean dressing, cover the wound, immobilise the limb as it lies and get urgent medical help. Do not try to push the bone back or straighten the limb, and do not move the person unless they are in danger.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Moving an injured limb to 'see' the break.
  • Trying to realign the bone.
  • Forgetting to check circulation and sensation beyond the break.
  • Assuming a normal first X-ray excludes a fracture.

Check yourself

Which fracture type is common in children?

Greenstick.

What makes a fracture open?

The bone breaks the skin or a wound communicates with the break.

What force often causes a spiral fracture?

A twisting force.

Quick revision points

  • Types: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, greenstick, open.
  • Open fractures need urgent care.
  • Immobilise, do not realign.
  • Check circulation beyond the injury.
  • The pattern guides treatment.

bones-their-nicknames-explained-simply.caption: A translation table of bone nicknames and anatomical names for quick testing.
bones-their-nicknames-explained-simply.body:
In short: This table version is built for testing yourself: cover one column, recall the other, then swap.

What the card shows

This version has a blue wave header and a different layout. A small skeleton sits above a table of rounded tags, each pairing a nickname with an arrow to the anatomical name: beauty bone → clavicle, shoulder blade → scapula, breast bone → sternum, knee cap → patella, heel bone → calcaneus, jaw bone → mandible, upper jaw → maxilla, cheek bone → zygomatic, tail bone → coccyx, funny bone → humerus, finger and toe bones → phalanges, brain box → cranium, and back bone or spine → vertebral column.

Why a table version

The skeleton versions teach where the bone is. This one teaches the translation, which is how most exam questions are written: they give one name and ask for the other.

How I use it

Cover one column and test yourself, then swap. Pair up with a classmate and take turns reading a nickname for the other to answer. Notice the patterns too: many names come from Latin or Greek words for something familiar. Scapula and clavicle sound technical, but "shoulder blade" and "little key" describe what they look like. Once you spot that, the formal names stop feeling like random words. Keep this card on your phone for quick checks between lectures.

Why a table helps

Exam questions often give one name and ask for the other. A two-column table matches that format exactly, so practising it feels like the real thing. It also makes patterns visible: bones named after shapes (scapula, patella), places (clavicle) or Latin words for ordinary objects.

Add a third column of your own: where the bone is and one fact, such as 'femur: longest bone' or 'mandible: only movable skull bone'.

Study routine

Day 1: read and cover. Day 2: test from memory and mark wrong ones. Day 4: test only the ones you missed. Day 7: test all again. Spaced repeats beat a single long session because they force your memory to retrieve the information each time.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Learning the table by sight without actual recall.
  • Confusing similar-sounding names.
  • Skipping the third column of locations.
  • Studying only before the exam.

Check yourself

What is the zygomatic bone?

The cheek bone.

What is the sternum?

The breast bone.

What is the clavicle?

The collar bone, the 'beauty bone'.

Quick revision points

  • Cover one column and recall the other.
  • Add location and function facts.
  • Use spaced repeats.
  • Practise both directions.
  • Link the name to a place on your body.

common-pulse-sites.caption: Nine places where a pulse can be felt, and which one to use in routine and emergency care.
common-pulse-sites.body:
In short: A pulse is the pressure wave of each heartbeat felt in an artery. Knowing nine sites lets you check circulation almost anywhere.

What the card shows

Nine small panels in a three-by-three grid fill this graphic, each with a number, a drawing of the body part and a red mark where the pulse is felt. They are: 1 temporal (side of the forehead), 2 carotid (side of the neck), 3 apical (left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular), 4 brachial (inner elbow, medial antecubital), 5 radial (wrist, thumb side), 6 femoral (groin), 7 popliteal (behind the knee), 8 posterior tibial (behind the inner ankle) and 9 dorsalis pedis (top of the foot). The header says "Assess • Locate • Count".

Which one to use

The radial pulse is the usual routine site. The carotid and femoral are large central arteries, so they are the ones you check in an emergency when peripheral pulses fade. The apical pulse is counted with a stethoscope directly over the heart, and it is used for infants and for checking the heart rate against the radial rate. Brachial is the pulse of choice for infant CPR and blood pressure measurement.

Method

Use your first two fingers, never your thumb, because it has its own pulse. Press gently, count for a full minute if the rhythm is irregular, and note rate, rhythm and strength. Pulses below the knee and in the foot are checked after limb surgery and in positioning to confirm circulation is good.

Which site and why

Radial: easiest and used for routine checks. Brachial: used in infants and for blood pressure. Carotid and femoral: large central pulses used in emergencies because they remain palpable when peripheral ones fade. Apical: heard with a stethoscope over the heart. Temporal, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis help check circulation in the head and limbs.

A missing or weak pulse in a limb after surgery, a cast or a long period in one position can mean blood flow is threatened and needs urgent attention.

How to count properly

Use the pads of two or three fingers, not the thumb. Count for 30 seconds and double, or for a full minute if irregular. Note rate, rhythm (regular or irregular) and strength (weak, normal, bounding). Record the site and the time. Compare both sides when checking a limb.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using the thumb, which has its own pulse.
  • Pressing too hard and stopping the pulse.
  • Checking both carotids at once, which can reduce blood flow to the brain.
  • Counting for too short a time in an irregular rhythm.

Check yourself

Which pulse is used in infants?

Brachial or apical.

Which pulses are checked in an emergency?

Carotid and femoral.

Where is the dorsalis pedis?

On the top of the foot.

Quick revision points

  • Radial is the routine site.
  • Carotid and femoral are central pulses for emergencies.
  • Use fingers, not thumb.
  • Record rate, rhythm and strength.
  • Compare limbs after surgery or trauma.

types-of-surgical-incisions.caption: Seven common abdominal incisions, what each is used for and why shape matters.
types-of-surgical-incisions.body:
In short: The incision is the surgeon's doorway. Different shapes give different access and healing, and theatre staff should recognise them.

What the card shows

Seven small abdomen outlines with the incision drawn in red fill this graphic, with me looking up from the bottom left. The top row shows Kocher (subcostal), McBurney (oblique in the right lower quadrant), Lanz and Pfannenstiel (suprapubic transverse). The bottom row shows midline vertical, transverse and chevron (roof-top).

What each is used for

The Kocher incision runs under the ribs on the right and is used for gallbladder and liver surgery. McBurney and Lanz are small cuts in the right lower abdomen used for appendicectomy, with Lanz placed more transversely and often giving a neater scar. Pfannenstiel is a curved cut low above the pubic bone, commonly used for caesarean section and gynaecological surgery. A midline vertical incision gives wide access to the whole abdomen. Transverse cuts follow skin lines, and the chevron gives broad access to the upper abdomen.

Why shape matters

Surgeons choose an incision for access, healing, cosmetic result and the risk of a hernia. Muscle-splitting and transverse incisions often heal strongly, while a long midline cut gives the best exposure in an emergency.

For theatre students

Knowing the incision helps you predict the instruments, the drapes and the closure layers. See the 7 Layers Closed in C-Section card for what a Pfannenstiel opens.

Why so many incisions

The surgeon chooses an incision to reach the target organ, avoid important nerves and vessels, follow natural skin lines where possible and allow strong healing. A midline cut offers fast, wide access for emergencies and exploration but can heal with a higher hernia risk. Transverse and oblique cuts follow muscle fibres and skin lines and often heal strongly with better cosmetic results.

The patient's body shape, previous scars, the urgency and the surgeon's training also shape the choice.

Predicting your set-up

Knowing the incision helps you anticipate the retractors, the length of sutures and the number of layers to close. For example, a Pfannenstiel for caesarean section means a low curved cut and several layers; a McBurney's incision for appendicectomy is smaller and calls for smaller retractors. Always follow the surgeon's request and the planned procedure on the list.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Mixing up Lanz and McBurney incisions.
  • Assuming every abdominal operation is via a midline cut.
  • Forgetting to check previous scars when positioning and prepping.
  • Not tailoring the set to the incision.

Check yourself

Which incision is used for caesarean section?

Pfannenstiel.

Which incision is under the right ribs?

Kocher (subcostal).

Why might a surgeon choose a transverse incision?

It follows skin lines and heals well.

Quick revision points

  • Kocher: under the ribs; McBurney or Lanz: appendix.
  • Pfannenstiel: low transverse for C-section.
  • Midline: wide, fast access.
  • Shape affects healing and hernia risk.
  • Know the incision to predict instruments.

anatomy-of-the-lower-limb.caption: A labelled map of the lower limb from pelvis to toes: bones, joints and what each does.
anatomy-of-the-lower-limb.body:
In short: The lower limb carries your body weight, so it is built from strong bones and large joints. This card shows them in order from top to bottom.

What the card shows

A coloured skeleton of the whole lower limb runs down the middle of this graphic, with a banner reading "Anatomy of Lower Limb" across the top. Each bone or joint has a coloured label with a leader line: pelvis (blue), hip joint (green), thigh (pink), femur (red), knee joint (green), patella (light blue), leg (purple), tibia (pink), fibula (orange), ankle joint (green), foot (light blue), and the foot bones, tarsals (purple), metatarsals (teal) and phalanges (yellow).

Reading it from top to bottom

Follow the limb down: the pelvis holds the hip joint, the femur is the thigh bone and the longest bone in the body, the patella sits in front of the knee, the tibia and fibula form the leg, and the foot is built from tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges.

Why it matters in theatre

Orthopaedic cases, fractures, amputations and positioning all depend on this anatomy. The thigh, the knee and the ankle are the joints you will hear named most. Colour-coding helps your memory: pair each colour with a region and quiz yourself by covering the labels. Once the bones are automatic, the muscles, nerves and blood vessels of the limb are much easier to add on top.

From hip to toes

The pelvis connects to the femur at the hip, a ball-and-socket joint. The femur is the longest and strongest bone. At the knee, the femur meets the tibia, with the patella in front, and the fibula runs alongside the tibia. At the ankle, the tibia and fibula meet the talus. The foot contains tarsal bones (including the calcaneus or heel), metatarsals and phalanges.

Muscles, nerves and blood vessels run along these bones, and the main arteries can be felt at the groin, behind the knee, behind the inner ankle and on top of the foot.

Why theatre staff need it

Hip fractures, knee replacements, tibial fractures, amputations and many vascular operations involve this anatomy. Positioning for lower limb surgery requires protecting the peroneal nerve at the knee and the heels. When you know the bones you understand the instruments and implants: femoral nails, tibial plates, knee components.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Confusing tibia (shin, weight-bearing) with fibula (slender, lateral).
  • Forgetting the patella as part of the knee.
  • Mixing tarsals and metatarsals.
  • Ignoring nerve and blood supply when positioning.

Check yourself

What is the longest bone?

The femur.

Which bone is the shin bone?

The tibia.

Name the tarsal bone forming the heel.

The calcaneus.

Quick revision points

  • Pelvis, femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges.
  • Hip is ball-and-socket; knee is a hinge.
  • Femur is the longest bone.
  • Protect nerves and heels when positioning.
  • Know the pulses at groin, knee, ankle and foot.

types-of-anesthesia.caption: General, regional, local and monitored anaesthesia care: what each involves and when it is used.
types-of-anesthesia.body:
In short: Anaesthesia is not one thing. Choosing the type depends on the operation, the patient and the anaesthetist's judgement. This card sets out the four main types.

What the card shows

Four rounded cards with icons run down the right of this graphic while General: unconscious, the whole body is affected, used for major surgery. Regional (spinal or epidural): a large area is numbed, the patient is awake and the numbness is from the waist down. Local: a small area is numbed, the patient is awake, used for minor procedures. Monitored anaesthesia care (MAC): sedation, the patient is calm, and aware but relaxed.

Choosing between them

The choice depends on the operation, the patient's health, their preference and the anaesthetist's judgement. A skin lesion needs only local, a caesarean section often uses spinal and a long abdominal operation usually needs general.

What each one involves

General anaesthesia means loss of consciousness, usually with a breathing tube or airway device and close monitoring. Regional anaesthesia blocks nerves in a region of the body. Local blocks only the nerves in the small area. MAC adds monitored sedation to a local or regional block to keep the patient comfortable.

The theatre team's role

Prepare the right equipment for the type, keep emergency drugs and airway equipment ready and watch the patient with the anaesthetist.
