Regional and local anaesthetics have maximum safe doses, so the amounts are always recorded. See the Recovery Position and Anaesthesia card for what happens afterwards.

How each type works

General anaesthesia uses drugs that make the patient unconscious and unable to feel pain, usually with airway support and artificial ventilation. Regional anaesthesia blocks nerves for a large area: a spinal or epidural numbs the lower body, and nerve blocks numb a limb. Local anaesthesia numbs a small area by injecting a drug around the nerves there. Monitored anaesthesia care adds sedation and monitoring to local or regional techniques, keeping the patient relaxed.

Each has benefits and risks that the anaesthetist explains to the patient before surgery.

What changes in theatre

General anaesthesia needs airway equipment, ventilator, suction and drugs ready. Spinals can drop blood pressure, so fluids and vasopressors are prepared. Local anaesthetic doses must be recorded and kept below safe limits because too much can cause toxicity. In all cases, monitoring and emergency equipment must be ready, and the team should be prepared to convert to general anaesthesia if needed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Forgetting that regional anaesthesia can still need airway equipment on standby.
  • Not recording local anaesthetic doses.
  • Assuming an awake patient does not hear the team.
  • Leaving the patient alone during sedation.

Check yourself

Which type makes a patient unconscious?

General anaesthesia.

What does a spinal numb?

The lower body, typically from the waist down.

Why record local anaesthetic doses?

Because there is a maximum safe dose.

Quick revision points

  • General: unconscious; regional: a large area numb.
  • Local: a small area; MAC: sedation with monitoring.
  • Choice depends on the operation and patient.
  • Keep airway and emergency equipment ready.
  • Awake patients can hear the team.

bones-and-their-nicknames-explained-simp.caption: The skeleton diagram used region by region to learn bone nicknames and names.
bones-and-their-nicknames-explained-simp.body:
In short: Instead of memorising a flat list, walk down the body one region at a time. This card shows how.

What the card shows

This is the same skeleton diagram as the first Bones card, but I want to use it differently here. The skeleton stands on the left, and leader lines connect each body region to a labelled tag: the head and face carry brain box, upper jaw, jaw bone and cheek bone; the shoulder girdle carries beauty bone and shoulder blade; the chest carries breast bone; the arm carries funny bone and finger and toe bones; the trunk carries back bone and tail bone; and the legs carry knee cap and heel bone. My arms are crossed on the right.

Study it by region, not by list

Instead of memorising a flat list, walk down the body. Start with the skull and face, move to the shoulder, chest and arm, then the spine, then down the leg to the heel. Each region gives you two to four names, which is a small enough bite to hold in working memory.

Turn it into a game

Say the nickname, point to the place on your own body, then say the proper name. The upper jaw is the maxilla, the lower jaw is the mandible, and the collarbone is the clavicle. Doing it on yourself builds the link between the name and the real position. Ten minutes a day for a week is usually enough for a lasting hold, and spaced repeats beat one long session.

Why region by region works

Your working memory can only hold a handful of items at once. Grouping the names by region (head and face, shoulder, chest, arm, trunk, leg) breaks 13 names into small chunks of two to four, which is much easier to hold. Each chunk is anchored to a place on the body, which gives your memory a location to attach to.

When you practise, point to the bone on yourself and say both names. Touching the bone adds a physical memory to the verbal one.

Next steps after the nicknames

Once the names stick, add the next layer: the type of bone (long, short, flat, irregular), key landmarks and what attaches to it. For example, the clavicle is a long bone, easily felt and commonly fractured; the sternum is a flat bone that protects the heart and is split in some open heart operations.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Trying to learn all names in one sitting.
  • Only reading, not saying them aloud.
  • Ignoring the formal names.
  • Never testing yourself on a real body or model.

Check yourself

Which names belong to the head and face?

Cranium, maxilla, mandible and zygomatic bone.

Which is the tail bone?

The coccyx.

What is the breast bone?

The sternum.

Quick revision points

  • Learn by region.
  • Point and say both names.
  • Space your practice over days.
  • Add bone type and landmarks.
  • Test yourself on a model or a partner.

sharps-safety.caption: How to prevent needle and blade injuries, and exactly what to do if one happens.
sharps-safety.body:
In short: Sharps injuries can pass on blood-borne viruses. This card covers the risk, safe handling, disposal and the steps after an injury.

What the card shows

Four chevron-shaped boxes run down the left of this graphic, with me on the right with arms folded and a finger raised to my chin. Risk: HIV, HBV and HCV from scalpels and needles. Safe Handling: no recapping, use the tray pass and use one hand. Disposal: immediately in a puncture-proof sharps bin. If Injury: wash, let it bleed, report and follow the PEP protocol. The title Sharps Safety runs along the bottom.

Why sharps injuries matter

A needle or blade that has been in a patient can carry blood-borne viruses. The risk of infection from any one injury varies with the virus, the depth of the injury and the source, but it is never zero, which is why prevention and reporting are both taken so seriously.

The four boxes in practice

No recapping, because recapping is when most needle injuries happen. Use a tray to pass sharps so that two people never hold the same sharp. Work with one hand where possible. Dispose of the item yourself, at once, in a rigid container that does not leak or puncture and is closed at about three-quarters full.

If it happens to you

Wash with soap and water, let it bleed gently, do not squeeze or scrub with bleach, tell your supervisor and get a post-exposure assessment as soon as possible. Hepatitis B vaccination before you start attachment is one of the best protections. The Needle Stick Injury Protocol card has the detailed steps.

The risk behind the rules

Needles, blades and broken glass that have touched blood can carry hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. The chance of infection after one injury depends on the virus, the depth of the injury, the amount of blood and the source patient's status, so each injury is assessed individually. Prevention is far better than treatment, and vaccination against hepatitis B before clinical work is a key protection.

Most injuries are avoidable: they occur during recapping, passing sharps hand to hand, overfilled boxes, or working in a rush.

If an injury happens

Wash the area with soap and running water, let it bleed gently, do not squeeze or scrub, report to the supervisor immediately and attend the designated service for assessment and, where indicated, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which works best when started early. Document the incident. Many places also test the source patient with their consent and according to policy.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Recapping needles.
  • Carrying sharps in a pocket or in the hand across the room.
  • Overfilling the sharps box or pushing sharps down with fingers.
  • Hiding an injury to avoid trouble.

Check yourself

When should a sharps box be closed?

At about three-quarters full.

Why report an injury quickly?

PEP and assessment work best early.

What should you not do to a needle-stick wound?

Squeeze it or scrub it with bleach.

Quick revision points

  • Never recap; use a tray or neutral zone.
  • Dispose of sharps immediately in a rigid box.
  • Vaccinate against hepatitis B.
  • Wash, let it bleed, report, get assessed.
  • Follow your hospital's PEP policy.

ventilator-alarms-what-they-mean.caption: What common ventilator alarms mean and a safe first response to each.
ventilator-alarms-what-they-mean.body:
In short: Ventilator alarms are the machine's way of saying something has changed. This card links each alarm to its likely cause and first action.

What the card shows

Seven coloured cards in a grid fill this graphic, with a ventilator icon at the top and me pointing up at the bottom right. High pressure alarm: caused by a kinked tube, secretions, biting the tube or coughing, so check the tube for a kink and suction secretions. Low pressure alarm: caused by a disconnection or a leak in the circuit or cuff, so check all connections and the cuff. Apnoea: no breath detected, so stimulate the patient and assess. Low tidal volume: caused by a leak or a disconnection, so check for leaks. High respiratory rate: the patient is anxious or in pain, so assess pain, anxiety and sedation. Low FiO₂: an oxygen supply issue, so check the source. High FiO₂: oxygen set too high, so lower it to the prescribed level.

Reading the pattern

High pressure means something is blocking the flow, such as a kink or secretions. Low pressure means air is escaping, as with a disconnection or leak. Everything else follows from those two ideas.

First response

Look at the patient first, not the machine. If the patient is not ventilating well, disconnect and give breaths by hand with a bag, call for help and then trace the fault. Never silence an alarm without finding its cause. Alarm limits and responses differ by machine and unit, so follow the local protocol and the anaesthetist's directions.

Think in pairs

High pressure means the air cannot get in easily: a kinked tube, secretions, coughing, the patient biting the tube or a blocked filter. Low pressure or low volume means air is escaping or has been lost: a disconnection, a leaking cuff, a hole in the circuit. Apnoea means no breath has been detected. Oxygen alarms point to supply or settings.

The fastest safe approach is 'Patient first': look at the chest, colour and monitor, then check the circuit from the patient back to the machine.

What staff and students do

If the patient is in trouble, disconnect from the ventilator and give breaths by hand with a bag, call for help and fix the cause afterwards. Never silence an alarm without understanding it, and do not change settings unless asked by the person responsible. Learn the common alarms for your own machines, because layouts and thresholds differ.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Silencing the alarm and carrying on.
  • Fixing the machine before looking at the patient.
  • Ignoring the cuff leak because oxygen levels still look fine.
  • Changing alarm limits to stop nuisance alarms.

Check yourself

What causes a high pressure alarm?

Kinks, secretions, coughing or a blocked tube.

What does a low pressure alarm usually mean?

A leak or disconnection.

What is the first step in a serious alarm?

Check the patient and support breathing by hand if needed.

Quick revision points

  • High pressure: blockage; low pressure: leak.
  • Patient first, machine second.
  • Bag the patient if breathing is inadequate.
  • Do not silence alarms without cause.
  • Follow local protocols for each machine.

biomedical-waste-segregation.caption: The four-bin colour system for sorting healthcare waste at the point where it is made.
biomedical-waste-segregation.body:
In short: Sorting waste correctly protects staff, cleaners and the community and keeps costs down. This card shows four bins and what goes in each.

What the card shows

Four bins are drawn in a two-by-two grid with me pointing at them from the left. The red bin holds contaminated plastic such as IV sets, the yellow bin holds infectious anatomical and pathological waste, the black bin holds general non-infectious waste such as paper, packaging and food, and the white puncture-proof container holds sharps such as needles, scalpels and broken glass. The subtitle says "4 bins • Colour-coded • WHO standard".

The idea behind colour coding

Segregating at the point of generation keeps dangerous waste out of the general stream, protects cleaners and waste handlers, and cuts disposal costs, because only the infectious portion needs expensive treatment. Mixing a little infectious waste into a black bin turns the whole bin into a hazard.

Practical rules I follow

Decide the bin before you throw. Never recap needles, and place sharps in the puncture-proof box immediately. Close containers when about three-quarters full. Do not push waste down with your hands. Wash your hands after handling any waste. Colour schemes can differ slightly between countries and hospitals, so learn your own facility's chart and keep it on the wall where staff can see it. This graphic is the base version, and the Waste Segregation in Theatre card goes deeper for attachment students.

Why segregation matters

Healthcare waste is a mixture of harmless and hazardous items. If everything is mixed, all of it must be treated as hazardous, which costs more and increases the chance of exposure. Sorting at the point of generation, by the person who made the waste, is the only reliable way to keep dangerous items in the right stream.

Main categories are general waste, infectious waste, sharps, anatomical or pathological waste and chemical or pharmaceutical waste. Each has a handling, storage and disposal route.

Good habits

Know the colour code before you start. Place a bin close to where waste is produced. Do not overfill. Seal bags properly and label them when required. Never reach into a bin. Wear gloves and wash hands afterwards. Report spills and injuries immediately. If your hospital's colours differ from the card, follow the hospital's chart.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Throwing sharps into general waste.
  • Putting infectious waste in the black bin.
  • Overfilling bins so lids do not close.
  • Letting visitors or patients dump items in clinical bins.

Check yourself

Where do needles go?

In a puncture-proof sharps container.

Why sort at the point of generation?

It prevents mixing and exposure later.

At what level should containers be closed?

About three-quarters full.

Quick revision points

  • Four streams: general, infectious, sharps, anatomical/pathological.
  • Colour codes differ by hospital; learn yours.
  • Sort where the waste is made.
  • Never reach into bins.
  • Wash hands after handling waste.

hypothermia-prevention.caption: Why surgical patients get cold, how it harms them and how to keep them warm.
hypothermia-prevention.body:
In short: Even a mild drop in temperature raises the risk of bleeding and infection. This card shows the causes, the prevention and what to monitor.

What the card shows

Four teal panels with shield icons stack on the right of this graphic while Causes: exposure to a cold theatre and anaesthesia. Prevention: warm blankets, a fluid warmer and room temperature around 24 °C. Monitoring: core temperature every 30 minutes. Complications: coagulopathy, arrhythmia and infection.

Why patients get cold

Anaesthesia switches off the body's normal shivering and blood vessel responses, exposed skin loses heat, cold fluids and prep solutions add to it, and theatres are kept cool for the comfort of the gowned team. Even a mild drop in temperature changes how the body behaves.

Why it matters

Cold patients bleed more because clotting slows, heal more slowly and have more wound infections, and their hearts are more likely to develop rhythm problems. They also wake more slowly and shiver, which raises oxygen demand.

What we do about it

Start warming before surgery, not after it, cover everything that does not need to be exposed, use forced-air warming blankets and warmed fluids, and monitor the temperature at regular intervals. The card says every 30 minutes, but your own protocol may differ with the length and type of the case. Pair this with the Body Temperature card, which gives the ranges and what they mean.

The science of getting cold

Anaesthetic drugs reset the body's thermostat and widen blood vessels, which sends warm blood from the core to the cooler skin. Add a cool theatre, exposed skin, cold skin prep, cold fluids and open body cavities, and the core temperature can fall by one or two degrees in the first hour.

Hypothermia in surgery is generally defined as a core temperature below 36 °C, and it is common unless prevented.

Prevention is easier than rescue

Warm the patient before surgery, keep the theatre temperature suitable, cover everything that does not need to be exposed, use forced-air warming and warmed intravenous and irrigation fluids, and monitor temperature through the case and in recovery. Shivering in recovery can be a sign the patient is cold, and increases oxygen demand. Local policies set target temperatures and monitoring intervals.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Turning the room cold to keep the team comfortable and forgetting the patient.
  • Starting warming only after the patient is already cold.
  • Using cold prep and irrigation fluids.
  • Forgetting to monitor temperature on short cases.

Check yourself

Name two ways to keep a patient warm.

Forced-air blankets and warmed fluids.

Why do cold patients bleed more?

Clotting slows at lower temperatures.

When should warming start?

Before or at the start of surgery, not after.

Quick revision points

  • Anaesthesia and exposure cause heat loss.
  • Cold raises bleeding, infection and heart risks.
  • Cover, warm and monitor.
  • Warm fluids and forced-air warmers help.
  • Follow local temperature protocols.

who-surgical-safety-checklist.caption: The three pauses of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: Sign In, Time Out and Sign Out.
who-surgical-safety-checklist.body:
In short: The checklist has three pauses designed to catch mistakes before they reach the patient. This card shows what happens at each.

What the card shows

A navy header with the WHO logo reads "WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, 3 phases", and three teal cards run down the right, with me pointing up at the left. 1 Sign In, before anaesthesia induction: patient identity confirmed, procedure and consent verified, anaesthesia safety check complete. 2 Time Out, before incision: team introductions of surgeon, anaesthesia and nurse, confirmation of patient, site and procedure, antibiotics given and imaging reviewed. 3 Sign Out, before the patient leaves the OR: instrument and sponge counts confirmed, specimen labelled correctly, equipment issues recorded and a recovery and handoff plan shared. The footer says never skip the checklist, because it prevents wrong-site surgery.

Why three pauses

Each pause happens at a point where an error can still be caught. Before anaesthesia, the right patient and procedure can be confirmed. Before incision, everyone in the room agrees what is about to happen. Before leaving, nothing is left behind or lost.

How to make it work

The checklist works only when everyone stops and listens. The circulating nurse often reads it, but any team member may speak. If the list is skipped or rushed, the safety benefit disappears. Hospitals may adapt the wording, and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist Explained blog post goes through each item.

What students can do

Learn all three phases, listen attentively and speak up if you see something wrong.

Where the checklist came from

The WHO introduced the Surgical Safety Checklist as part of its Safe Surgery programme to reduce avoidable harm worldwide. It is a short, practical tool designed to be adapted to local settings, and studies and hospital experience have linked its proper use with fewer complications and deaths.

Its power comes from teamwork: it makes the whole team stop, speak and listen.

The three phases

Sign In (before anaesthesia): confirm identity, procedure, site and consent, check the anaesthesia machine and medicines, and discuss allergies and airway risk. Time Out (before incision): everyone introduces themselves, confirms the patient, procedure and site, discusses critical steps, antibiotic timing and imaging, and any equipment concerns. Sign Out (before the patient leaves): confirm the procedure recorded, instrument, sponge and needle counts, specimen labelling, equipment problems and recovery plan.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Reading it out while others carry on working.
  • Ticking boxes without asking the questions.
  • Skipping the checklist in emergencies.
  • Having only one person take part.

Check yourself

When is the Time Out done?

Before the skin incision.

Name one thing confirmed at Sign Out.

Counts, specimen labelling or the recovery plan.

Who can speak up during the checklist?

Any member of the team.

Quick revision points

  • Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out.
  • Everyone stops and listens.
  • Confirm patient, site and procedure.
  • Counts and specimens at Sign Out.
  • Adapt wording, never skip it.

blood-groups-who-can-give-to-whom.caption: The ABO and Rh compatibility table for red cell donation, with an explanation of why it works.
blood-groups-who-can-give-to-whom.body:
In short: Giving the wrong blood type can be fatal. This card shows the red cell compatibility chart and the logic behind it.

What the card shows

A compatibility table sits on the right of this graphic with a blood-drop icon beside each row. O negative is labelled the universal donor and can give to all eight groups. O positive gives to O+, A+, B+ and AB+. A negative gives to A−, A+, AB− and AB+. A positive gives to A+ and AB+. B negative gives to B−, B+, AB− and AB+. B positive gives to B+ and AB+. AB negative gives to AB− and AB+. AB positive is the universal recipient, able to receive from every group. A tip at the bottom says Rh negative can donate to Rh positive and Rh negative, but Rh positive can only donate to Rh positive.

How to read it

Match the antigen: a person can only receive red cells that lack the antigens their own plasma would attack. Group O cells have neither A nor B antigen, so they go anywhere, and AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B, so AB can receive anywhere.

Important note

This chart is about red cell donation. Plasma compatibility runs the other way, and in real practice blood is always cross-matched and checked at the bedside before transfusion. Never rely on a poster for a clinical decision.

The logic of antigens and antibodies

Red cells carry antigens on their surface: A, B, both (AB) or neither (O), and Rh (D) positive or negative. Plasma carries antibodies against the antigens the person does not have. A recipient's antibodies attack red cells with a foreign antigen, so you only give cells that the recipient's plasma will not attack.

O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh D antigens and can be given to most people in an emergency. AB positive recipients have no anti-A or anti-B antibodies and can receive red cells from any ABO group.

In practice

The chart is a teaching aid. Real transfusion always begins with correct patient identification, a sample, grouping and cross-matching or electronic matching, and bedside checks by two staff. Plasma and platelets follow different compatibility rules. Many errors come from patient or sample identification mistakes, not from the chart.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming O negative is always safe for everyone.
  • Mixing up red cell and plasma compatibility.
  • Skipping the bedside check.
  • Labelling a blood sample for the wrong patient.

Check yourself

Who is the universal red cell donor?

O negative.

Who is the universal red cell recipient?

AB positive.

What must always be done before transfusion?

Cross-match and bedside identity checks.

Quick revision points

  • O negative is the universal red cell donor.
  • AB positive is the universal recipient.
  • Rh negative patients should receive Rh negative blood where possible.
  • Plasma compatibility is reversed.
  • Never rely on a chart for a clinical decision.

stages-of-wound-healing.caption: The four overlapping stages of wound healing and what supports or slows each.
stages-of-wound-healing.body:
In short: Wounds heal in stages that overlap. Knowing them helps you understand dressings, delayed healing and what the patient should do.

What the card shows

Four soft panels with small illustrations sit in a two-by-two grid on the right of this graphic, with me pointing from the left. 1 Hemostasis: zero to minutes, with clotting and a platelet plug. 2 Inflammatory: days 1 to 5, with redness, swelling and white-cell clean-up. 3 Proliferative: days 4 to 21, with granulation tissue, new vessels and collagen. 4 Remodelling: from day 21 up to two years, with maturation, scar formation and strengthening.

What is happening in each stage

First the bleeding stops. Then the body sends white cells to clear germs and debris, which is why a fresh wound looks red, warm and swollen. Next, new tissue and blood vessels fill the gap, and collagen gives it strength. Finally, the collagen reorganises and the scar slowly becomes stronger, though never quite as strong as the original skin.

The stages overlap

The dates are guides, and the stages merge into each other. A wound can stay stuck in the inflammatory stage if it is infected or if the patient has poor circulation, diabetes or poor nutrition.

What helps healing

Protein, vitamin C, zinc, good blood sugar control, not smoking, clean dressings and keeping the wound moist and protected all help. This is why the postoperative advice about eating, resting and wound care matters. See the Stages of Wound Healing blog post for more detail.

What happens in each stage

Haemostasis: platelets and clotting stop bleeding within minutes. Inflammation: white cells clean the wound; redness, warmth and swelling are normal here. Proliferation: new tissue (granulation), new blood vessels and collagen fill the wound and skin edges pull together. Remodelling: collagen reorganises and strengthens for months, and scar tissue matures but never quite matches the original strength.

Primary intention is when a clean wound is closed with sutures; secondary intention is when it heals from the base up; tertiary intention is delayed closure.

What delays healing

Infection, poor circulation, diabetes, smoking, poor nutrition, steroids, tissue tension and repeated trauma. Support healing with good nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), blood sugar control, not smoking, gentle handling, correct dressings and early reporting of infection signs: increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, smell or fever.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating normal inflammation as infection, or the reverse.
  • Removing dressings too often.
  • Ignoring nutrition and smoking.
  • Expecting a scar to be as strong as skin immediately.

Check yourself

Which stage involves granulation tissue?

Proliferation.

Which stage lasts longest?

Remodelling.

Name two factors that slow healing.

Infection and diabetes (or smoking or poor nutrition).

Quick revision points

  • Four stages: haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodelling.
  • Stages overlap.
  • Infection and poor circulation delay healing.
  • Nutrition and clean dressings help.
  • Report increasing pain, redness, pus or fever.

sterilization-methods.caption: Five sterilisation methods and which items each is suitable for.
sterilization-methods.body:
In short: Different items need different methods. This card compares steam, dry heat, ethylene oxide, radiation and chemical sterilisation.

What the card shows

Five pale cards with icons run down the right of this graphic, with me on the left with a hand on my chest. Steam autoclave: pressurised steam at 121 to 134 °C, which kills bacteria, viruses and spores, common for surgical instruments. Dry heat: hot air at 160 to 170 °C for one to two hours, with no moisture, used for glassware and powders. Ethylene oxide: a low-temperature gas for heat-sensitive devices that needs aeration to remove residue. Gamma radiation: ionising radiation for disposable supplies, with no heat and penetration through packaging. Chemical glutaraldehyde: a liquid sterilant for soaking endoscopes and instruments, cold sterilisation for sensitive equipment.

Choosing the method

Match the method to the item. If it tolerates heat and moisture, use steam, because it is fast, cheap and reliable. If it tolerates heat but not moisture, use dry heat. If it cannot take heat, use gas, radiation or a chemical.

The trade-offs

Ethylene oxide is toxic, so items must be aerated before use. Gamma radiation is an industrial process for manufacturers, not a hospital machine. Glutaraldehyde needs strict contact times, good ventilation and thorough rinsing, and it is sometimes used for high-level disinfection rather than true sterilisation depending on time and policy. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions for each instrument.

Matching method to material

Steam under pressure is the first choice for anything that tolerates heat and moisture because it is fast, cheap and reliable. Dry heat suits items that moisture damages, such as powders, oils and some glassware, but needs a higher temperature and longer time. Ethylene oxide gas and low-temperature processes treat heat-sensitive devices; gas must be aerated afterwards. Gamma radiation is used industrially for single-use items. Liquid chemical sterilants are used when no other method is suitable and need strict contact times and rinsing.

Cleaning must always come first: dirt shelters microorganisms and protects them from the process.

Verifying sterility

Each method has its own monitors: mechanical readouts, chemical indicators and biological indicators. Items must be packaged correctly, loaded properly, labelled and stored in a clean dry place. Always check the instrument manufacturer's instructions, since some delicate equipment cannot take steam.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Sterilising an uncleaned instrument.
  • Using steam on heat-sensitive items.
  • Skipping aeration after ethylene oxide.
  • Using a chemical soak for items that can be steam sterilised.

Check yourself

Which method is preferred for heat-stable instruments?

Steam autoclave.

Why is cleaning done first?

Dirt protects microbes from the sterilising agent.

Why must ethylene oxide items be aerated?

To remove toxic residue.

Quick revision points

  • Steam first when the item allows.
  • Dry heat for moisture-sensitive items.
  • Low-temperature methods for heat-sensitive items.
  • Clean before sterilising.
  • Follow manufacturer instructions.

hand-scrub-technique.caption: A four-step overview of the surgical hand scrub: prepare, wash, scrub, rinse and dry.
hand-scrub-technique.body:
In short: The scrub is the first act of sterile technique. This card gives a simple four-step overview.

What the card shows

Four teal numbered panels run across the bottom of this graphic with me standing above them. 1 Preparation: remove jewellery, trim nails and check your hands. 2 First wash: wash hands and forearms up to two inches above the elbow for two minutes. 3 Scrub: systematic from nails to fingers to hands to arms, for three minutes with antiseptic. 4 Rinse and dry: hands up, rinse from fingertips towards the elbow, then dry with a sterile towel.

What each step is doing

Preparation removes the places where germs hide. The first wash removes visible dirt and loosens skin oils. The scrub with antiseptic reduces the number of germs on the skin to a safe level. Rinsing in the right direction means the water flows from the cleanest part, the fingertips, down to the dirtier elbow, never back up to the hands.

Keep these rules in mind

Hands stay up and in front, above the elbows, and never drop below the waist. Move from the cleanest area to the less clean, and treat each finger as having four sides. Use the scrub time your hospital requires, which is why the card shows a basic pattern, and follow the product's instructions for contact time. This is the simple four-step overview, so see the Surgical Hand Scrub 6 Steps and Scrub Technique cards for more detail.

What the scrub achieves

Surgical hand antisepsis removes dirt and transient bacteria and lowers the number of resident bacteria on the hands and forearms before gloving. It also leaves a residual effect: the antiseptic keeps suppressing bacterial growth under the glove during the operation.

Whether you use a traditional scrub with antiseptic soap and a brush or a waterless alcohol-based rub, the principle is the same: cover every surface for the time recommended on the product and by your hospital.

Keys to doing it well

Clean nails and keep them short. Remove jewellery and any watch. Keep hands above the elbows. Rinse so water runs from fingertips to elbow. Dry with a sterile towel without returning to the hands. Do not touch anything non-sterile after scrubbing; if you do, scrub again. Use the contact times set by local policy and the antiseptic's manufacturer.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Rushing the nails and between the fingers.
  • Letting hands drop below the waist.
  • Touching the tap or door after scrubbing.
  • Skipping the rinse direction.

Check yourself

Which direction does water flow when you rinse?

From fingertips toward the elbow.

Why remove jewellery?

Germs hide under it and it can tear gloves.

What do you do if you touch a non-sterile surface?

Scrub again.

Quick revision points

  • Prepare, wash, scrub, rinse and dry.
  • Hands up and elbows down.
  • Clean to less clean.
  • Follow your hospital's contact times.
  • If contaminated, re-scrub.

suture-materials.caption: Absorbable versus non-absorbable sutures, and how cutting and taper needles differ.
suture-materials.body:
In short: The right suture and needle combination matters for healing. This card gives the main types and where each is used.

What the card shows

Two large boxes sit at the top of this graphic: absorbable (Vicryl and catgut, which dissolve naturally, need no removal and are used inside body tissues) and non-absorbable (nylon, silk and Prolene, which need removal once healed and are used for skin or surface closures). Below, a Needle Types box separates cutting or reverse-cutting needles, with a sharp edge for skin, from taper or blunt needles, rounded for bowel and vessels.

Absorbable and non-absorbable

Absorbable sutures lose strength and disappear over days to weeks, so they are used where nobody can take them out later, such as muscle layers and deep tissue. Non-absorbable sutures keep their strength, so they are used for skin and for tissues that need long-term support.

A nuance

The card simplifies things. Some non-absorbable materials, such as Prolene, are placed deliberately inside the body, for example in blood vessel repairs, and silk loses its strength slowly over a long time.

Matching the needle

A cutting needle has a sharp edge to pass through tough tissue like skin, while a taper-point needle spreads tissue without cutting it, which is gentler on bowel and vessels. When you prepare the tray, always read the pack label for material, size and needle shape, and check the expiry. The Sutures and Needles Basics blog post covers sizes and handling.

How to choose a suture

Surgeons consider the tissue, how long it needs support, the risk of infection and the cosmetic result. Absorbable sutures are broken down by the body over days to weeks, so they suit internal tissues that heal fast. Non-absorbable sutures remain until removed, and are used for skin, tendons and sites needing long-term strength. Monofilament sutures are smooth and resist bacteria; braided sutures handle well but can harbour bacteria.

Suture size is written as a number of zeros: a larger number of zeros (for example 6-0) means a finer thread, and 1 or 2 is thicker.

Matching the needle

Cutting and reverse-cutting needles have sharp edges and pass through tough tissue like skin and fascia. Taper-point needles slide through softer tissue such as bowel and vessels. Needle curvature and size change how it moves through tissue. Always read the pack for material, size and needle type, check the expiry and confirm with the surgeon before opening it.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Opening a suture before confirming the exact type and size.
  • Confusing suture sizes (2-0 vs 0).
  • Passing the needle without controlling the point.
  • Not counting needles.

Check yourself

Which sutures need removal?

Non-absorbable ones used on skin.

What does 6-0 mean?

A very fine suture.

Which needle is used for bowel?

Taper-point.

Quick revision points

  • Absorbable: dissolve; non-absorbable: stay or removed.
  • More zeros means finer thread.
  • Cutting needles for skin; taper for soft tissue.
  • Count needles.
  • Read the pack label every time.

7-layers-closed-in-c-section.caption: The seven tissue layers a surgeon passes through and closes in a caesarean section.
7-layers-closed-in-c-section.body:
In short: Knowing the layers lets you follow the operation, prepare the right sutures and understand what is being repaired. This card lists them from skin to uterus.

What the card shows

This graphic stacks the seven tissue layers of a caesarean section on the right, with me pointing at them from the left. The list is numbered from the outside in: 1 skin (the outermost protective layer), 2 subcutaneous tissue (the fatty layer, with Camper's and Scarpa's fascia noted), 3 rectus sheath fascia (the white fibrous layer), 4 the rectus abdominis muscle (drawn in red), 5 parietal peritoneum, 6 the uterine muscle (myometrium) and 7 the visceral peritoneum covering the uterus. A summary box underneath repeats the layers in order.

How to read the order

The surgeon passes through these layers in the order 1 to 7 on the way in, and the closure works back out in the opposite direction, uterus first and skin last. That is why the graphic says "bottom to top". The colours help: yellow fat, red muscle, pale membranes.

What to remember as a theatre student

Know the names well enough to follow the surgeon's commands and to prepare the right sutures and instruments for each stage. In real practice the layers closed vary with the surgeon's technique, and many surgeons choose not to close the peritoneum at all, so treat this as the anatomy map rather than a fixed rule. A quick memory trick is to say the layers aloud as skin, fat, fascia, muscle, peritoneum, uterus, uterine covering.

Walking through the layers

Skin and subcutaneous fat are first. Beneath lies the rectus sheath (fascia), a strong layer that provides the main strength of the closure. The rectus muscles are usually separated rather than cut. Then comes the peritoneum, the thin membrane lining the abdomen, and the bladder flap is gently moved down. The uterus is opened in the lower segment, and the baby is delivered. Closure then retraces the steps: uterus, sometimes peritoneum, fascia, subcutaneous tissue and skin.

The exact technique varies with the surgeon, the urgency and the patient, so treat this as a map.

What the theatre team does

Before the case, prepare the set, check counts and have suture types ready for the uterus, fascia and skin. Warm fluids, oxytocic drugs per protocol, newborn resuscitation equipment and blood should be ready. Counts are especially important because swabs can be hidden in the wound, so count at the start, before closing the uterus and again before the skin is closed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming every surgeon closes the same layers.
  • Forgetting counts before closing the uterus.
  • Not preparing for newborn resuscitation.
  • Opening instruments before the team is ready.

Check yourself

Name the layer that gives the main strength to the closure.

The rectus sheath (fascia).

What incision is typical?

A Pfannenstiel transverse low abdominal incision.

When are counts performed?

Before incision, before closure and at the end.

Quick revision points

  • Layers: skin, fat, fascia, muscle, peritoneum, uterus.
  • Closure reverses the opening.
  • Fascia gives strength.
  • Count carefully.
  • Technique varies by surgeon.

body-temperature.caption: The temperature ranges from hypothermia to hyperpyrexia and what each means.
body-temperature.body:
In short: Body temperature is a vital sign that tells you about infection, inflammation, shock and anaesthesia effects. This card gives the main bands.

What the card shows

A colour-coded thermometer ladder runs down this graphic from hot to cold, with me at the top right with a hand on my chin. The rows are hyperpyrexia at or above 41.5 °C (life-threatening, a medical emergency), very high fever at or above 40.0 °C (serious, needs evaluation), fever at or above 38.0 °C (higher than normal, monitor and treat), normal at 36.1 to 37.7 °C (typical for healthy adults) and hypothermia below 35.0 °C (abnormally low, a medical emergency). The heading reads "Know the ranges • When to seek care • Stay informed".

Reading the ladder

Red and orange mean act, green means normal, blue means too cold. Each band includes a short note on risk: organ damage and seizures at the top, dehydration in the middle, and the dangers of cold at the bottom.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthesia, cold theatres and open body cavities all push patients toward hypothermia, which raises bleeding, infection and heart risks, so temperature is monitored and warming measures are used. Fever after surgery can be an early sign of infection. Different references use slightly different normal ranges, for example 36.5 to 37.5 °C in the Normal Vital Signs card, so learn the range your hospital uses and always take temperature trends together with the whole patient picture.

How the body controls temperature

The hypothalamus works like a thermostat. When we are too hot, we sweat and widen skin vessels; when we are too cold, we shiver and narrow them. Fever is a raised set-point in response to infection or inflammation. Hyperthermia is different: the body is overwhelmed by heat, as in heat stroke or malignant hyperthermia.

Low temperature (hypothermia) slows the heart, clotting and drug breakdown.

Measuring accurately

Methods include tympanic (ear), oral, axillary (armpit), temporal and core probes (oesophageal, bladder, nasopharyngeal). Each reads slightly differently, so use the same site for trends and follow your hospital's practice. Record the site, time and any action taken. In theatre, core temperature probes are commonly used in longer cases.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Comparing readings taken at different sites.
  • Treating every fever with the same drug without finding the cause.
  • Ignoring low temperature in a patient who is shivering.
  • Forgetting that infants and older adults regulate temperature poorly.

Check yourself

What is a typical normal range?

About 36.1 to 37.7 °C, depending on the reference.

What does hypothermia mean?

Abnormally low body temperature.

Why record the site of measurement?

Different sites read differently.

Quick revision points

  • Know the normal range for your hospital.
  • Fever means a raised set-point.
  • Hypothermia slows clotting and the heart.
  • Use the same site for trends.
  • Report extreme values immediately.

laser-safety-in-ot.caption: The four main laser hazards in theatre and the precautions that control them.
laser-safety-in-ot.body:
In short: Surgical lasers cut and coagulate tissue using light energy. This card covers eye protection, fire, smoke and records.

What the card shows

Four teal panels with icons stack on the right of this graphic, and Eye Protection: use wavelength-specific goggles for all staff and the patient. Fire Risk: no alcohol prep and keep wet towels around the laser. Smoke Plume: use an evacuator and an N95 mask, with suction close to the site. Documentation: record the laser type, power and duration, and complete the safety checklist.

Why goggles must match the laser

Different lasers work at different wavelengths, and a goggle that blocks one wavelength may do nothing against another. That is why the card says wavelength-specific, and why the goggles should be checked for the right label before the laser is switched on.

The other three hazards

Lasers produce heat, so alcohol-based prep and dry drapes are fire risks, and wet towels help to contain any spark. The smoke plume from vaporised tissue contains particles and chemicals that should not be inhaled, so a smoke evacuator and a proper N95 mask matter. Finally, the record of what was used and how much is part of the legal and clinical file. Warning signs on the door, covered windows and a trained laser safety officer are also standard in many hospitals. As a student, stay clear of the beam path and follow the team's instructions.

Understanding the hazards

Laser light is concentrated and can burn skin and eyes even from reflection off metal. Different lasers have different wavelengths, so protective eyewear must match the laser in use. Lasers can ignite drapes, alcohol and anaesthetic gases. The plume produced when tissue is vaporised contains particles and chemicals that can irritate the lungs.

Laser safety is usually overseen by a trained laser safety officer who sets local rules.

How the team stays safe

Post warning signs on the door and cover windows if needed. Everyone present wears matching eyewear, and the patient's eyes are covered. Use non-reflective instruments where required, keep the laser on standby when not in use, have water or saline ready, use smoke evacuation and a high-filtration mask, and record the details. Only trained people operate the laser.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using the wrong goggles for the laser wavelength.
  • Leaving the laser armed when not in use.
  • Ignoring the smoke plume.
  • Using alcohol-based prep that has not dried.

Check yourself

Why must goggles match the laser?

Wavelengths differ, and eyewear protects only against specific ones.

What is the fire risk?

Drapes, alcohol and oxygen-rich gases can ignite.

What is a smoke evacuator for?

To remove the plume containing harmful particles.

Quick revision points

  • Wavelength-specific eye protection.
  • Fire precautions: dry prep, wet towels.
  • Smoke evacuation and a proper mask.
  • Warning signs and trained operators.
  • Record laser settings and duration.

types-of-surgical-scissors.caption: Six types of surgical scissors and what each is designed to cut.
types-of-surgical-scissors.body:
In short: Using the right scissors protects both the tissue and the instrument. This card shows six common types.

What the card shows

Six pairs of scissors are drawn in two columns, each with a short caption, and 1 Mayo: heavy and semi-blunt for dense tissue and fascia. 2 Metzenbaum: delicate and thin for fine tissue dissection. 3 Iris: small and sharp for ophthalmic and fine microsurgery. 4 Bandage or Lister: an angled blunt tip for cutting bandages and dressings safely. 5 Suture removal: a sharp, pointed tip for removing stitches. 6 Operating scissors, straight: sharp or blunt for general tissue cutting. A note says it is an educational infographic, not to scale.

How to tell them apart

Look at the blades and the tips. Mayo scissors are short and strong, Metzenbaum are long with thin, delicate blades, and iris scissors are the smallest. Bandage scissors have a blunt, angled tip to slide under a dressing without cutting the skin.

Why each has its own job

Using fine scissors on thick tissue blunts and damages them, and using heavy scissors on delicate tissue is rough on the patient. A good tip is that Mayo scissors cut tough tissue and fascia, while Metzenbaum scissors are kept for delicate tissue only.

For students

Learn the shapes first, then the names, then which tray holds which. Never use tissue scissors to cut sutures or dressings, and hand every pair handle first. See the Safe Instrument Handling card.

Reading the design

The blade shape, length and tip tell you the job. Mayo scissors are heavy and short for dense tissue such as fascia and for cutting sutures in some trays. Metzenbaum scissors are long and delicate for dissecting fine tissue and should not be used on suture or heavy structures. Iris scissors are small and sharp for fine work. Lister bandage scissors have an angled blunt tip. Straight or curved shapes affect access and visibility. Tips may be sharp or blunt.

Tungsten carbide inserts make some scissors stay sharper for longer, usually marked by gold handles.

Care and handling

Pass scissors handle first with the tips closed. Wipe blood off during use, never use them on wire or pins, and do not drop them. In processing, open the box lock and clean carefully; check sharpness and alignment, test them on gauze, and send for sharpening or repair if needed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using fine dissecting scissors to cut suture or tough tissue.
  • Closing tips on gauze fibres and tearing the blades.
  • Dropping instruments.
  • Putting scissors in the wrong tray.

Check yourself

Which scissors are used for delicate tissue?

Metzenbaum.

Which have an angled blunt tip for dressings?

Lister bandage scissors.

What do gold handles often indicate?

Tungsten carbide inserts.

Quick revision points

  • Mayo: tough tissue; Metzenbaum: delicate tissue.
  • Iris: fine work; Lister: bandages.
  • Use each for its purpose only.
  • Pass handle first.
  • Check sharpness after processing.

types-of-anemia.caption: Four types of anaemia classified by cause and cell size, with typical clues.
types-of-anemia.body:
In short: Not all anaemia is the same. Naming the type guides treatment, and cell size on a blood test is a key clue.

What the card shows

Four cells in a two-by-two panel carry the types, each with a red blood cell drawing, and Iron deficiency: microcytic, with small pale cells, low iron and poor diet. Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: macrocytic, with larger cells, fatigue and tingling or numbness. Aplastic: pancytopenia from bone marrow failure, with all blood cells reduced, weakness and bleeding risk. Haemolytic: destruction of red cells, such as sickle cell, with cells breaking apart, jaundice and pain episodes. A tip at the bottom lists the common symptoms: fatigue, pale skin, shortness of breath and dizziness.

Reading the cell sizes

Microcytic means small cells and macrocytic means large cells. Cell size is one of the first clues on a blood test, and helps point to the cause.

What each type means

Iron deficiency is the most common worldwide, and diet or blood loss is often behind it. B12 and folate deficiency affect cell maturation and can damage nerves, which explains the tingling. In aplastic anaemia the marrow stops making enough cells of every kind. In haemolytic anaemia, cells are destroyed faster than they are made.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaemia lowers a patient's reserve for bleeding, so the cause should be found and treated before elective surgery. This card follows on from the Anaemia Simple Overview.

Reading the clues

Microcytic anaemia (small cells) is most often caused by iron deficiency or chronic blood loss. Macrocytic anaemia (large cells) points to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Normocytic anaemias can follow chronic disease or acute blood loss. Aplastic anaemia is failure of the bone marrow to produce enough cells. Haemolytic anaemia means red cells are destroyed too quickly, as in sickle cell disease, some infections and inherited conditions.

Tests include a full blood count, a blood film, iron studies and sometimes bone marrow examination.

Treatment overview

Iron deficiency is treated with iron and by finding the source of loss. B12 or folate deficiency is treated with replacement. Aplastic and severe haemolytic anaemias need specialist care, possibly transfusion or other treatments. Because causes differ, never assume that iron tablets fit every case.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Giving iron to a patient with a different type of anaemia.
  • Not looking for the source of blood loss.
  • Ignoring tingling or numbness in B12 deficiency.
  • Overlooking sickle cell crises in surgery planning.

Check yourself

What does microcytic mean?

Small red blood cells.

Which deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia?

Vitamin B12 or folate.

What happens in haemolytic anaemia?

Red cells are destroyed too quickly.

Quick revision points

  • Iron deficiency: small cells.
  • B12 or folate deficiency: large cells.
  • Aplastic: marrow failure.
  • Haemolytic: premature destruction.
  • Treat the cause, not just the number.

fire-triangle-in-ot.caption: The three ingredients of fire and how to keep them apart in the operating theatre.
fire-triangle-in-ot.body:
In short: Operating theatres contain oxygen, fuel and ignition sources in close contact. This card explains the triangle and the five key preventions.

What the card shows

A green triangle sits in the middle of this graphic with a corner for each ingredient of fire. Fuel at the top lists surgical drapes, alcohol prep, hair and bowel gases. Ignition at the bottom left lists electrocautery, laser and fibre-optic light. Oxidizer at the bottom right lists oxygen and nitrous oxide. Below the triangle a prevention box lists five tips: let prep dry before draping, use the lowest oxygen concentration possible, avoid pooling of alcohol prep, check that electrocautery is holstered when not in use, and keep wet towels ready at the sterile field.

The triangle idea

Fire needs all three corners. Remove any one of them and it cannot start. In theatre we cannot remove all three, because we always have oxygen, tools that make heat and flammable materials, so our job is to keep them apart and keep the risks small.

The risky combination

The classic danger is an oxygen-rich space under the drapes near the head and neck, where an electrocautery spark meets alcohol-based skin prep that has not dried. Letting prep dry fully, reducing oxygen where possible and holstering the pencil stop almost all of these events.

In an emergency

Know where the fire extinguisher, the oxygen shut-off and the evacuation routes are before the case begins. Follow your hospital's fire plan, and use the wet towels or saline to smother small flames at the field.

The triangle in a theatre setting

An oxidiser such as oxygen or nitrous oxide makes fires burn faster. Fuels include drapes, gauze, alcohol-based prep, hair, gowns, and some anaesthetic equipment such as tubing. Ignition sources include diathermy, lasers, fibre-optic light cables and defibrillator paddles. The most dangerous zone is the airway and head and neck, where oxygen can pool under drapes and ignite with a small spark.

A surgical fire can cause serious burns to patients and staff in seconds.

Prevention and response

Let alcohol-based prep dry fully, avoid pooling, use the lowest effective oxygen concentration, keep diathermy and light cables in holsters or off when not used, and keep saline or wet gauze ready. If a fire occurs, remove the burning material, stop gas flow, extinguish or smother the flames, and care for the patient first. Know your fire plan and drill it regularly.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using diathermy before the prep dries.
  • Leaving the active electrode switched on or in the drapes.
  • Ignoring oxygen concentration around the face.
  • Not knowing the location of extinguishers and exits.

Check yourself

Name the three sides of the fire triangle.

Oxidiser, fuel and ignition.

Where is the fire risk highest?

The airway and head and neck area under the drapes.

What is a first response to a small drape fire?

Remove or smother the fire and stop gas flow, then care for the patient.

Quick revision points

  • Fire needs oxidiser, fuel and ignition.
  • Let prep dry.
  • Holster diathermy.
  • Reduce oxygen concentration where possible.
  • Know your fire plan.

sterilization-indicators.caption: Mechanical, chemical and biological checks that prove a sterilisation cycle worked.
sterilization-indicators.body:
In short: No single check is enough. This card shows how mechanical, chemical and biological indicators work together.

What the card shows

A large teal circle with a shield in the middle of this graphic is labelled Sterilization Indicators, with four boxes around it and me standing at the edge. Mechanical: the printout, with temperature, pressure and time checked. Chemical: a Type 5 integrator that changes colour on every pack. Biological: a spore test, the gold standard, done weekly. Documentation log: load the Bowie-Dick test and record the result.

Three layers of proof

The mechanical check says the machine did what it was set to do. The chemical indicator shows that the pack itself was exposed to the right conditions. The biological indicator proves that living spores did not survive. Each one catches a different kind of failure, so the three are used together.

Bowie-Dick and the log

The Bowie-Dick test is used with prevacuum autoclaves to check that air has been removed properly, because trapped air stops steam from reaching the load. Every cycle is recorded so that a failed result can be traced to every pack that was in the machine.

What to do with a failure

Do not use the load, quarantine it, report it and re-process once the machine is checked. Expiry and indicator strips should be stored correctly. The OT Fun Quiz is built on the same idea, so try it, and then see the Autoclave and Sterilization Methods cards.

Different checks for different failures

Mechanical readings show the machine met its set temperature, pressure and time. Chemical indicators placed inside packs show the contents were exposed to the conditions. Biological indicators use spores that must be killed. Class 5 chemical integrators respond to several conditions and match the performance of biological indicators more closely than simple tapes.

The Bowie-Dick or air removal test checks that a pre-vacuum steam steriliser removes air, because trapped air prevents steam contact.

Acting on results

Record each cycle with load contents. If any indicator fails, do not release the load, quarantine and investigate. For implants, many policies require waiting for the biological result before use. Storage, shelf life and packaging integrity also matter: a sterile pack that is torn, wet or past its date is not safe to use.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using a chemical tape as the only proof.
  • Ignoring a failed Bowie-Dick test.
  • Failing to record load numbers.
  • Using packs with broken seals.

Check yourself

What does the Bowie-Dick test check?

Air removal in a pre-vacuum steriliser.

Which indicator proves spores were killed?

The biological indicator.

What do you do with a failed load?

Quarantine and re-process after investigation.

Quick revision points

  • Mechanical, chemical and biological checks together.
  • Biological is the gold standard.
  • Bowie-Dick tests air removal.
  • Record every cycle.
  • Failed load: do not use.

incidents-in-ot.caption: Types, causes, prevention and management of incidents in the operating theatre.
incidents-in-ot.body:
In short: Incidents happen in every hospital. What matters is preventing them and learning from them. This card sets out a six-part approach.

What the card shows

Six pastel boxes are arranged in a grid on the right of this graphic while 1 Types: wrong site, retained swab, anaesthesia error, fall and burn. 2 Causes: poor communication, fatigue and not using the checklist. 3 Prevention: the WHO checklist, counts, time-out and team briefing. 4 Immediate action: stop, secure the patient and inform the surgeon. 5 Reporting: incident form, documentation and disclosure. 6 Management: debrief, root cause analysis and corrective action.

How to read the grid

The first three boxes are about stopping incidents before they happen. The last three are about what to do if one does. Notice that the same causes show up again and again: people not talking to each other, people who are tired, and checks that get skipped.

What I take from it

When something goes wrong, the first priority is the patient. Stop what you are doing, make the patient safe and tell the surgeon and the team leader. After that, write an honest incident report with facts, not blame. Hospitals run root cause analysis because most incidents come from a chain of small system weaknesses, not one bad person. Students should report near-misses too, because they are free lessons. Always follow your hospital's incident reporting policy.

A systems view

Most incidents come from a chain of small weaknesses: poor communication, fatigue, rushed handovers, unclear roles, missing equipment or skipped checks. Blaming one person rarely prevents the next event. Safety culture means people report problems, near-misses are discussed openly and the system is improved.

Common incident types include wrong-site or wrong-patient surgery, retained items, burns, falls, medication errors, equipment failure and sharps injuries.

When something goes wrong

Stop and make the patient safe, call for help, tell the surgeon and team leader, document facts promptly and report through the incident system. Be honest with the patient and family as policy directs. Afterwards, a team debrief and root cause analysis look at why it happened and what should change. Students should report near-misses, because they teach the same lessons without harm.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Hiding or delaying reporting.
  • Writing blame instead of facts.
  • Skipping the debrief.
  • Assuming a near-miss is not worth reporting.

Check yourself

Name two causes of incidents.

Poor communication and fatigue.

What is the first priority after an incident?

Patient safety.

What is root cause analysis?

A review of why the incident happened, to fix the system.

Quick revision points

  • Most incidents have system causes.
  • Stop, secure, tell, report.
  • Document facts, not blame.
  • Debrief and learn.
  • Report near-misses.

antimicrobial-resistance-amr-awareness.caption: What antimicrobial resistance is, how it develops and what health workers can do.
antimicrobial-resistance-amr-awareness.body:
In short: When antibiotics stop working, even simple surgery becomes dangerous. This card explains the causes and the steps we can all take.

What the card shows

Six numbered cards, each in a different colour, form the main body of this graphic: 1 what AMR is (microbes resist drugs, so antibiotics fail), 2 causes (overuse, misuse, incomplete courses, self-medication), 3 impact (longer illness, higher cost, more deaths), 4 prevention (rational use, culture and sensitivity, hygiene, vaccination), 5 antibiotic stewardship (right drug, right dose, right duration) and 6 the nurse's role (educate, monitor adherence, infection prevention and control, report). A red banner at the bottom warns "Superbugs alert • Misuse today = no cure tomorrow".

The core idea

Every time an antibiotic is used, some germs survive and learn to resist it. Using antibiotics when they are not needed, or stopping a course early, speeds that up.

What it means in theatre

Surgical patients depend on antibiotics to prevent infection, so resistance threatens every operation. Good hand hygiene, sterile technique and correct timing of prophylactic antibiotics all reduce how much antibiotic the hospital needs. Students can help by never encouraging self-medication, reminding patients to finish prescribed courses, and reporting infection patterns. Remember the banner: saving antibiotics today is how we keep surgery safe tomorrow.

What you can do today

Take antibiotics only when a clinician prescribes them, finish the course as directed and never share or save leftover tablets. Wash your hands, keep vaccinations up to date and ask questions if you are unsure why an antibiotic is needed.

How resistance develops

Bacteria that survive an antibiotic can multiply, and over time resistant strains become common. Using antibiotics for viral illnesses, not completing prescribed courses, using the wrong drug or dose, sharing leftover tablets, over-the-counter sales without prescription and overuse in farming all speed it up.

Resistant infections are harder and costlier to treat, and some can no longer be treated with first-line drugs.

What helps

Prevent infection in the first place with hand hygiene, vaccination and clean water; use antibiotics only when needed, in the right dose, route and duration; send cultures before treatment where possible; give prophylactic antibiotics at the right time before surgical incision and do not continue them unnecessarily; and educate patients. In theatre, good sterile technique reduces infections and therefore antibiotic use.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Asking for antibiotics for colds.
  • Stopping a course early without advice.
  • Keeping leftover antibiotics.
  • Giving prophylaxis at the wrong time.

Check yourself

Why does stopping antibiotics early matter?

Survivors may become resistant.

Do antibiotics treat viral infections?

No.

How does hand hygiene help with AMR?

It prevents infections and reduces antibiotic use.

Quick revision points

  • AMR means microbes resist drugs.
  • Misuse and overuse drive it.
  • Right drug, dose, duration.
  • Prevent infection to reduce antibiotic need.
  • Educate patients.

ot-lamps.caption: How surgical lights are designed, handled and maintained.
ot-lamps.body:
In short: A surgical light must give bright, shadow-free light without heating the field. This card covers types, parts and care.

What the card shows

A drawing of a surgical light with multiple LED domes fills the centre of this graphic, with five coloured boxes around it and me pointing up from the corner. Types: single dome, double dome, mobile and wall. Features: shadowless, cold light, adjustable intensity and colour temperature of 4000 K. Parts: dome, arm, handle, LED bulb and controls. Maintenance: clean the lens, check the bulb, check the arm lock and test the backup battery. Positioning: about one metre above the field, focus, and avoid contamination.

Why the light is special

Surgeons need to see colour and detail, so the lamp must give bright, even light that does not cast their hand shadows into the wound. Multiple domes and overlapping beams achieve that, and cool LEDs avoid heating tissue or the team.

Handling it safely

In many setups, only the sterile handle cover or a sterile handle is touched by the sterile team, while the circulating nurse adjusts the rest. Never touch the lamp body with sterile gloves unless it is a sterile handle. Check the arm locks so the lamp does not drift, and keep the lens clean and dry.

Quick checks

Before the list begins, test every lamp, check the backup battery and note any dead LEDs for maintenance. If a lamp fails mid-case, a mobile light must be ready. Positioning lamps well is a skill, so ask to practise during setup.

What makes a good surgical light

Multiple light heads overlap their beams so that if one is blocked, the others still illuminate the wound. LED technology provides cool, bright light with good colour rendering, so tissues look natural. Intensity can be adjusted, and some lamps offer different colour temperatures. Arms and handles allow positioning, and some lamps have cameras or battery backup.

Good light reduces surgeon fatigue and errors.

Handling and care

Position the lamp before draping, focus it on the field and avoid moving it over the sterile area. Use sterile handle covers or removable sterile handles where fitted. Clean lamp surfaces according to policy using approved agents, avoid harsh chemicals that fog the lens and check the arm locks and bulbs. Know where the backup light is and how to use it.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Touching a non-sterile lamp handle with sterile gloves.
  • Positioning the lamp directly over the sterile field in a way that drops dust.
  • Using strong solvents that damage lenses.
  • Ignoring flickering lights.

Check yourself

Why use multiple domes?

To reduce shadows and maintain light if one is blocked.

What is a benefit of LED lamps?

Cool, bright light with good colour rendering.

What should be checked before a case?

Function, arm locks and backup power.

Quick revision points

  • Shadow-free, bright, cool light.
  • Check arms, locks and backup before a case.
  • Handle only sterile handles when sterile.
  • Clean with approved agents.
  • Report flickering.

scrub-technique.caption: A six-step counted-stroke scrub method and the principles behind it.
scrub-technique.body:
In short: Counting strokes keeps the scrub consistent and complete. This card gives six steps and three principles.

What the card shows

Six numbered steps with small icons run down the left of this graphic while Step 1: remove jewellery and keep nails short. Step 2: wet the hands and forearms up to the elbow. Step 3: scrub the nails with five strokes, then the fingers and palms. Step 4: scrub the arms with ten strokes on each side. Step 5: rinse with hands up and elbows down so the water flows downward. Step 6: dry with a sterile towel, then gown and glove. A blue Principles box adds that the first scrub of the day is five minutes and later scrubs are three minutes, that you move from the cleanest to the less clean areas and that hands stay higher than the elbows throughout.

Why strokes are counted

Counting strokes, such as five on each nail and ten on each side of the arm, makes the scrub consistent from one person and one day to the next. It also stops us from rushing or scrubbing one area too long.

Direction matters

Rinsing with fingertips highest means water and soap run towards the elbow, which is the less clean region, not back towards the hands. Drying should also move from the hands to the elbow without returning.

Compare with the other scrub cards

This card is the technique with strokes, the Hand Scrub Technique card is the four-step overview and the Inside the Operating Theatre card gives the six hand movements. Exact times and products depend on your hospital's policy.

The stroke-count method

The counted-stroke method assigns a number of strokes to each part of the hand and arm so that every surface gets the same effort every time. It is an older, structured approach used in training and in some hospitals, while the timed method simply sets total contact time. Both aim to cover all surfaces. Newer guidance also supports alcohol-based surgical hand rubs applied for the manufacturer's contact time on clean, dry hands.

Nails and fingertips deserve extra attention because they harbour many bacteria.

Following the principles

Start at the cleanest area, the fingers, and move up the arm. Keep hands above elbows so water runs away from the clean area. Do not return to the hands once you have moved up the arm. Rinse thoroughly. Dry with a sterile towel in a single direction. Follow your hospital's method and times.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Skipping the nails.
  • Scrubbing too fast to count properly.
  • Letting the water run back to the hands.
  • Touching anything after drying.

Check yourself

Why count strokes?

To scrub every area consistently.

Which part gets extra attention?

Nails and fingertips.

Why keep hands above the elbows?

So water flows from clean to less clean areas.

Quick revision points

  • Count strokes for consistency.
  • Fingertips and nails first.
  • Hands above elbows.
  • One direction when drying.
  • Follow local times and products.

postoperative-phase.caption: The six jobs of postoperative care: recovery, pain, wound, fluids, complications and discharge.
postoperative-phase.body:
In short: Care does not end when the last stitch goes in. This card shows what happens after surgery and what to watch for.

What the card shows

Six coloured bars run down the right of this graphic, with me gesturing with an open hand. 1 Recovery in PACU: vitals every 15 minutes, airway and consciousness. 2 Pain management: assessment, analgesics and positioning. 3 Wound care: dressing, drain and signs of infection. 4 Fluid and nutrition: IV fluids, intake and output chart and moving from nil by mouth to oral. 5 Complications: bleeding, fever, DVT and atelectasis. 6 Discharge: education, medicines, follow-up and documentation.

What happens in recovery

The patient is watched closely until they wake and are stable. Airway, breathing, circulation and level of consciousness come first, then pain, nausea and the wound. The frequency of vital checks is highest at the start and spaces out as the patient settles.

Looking out for problems

Bleeding shows up as a rising pulse and falling blood pressure, or as soaked dressings. A fever may signal infection. Calf pain and swelling can mean DVT, and breathing problems or a low-grade fever in the first days can reflect atelectasis, a collapse of small parts of the lung. Early mobilisation and deep breathing help prevent both.

Discharge

Patients leave with clear instructions: how to care for the wound, which medicines to take, which signs to report and when to come back. Writing it down matters, because people forget what they were told when they are drowsy. Frequencies and policies vary by unit.

Recovery and what is monitored

In the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU), nurses check airway, breathing, circulation, consciousness, temperature, pain, nausea and the wound at set intervals. Oxygen is given as needed. Patients are moved to the ward when they meet discharge criteria, such as being awake, stable and comfortable.

On the ward, early walking, deep breathing and leg exercises help prevent chest infection and blood clots.

Common complications and warning signs

Bleeding (rising pulse, falling blood pressure, soaked dressings), infection (fever, redness, pus), clots in the legs (painful swollen calf), chest problems (cough, breathlessness), urinary retention and nausea. Pain should be assessed regularly and treated with the plan prescribed. Fluid balance and return of bowel function are watched after abdominal surgery. Clear discharge advice and follow-up complete the pathway.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming a patient is stable because they are quiet.
  • Missing early signs of bleeding.
  • Delaying mobilisation.
  • Not giving written discharge advice.

Check yourself

Where are patients monitored immediately after surgery?

In PACU or recovery.

Name a sign of bleeding.

Rising pulse and falling blood pressure.

Why mobilise early?

To prevent clots and chest problems.

Quick revision points

  • Recovery, pain, wound, fluids, complications, discharge.
  • Watch airway, breathing, circulation first.
  • Know signs of bleeding and infection.
  • Early mobilisation helps.
  • Give clear written advice.

full-personal-protective-equipment-ppe.caption: The full set of PPE and the order for putting it on and taking it off.
full-personal-protective-equipment-ppe.body:
In short: PPE protects staff and patients, but only if it is worn and removed correctly. This card lists the items and the sequence.

What the card shows

A numbered list of seven coloured boxes runs down the right of this graphic with me raising a finger on the left. They are: 1 hand hygiene (soap and water or alcohol rub), 2 fluid-resistant gown, 3 mask (N95 or surgical, N95 for airborne and surgical for droplets), 4 goggles or face shield, 5 gloves (sterile nitrile, changed between patients), 6 cap and shoe covers, and 7 donning and doffing order. The order box says: DON hand wash, gown, mask, goggles, gloves; DOFF gloves, goggles, gown, mask, hand wash. A blue footer reads "Perioperative nursing care".

Why the order matters

Putting PPE on in the right order means the layers fit together without gaps. Taking it off in the right order matters even more, because the outside is contaminated. Removing gloves first and finishing with hand hygiene stops you carrying germs onto your face or clothes.

A note on protocols

Different guidelines list slightly different doffing sequences, for example some remove the gown and gloves together, so follow the sequence taught by your own hospital. What never changes is the principle: touch the clean inside surfaces only, go slowly, and clean your hands afterwards. Check masks for fit, replace wet or torn items immediately, and never wear PPE outside the area where it is needed. The PPE Donning and Doffing card in the Inside the Operating Theatre series goes deeper on the common errors.

What each item protects

Gown or apron protects clothes and skin from fluids. Mask protects the nose and mouth: surgical masks protect against droplets and splashes; N95 or similar respirators are used for airborne diseases. Eye protection protects against splashes. Gloves protect the hands and prevent carrying germs between patients. Caps and shoe covers help keep the theatre clean.

Remember that PPE is the last line of defence after good hygiene, safe systems and clean practice.

Doffing is where mistakes happen

Contamination happens most often during removal. Take off the most contaminated items first, avoid touching the outside, pull items away from your body, discard in the right bin and clean your hands immediately. Practising with a partner who watches helps catch errors. Different guidelines recommend slightly different sequences; use your hospital's.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Touching your face with used gloves.
  • Wearing PPE outside the work area.
  • Reusing single-use items.
  • Removing the mask first.

Check yourself

Which mask is used for airborne infections?

N95 or equivalent respirator.

Why is doffing risky?

The outside is contaminated.

What always comes last?

Hand hygiene.

Quick revision points

  • Don: hand hygiene, gown, mask, eye protection, gloves.
  • Doff: gloves, goggles, gown, mask, hand hygiene (follow local order).
  • Avoid touching the front of used PPE.
  • Replace damaged PPE immediately.
  • Do not wear PPE outside its area.

nosocomial-infections.caption: Hospital-acquired infections: what they are, who is at risk and how to break the chain.
nosocomial-infections.body:
In short: Patients come to hospital to get better, not to catch something new. This card shows the common types and how to prevent them.

What the card shows

Six coloured bars run down the right of this graphic with me pointing at them from the left. 1 Definition: infection acquired in hospital after 48 hours. 2 Types: urinary tract infection, surgical site infection, pneumonia and bloodstream infection. 3 Causes: poor hand hygiene and contaminated equipment. 4 Risk factors: long stay, invasive devices and antibiotics. 5 Prevention: hand hygiene, PPE, asepsis and sterilisation. 6 Nurse role: surveillance, reporting and education. A red banner says hospital infection is preventable, so break the chain, and hand hygiene is your vaccine.

What nosocomial means

It comes from the Greek for hospital. These infections, also called healthcare-associated infections, were not present or incubating when the patient arrived.

Why surgical patients are at risk

Surgery opens the body's barrier, and catheters, drains and ventilators give germs a route in. Long stays and antibiotic use change the patient's own bacteria and may favour resistant ones, which links to the AMR card.

Breaking the chain

Infection needs a source, a way to travel and a susceptible person. Hand hygiene, PPE, sterile technique, clean equipment and early removal of devices break each link. Everyone in the building has a role, from the cleaner to the surgeon. Report suspected infections early, and follow your infection prevention team's guidance.
