The Preventing Hospital-Acquired Infections blog post goes deeper into the same topic.

The chain of infection

An infection needs a source (a person, equipment or the environment), a way to spread (contact, droplets, air or contaminated items), an entry point (wounds, tubes) and a susceptible person. Break any link and the infection stops. Hand hygiene breaks the route of spread; sterile equipment removes the source; vaccination protects the susceptible person; removing tubes early removes the entry point.

Surgical site infections, catheter-associated urinary infections, ventilator or hospital-acquired pneumonia and bloodstream infections linked to lines are the most common types.

What staff can do every day

Clean hands at the five moments, use gloves and gowns appropriately, keep surfaces clean, handle waste and sharps safely, follow sterile technique, remove devices as soon as they are no longer needed, and stay home or report if you are unwell. Surveillance and feedback show where to improve.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Believing gloves replace hand hygiene.
  • Leaving urinary catheters in longer than necessary.
  • Reusing single-use equipment.
  • Ignoring early signs of infection.

Check yourself

What does nosocomial mean?

Acquired in hospital.

Name one infection linked to catheters.

Urinary tract infection.

What is the simplest prevention?

Hand hygiene.

Quick revision points

  • Hospital infections are largely preventable.
  • Break the chain of infection.
  • Hand hygiene is central.
  • Remove devices early.
  • Report and learn from infections.

8-routes-of-drug-administration.caption: Eight ways drugs enter the body and why the route changes speed and effect.
8-routes-of-drug-administration.body:
In short: The route is part of the prescription. This card lists eight routes and when each is used.

What the card shows

Eight colour-coded cards run down the right side of this graphic, each with a small icon: oral (tablets, capsules, swallowing), sublingual (under the tongue, fast absorption), buccal (between cheek and gum), rectal (suppositories), parenteral IV (directly into a vein), intramuscular IM (into muscle), subcutaneous SC (under the skin), and inhalation and topical (lungs and skin). A blue strip at the bottom reads "Right route = right effect" and reminds you to check the 10 rights.

Why the route matters

The same drug behaves differently depending on how it gets in. Sublingual and buccal routes skip the liver's first pass and work quickly. IV gives the fastest and most complete effect because nothing needs to be absorbed. IM and SC are slower and steadier, and oral is the most convenient but depends on a working gut.

How I remember them

I group them by speed and by body area: mouth routes (oral, sublingual, buccal), injections (IV, IM, SC), and surfaces (rectal, inhalation, topical). In theatre you will mostly see IV, IM and inhalation, because anaesthesia relies on them. Whatever the route, the check never changes: right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time, plus the other rights your school teaches. Always follow your institution's drug policy.

Speed and reliability

Intravenous drugs go straight into the blood and act fastest. Sublingual and buccal drugs absorb through mucous membranes and avoid the first pass through the liver. Oral drugs must be swallowed and absorbed, which takes time and can be affected by vomiting. Intramuscular and subcutaneous injections absorb more slowly. Rectal, inhaled and topical routes suit specific needs. Epidural and spinal routes are used in anaesthesia.

The route also affects side effects, so a drug may be safe by one route and dangerous by another.

Safe administration

Check the prescription, patient, drug, dose, route, time and expiry before every dose. Never give an intravenous drug by a route not intended, and never inject a drug meant for another route. Label syringes and drugs on and off the sterile field. If you are unsure, ask before giving anything. Students observe and assist as allowed and do not administer unless authorised.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Giving a medicine by the wrong route.
  • Assuming all drugs can be given orally.
  • Unlabelled syringes.
  • Skipping the identity check.

Check yourself

Which route acts fastest?

Intravenous.

Why do sublingual drugs act quickly?

Mucous membranes absorb them directly into blood.

What must be checked before giving any drug?

Patient, drug, dose, route and time.

Quick revision points

  • Route affects speed and effect.
  • IV is fastest.
  • Sublingual and buccal avoid first-pass metabolism.
  • Check the rights every time.
  • Label everything.

pre-general-surgery-ot-preparation.caption: A six-stage checklist for preparing the theatre, equipment, supplies and patient before general surgery.
pre-general-surgery-ot-preparation.body:
In short: Preparation is where safe surgery starts. This card gives six steps from cleaning to documentation.

What the card shows

Six coloured bars run down the right of this graphic, with me pointing at them from the left. 1 Theatre cleaning: dusting, fumigation and disinfection. 2 Equipment: suction, diathermy, OT light and anaesthesia machine. 3 Sterile set: instruments, gowns, gloves, drapes and sutures. 4 Patient: ID, consent, site marking, vitals and NPO status. 5 Team briefing: WHO time-out, roles and communication. 6 Documentation: OT register, counts and safety checklist. A tip bar at the bottom says a well-prepared OT is half the surgery done, sterility saves lives and check twice, cut once.

The order of preparation

First the room is made clean, then the machines are tested, then the sterile supplies are laid out and checked, and finally the patient arrives and the team briefs. Preparing in this order means no step is rushed while the patient is waiting.

What to check before the patient comes in

Suction works, diathermy and its pad are ready, the lamp is focused, the anaesthesia machine check is done and every sterile pack is within date and intact. The count sheet, register and checklist are on hand. Skipping any one of these means finding the problem later, with the patient already on the table. Preparation lists vary with the type of operation, so this is the general-surgery version, and your theatre may add items for its own cases.

A logical order

Clean the room first so everything that comes in is clean. Test the equipment so faults are found early. Prepare sterile supplies once the room is ready, so they are not exposed longer than necessary. Confirm the patient's details, consent, site marking and fasting. Hold a briefing to confirm roles, special needs and concerns. Document everything in the theatre register.

The WHO checklist covers many of the same points at specific pauses.

The small things that cause delays

A missing consent form, a suction that does not work, blood not crossmatched, an instrument tray that was not sent, an unfocused light. Many delays are avoided by reading the list the day before and making a short checklist for each specialty. Keep emergency items accessible and know where the nearest replacement for anything that fails is.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Opening supplies too early.
  • Not testing the diathermy and suction.
  • Not checking the consent form.
  • Skipping the briefing.

Check yourself

Why clean before preparing supplies?

So sterile supplies enter a clean environment.

What is checked on the patient before surgery?

Identity, consent, site marking, fasting and vitals.

Why brief the team?

To confirm roles and special requirements.

Quick revision points

  • Clean, test, prepare, confirm, brief, document.
  • Read the list the day before.
  • Check suction and diathermy.
  • Confirm consent and site marking.
  • Keep emergency equipment close.

diathermy-machine.caption: How electrosurgery works, its parts and the safety rules that prevent burns.
diathermy-machine.body:
In short: Diathermy cuts and seals vessels with heat from electric current. This card covers the principle, types and precautions.

What the card shows

Six coloured panels stack on the right of this graphic while Principle: a high-frequency electric current converts to heat to cut and coagulate tissue. Parts: generator, active electrode, return pad and foot switch. Types: monopolar and bipolar. Modes: cut, coag and blend. Uses: cutting tissue, haemostasis and dissection. Precautions: check the pad, avoid alcohol, no jewellery and inspect for burns.

How it works in plain words

The generator produces electrical current at a frequency high enough that it heats tissue without shocking the patient. In monopolar mode the current flows from the active electrode through the patient to the return pad, so the pad must stick well over a clean, dry, muscular area. In bipolar mode the current passes between two tips, so no return pad is needed and the effect is more localised.

Safety first

Most diathermy injuries come from poor pad contact, pooled alcohol or fluids that ignite, and metal contact. Always check the pad site and the skin afterwards. Keep the active electrode holstered when not in use. This card ties directly to the Fire Triangle card, because diathermy is one of the main ignition sources in theatre. Set the lowest effective power and follow the manufacturer's instructions for your machine.

How it works

High-frequency current passes through tissue, where electrical resistance turns energy into heat. Cutting mode concentrates heat to vaporise cells; coagulation mode produces less intense heat to seal small vessels. In monopolar diathermy, current passes from the active electrode through the patient to a return pad, so the pad must have good contact over a clean, dry, well-perfused area. In bipolar diathermy, current passes only between the tips of forceps and is used near nerves and in delicate surgery.

Use the lowest power that works.

Preventing burns and fires

Check the machine and cables before use. Apply the return pad firmly and avoid scars, bony areas, hair and jewellery contact. Keep the active electrode holstered when not in use. Make sure skin prep is dry. Do not allow the patient to touch metal. For patients with pacemakers or implants, special precautions apply; tell the anaesthetist and follow protocol. Smoke produced should be evacuated.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Placing the return pad over a wet or hairy area.
  • Using a high power setting for convenience.
  • Leaving the pencil in the field.
  • Forgetting pacemaker precautions.

Check yourself

What is the difference between monopolar and bipolar?

Monopolar needs a return pad; bipolar passes current between two tips.

Why must prep be dry?

Alcohol can ignite.

Where should the active electrode be placed when not in use?

In a holster.

Quick revision points

  • Heat from current cuts or coagulates.
  • Return pad contact is essential for monopolar.
  • Bipolar is more localised.
  • Holster the pencil.
  • Tell the team about pacemakers.

suction-machine.caption: How a suction machine works and how to check and care for it.
suction-machine.body:
In short: Suction clears blood, fluids and secretions so the surgeon and anaesthetist can see and the airway stays clear. This card covers its parts and care.

What the card shows

Five coloured panels stack on the right of this graphic, with me on the left clenching a fist to my chest. Parts: motor, collection bottle, tubing, suction catheter, vacuum gauge and filter. Mechanism: creates negative pressure, sucks fluid and air and has adjustable vacuum. Types: electric, foot-operated, manual and wall-mounted. Uses: airway clearance, the surgical field, amniotic fluid and blood. Care: empty the bottle, clean the tubing, check the filter and test the pressure.

How it works

The motor, or the wall system, creates a lower pressure inside the tubing and bottle than in the air outside, so fluid and air are drawn in through the catheter. The bottle collects the fluid and the filter protects the motor.

Why a student should know it

Suction is one of the first things checked before a case, because the anaesthetist may need it at any moment to clear vomit or secretions from the airway, and the surgeon uses it to keep the field clear. A machine that does not suck, or a bottle that is full, is an emergency in waiting.

Quick check

Switch on, block the tube with your thumb, read the gauge and release. Use the lowest effective pressure for delicate tissue and children. Empty and clean after each case, and treat the contents as infectious waste. Never adjust the settings without being asked, as the Touch vs Do Not Touch card explains.

Parts and principle

A vacuum source, either a pump or the hospital wall system, creates negative pressure in tubing and a collection container. A regulator controls the vacuum strength, a gauge shows it, a bacterial filter or float valve protects the machine, and various catheters or tips attach to the end. Different tips are used for the airway, the surgical field and wounds.

Too much vacuum can damage tissue; too little will not clear fluid.

Checking and caring for suction

Check before every list: connections tight, canister secure, filter dry, vacuum builds when the tube is blocked, and a second unit available. Replace or empty canisters according to policy, handle contents as infectious waste, and clean or replace tubing. For airway suction, use the right catheter size and limit suction time to avoid reducing oxygen.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Not testing the suction until it is needed.
  • Leaving a full canister.
  • Using high pressure on children.
  • Not having a backup suction.

Check yourself

How do you test suction?

Block the tube and check that the gauge rises.

What protects the machine from fluids?

A filter or float valve.

Why limit airway suction time?

It can lower oxygen levels.

Quick revision points

  • Suction removes fluid and air using negative pressure.
  • Test before every case.
  • Use appropriate pressure.
  • Empty and clean after use.
  • Have a backup.

intraoperative-phase.caption: The six core elements of the intraoperative phase, from the WHO checklist to documentation.
intraoperative-phase.body:
In short: The intraoperative phase is when the operation happens. This card shows six elements that keep it safe.

What the card shows

Six coloured cards run down the right of this graphic with me standing calmly on the left with my hands clasped. 1 WHO checklist: sign-in, time-out, sign-out. 2 Positioning: supine, prone, lithotomy and safe positioning. 3 Anaesthesia: general, spinal, local and monitoring. 4 Asepsis: scrubbing, gowning, gloving and draping. 5 Intra-op care: vitals, fluids, blood loss and counts. 6 Safety: electrosurgery safety, specimen handling and documentation.

What the intraoperative phase is

It is the part of the patient's journey that runs from the moment they are transferred into theatre until they are moved to recovery. It sits between the preoperative phase (preparation) and the postoperative phase (recovery), and each of the six cards on this graphic is a job that has to be done well during it.

How the six fit together

The checklist frames the whole case. Positioning and anaesthesia make the patient safe and ready, asepsis protects against infection, intra-op care tracks what the patient needs minute by minute, and safety closes the loop with equipment, specimens and records. If you take one thing from the card, take this: none of the six is optional, and none belongs to just one person. The surgeon, anaesthetist, scrub nurse and circulating nurse each own a part, and the patient's safety depends on everyone doing theirs. Use it together with the Perioperative Care and Postoperative Phase cards.

What runs through the case

The checklist frames the start, middle and end. Positioning protects the patient. Anaesthesia and monitoring keep them stable. Asepsis keeps infection out. Fluid balance, blood loss and counts are tracked throughout. Equipment, specimens and records are managed until the patient is handed to recovery.

The phase begins when the patient enters the operating room and ends when they are transferred to recovery.

Roles in the room

The surgeon leads the operation, the anaesthetist manages the patient's physiology, the scrub practitioner maintains the sterile field and passes instruments, and the circulating practitioner supports with supplies, counts, documentation and communication. Everyone has a voice in safety. Students observe, learn the flow and assist within their scope.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating the checklist as paperwork.
  • Forgetting fluid and blood loss tracking.
  • Allowing too many people into the room.
  • Handing over without a complete record.

Check yourself

When does the intraoperative phase start?

When the patient enters the operating room.

Who maintains the sterile field?

The scrub practitioner.

Name one safety task of the circulating practitioner.

Counts, documentation or fetching supplies.

Quick revision points

  • Checklist, position, anaesthesia, asepsis, monitoring, safety.
  • Counts and specimens are part of the case.
  • Everyone can speak up.
  • Limit traffic in the room.
  • Hand over clearly to recovery.

theatre-zones.caption: The four-zone layout of an operating theatre and why traffic flows one way.
theatre-zones.body:
In short: A theatre suite is divided so that clean and dirty activities do not meet. This card shows four zones.

What the card shows

Four coloured boxes run down the right of this graphic, with me pointing at them from the left. 1 Protective zone: reception, changing rooms and admin, where street clothes are allowed. 2 Clean zone: corridors, storage, recovery and clean supplies. 3 Sterile zone: operating rooms and the scrub area, with only sterile attire. 4 Disposal zone: dirty utility, waste disposal and decontamination.

The idea of zoning

A theatre complex is arranged so that movement goes from the least clean area to the most clean, and dirty items leave by a different route. This stops contaminated people and materials from crossing paths with sterile ones.

Familiar names

Many hospitals describe the same plan as unrestricted, semi-restricted and restricted zones. Unrestricted is where street clothes are fine, semi-restricted needs scrubs and a cap, and restricted needs full theatre attire including a mask. The card breaks it down into four functional areas, so learn which words your own hospital uses.

Rules that follow

Change before you cross the line, never carry dirty items through the clean area, use designated routes for waste and instruments after use and keep doors closed. A student who understands the zones understands why the rules exist, and so is less likely to break them by accident. The Theatre Cleaning and Welcome to Theatre cards give the layout from a student's view.

From outside in

Protective or unrestricted zone: reception, offices, changing rooms. Clean or semi-restricted zone: corridors, stores, recovery and clean preparation. Sterile or restricted zone: operating rooms and scrub area, with full theatre attire. Disposal zone: dirty utility, sluice and waste areas.

Movement is arranged so that staff, patients, clean supplies and dirty items follow separate routes where possible.

Why it matters

Air pressure and ventilation help: theatres are often kept at higher air pressure than corridors so air flows outwards, reducing entry of contaminants. Doors should stay closed, and the number of people in the room should be limited. When you understand the zones, rules about masks, caps, footwear and moving dirty items make sense.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Walking into the restricted zone in street clothes.
  • Carrying dirty items through clean corridors.
  • Propping doors open.
  • Crowding the operating room.

Check yourself

Where is full theatre attire required?

In the sterile or restricted zone.

Why are doors kept closed?

To maintain air pressure and cleanliness.

What happens in the disposal zone?

Handling of waste and decontamination.

Quick revision points

  • Four zones: protective, clean, sterile, disposal.
  • Clean to sterile flow.
  • Dirty items use separate routes.
  • Doors closed, minimal traffic.
  • Change attire between zones.

iv-fluid-types.caption: The main intravenous fluids, how tonicity works and where each is used.
iv-fluid-types.body:
In short: IV fluids replace losses and deliver drugs and nutrients. This card compares isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic fluids, crystalloids, colloids and blood products.

What the card shows

Seven coloured bars run down the right of this graphic, with me pointing at them from the left. 1 Isotonic: normal saline 0.9%, Ringer's lactate and Ringer's, which expand the extracellular fluid. 2 Hypotonic: 0.45% and 0.33% saline, which shift fluid into cells. 3 Hypertonic: D5NS, D5RL and 3% saline, which pull fluid out of cells. 4 Crystalloids: small molecules such as saline, RL and dextrose. 5 Colloids: large molecules such as albumin and dextran. 6 Blood products: whole blood, packed red cells and fresh frozen plasma. 7 Indications: dehydration, shock and electrolyte imbalance. The footer says "Know your fluids: right fluid, right patient".

Tonicity in one idea

Compare the fluid with the patient's blood. Isotonic matches it and stays in the blood vessels and the space around cells. Hypotonic is weaker, so water moves into cells. Hypertonic is stronger, so water is drawn out of cells.

Where you meet them

Isotonic crystalloids are the everyday fluids in theatre for replacing losses and keeping the patient hydrated. Colloids and blood products are used when there is major blood loss. Giving the wrong type or the wrong amount can harm the patient, for example by causing swelling or electrolyte problems, so the prescription must be checked each time. Always check the label, the expiry, the clarity of the fluid and the patient's identity before it is hung.

Tonicity made simple

Cells sit in fluid. An isotonic fluid has about the same concentration as blood, so water stays where it is. A hypotonic fluid is more dilute, so water moves into cells. A hypertonic fluid is more concentrated, so water moves out of cells. Choosing the wrong one can cause cells to swell or shrink.

Crystalloids contain small dissolved particles such as salt and sugar and move freely between compartments. Colloids contain larger molecules that stay in the blood vessels longer. Blood products replace specific components.

Safe use

Check the prescription, the fluid, volume, rate, expiry and the patient before hanging. Look at the fluid for cloudiness or particles. Measure input and output, watch for signs of overload (breathlessness, swelling) and keep lines and cannula sites clean. Never add medicines to a fluid unless authorised, and label any additive.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Giving too much fluid too fast to a patient with a weak heart.
  • Using the wrong fluid for the situation.
  • Ignoring signs of fluid overload.
  • Not checking the label.

Check yourself

Which fluid is isotonic?

Normal saline 0.9% or Ringer's lactate.

What happens to cells in hypotonic fluid?

Water moves into them.

What is a colloid?

A fluid with large molecules that stay in vessels longer.

Quick revision points

  • Isotonic: matches blood.
  • Hypotonic: water into cells; hypertonic: water out.
  • Crystalloids are common in theatre.
  • Check label, expiry and clarity.
  • Monitor for overload.

recovery-position-anaesthesia.caption: The recovery position, why it keeps an airway clear, and how it fits with different types of anaesthesia.
recovery-position-anaesthesia.body:
In short: Turning a breathing, unconscious person onto their side lets fluid drain from the mouth and keeps the tongue forward. This card explains when and how.

What the card shows

Four coloured boxes in a two-by-two layout occupy the graphic, with a small figure of me pointing from the top-left corner. Types: general, regional (spinal or epidural), local and conscious sedation. Indication: for an unconscious but breathing person, and after general anaesthesia, where it prevents aspiration and choking. Steps: arm up, knee flexed, turn lateral, head tilted and monitor. Relation: after GA, use the recovery position until awake; after regional, lie supine and monitor blood pressure; after local, if drowsy, place in lateral.

What the recovery position does

Turning an unconscious, breathing person onto their side lets the tongue fall forward and lets fluid drain out of the mouth instead of down the airway. That is how it prevents choking and aspiration.

How the steps work

You place the near arm up, bend the far knee, roll the person towards you onto their side, tilt the head back slightly to keep the airway open and then watch their breathing and colour. It is a first aid skill and also a routine position in the recovery area.

Matching position to anaesthesia

Because the effects differ, so does the position. After a spinal, the legs may be numb and blood pressure may drop, so you monitor closely. If the person is not breathing normally, they need CPR, not the recovery position. Follow your own protocol and training.

The steps and the reason

Kneel beside the person, place the nearer arm at a right angle, bring the far arm across the chest, bend the far knee, then roll them toward you onto their side. Tilt the head back slightly to keep the airway open and adjust the top leg for stability. Recheck breathing, and do not leave them alone.

This stops the tongue falling back and prevents vomit or saliva entering the lungs, a major cause of harm after sedation or anaesthesia.

After anaesthesia

After general anaesthesia, patients are positioned to protect their airway until they wake and respond; different units use side-lying or head-up positions. After spinal anaesthesia, patients often lie flat or with a small head tilt according to local protocol, with blood pressure monitored. After a local anaesthetic, normal positioning applies unless drowsy. If a person is not breathing normally, start CPR instead.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using the recovery position for someone who is not breathing.
  • Leaving the person unattended.
  • Rolling someone with a suspected spinal injury without care.
  • Forgetting to monitor the airway after turning.

Check yourself

Why is the recovery position used?

To keep the airway open and prevent aspiration.

Who should not be placed in it?

Someone who is not breathing normally.

What must you do after turning them?

Keep monitoring breathing.

Quick revision points

  • For unconscious but breathing people.
  • Roll on the side with the head tilted back.
  • Monitor continuously.
  • No breathing means CPR.
  • Follow local anaesthesia recovery protocols.

autoclave.caption: How a steam autoclave sterilises, what its parts do and how to load and monitor it.
autoclave.body:
In short: The autoclave is the workhorse of sterile services. This card explains the principle, parts, cycles and checks.

What the card shows

Six coloured panels stack down the right side of this graphic with me pointing upward on the left: principle (moist heat under pressure, steam at 121 °C and 15 psi kills spores), parts (chamber, lid, pressure gauge, safety valve, heater), types (gravity, prevacuum, high speed), controls (temperature, pressure, time), steam cycle (121 °C for 15 minutes or 134 °C for 3 to 7 minutes) and monitoring (Bowie-Dick test, chemical indicator, biological indicator).

Why steam works

Steam under pressure reaches temperatures higher than boiling water, and moist heat destroys microbial proteins far more efficiently than dry heat. That is why the autoclave is the workhorse of sterilisation for heat-stable instruments, linen and glassware.

Putting the panels together

Think of the autoclave as three questions: what is it doing (principle and cycle), what is it made of (parts and types) and how do we know it worked (controls and monitoring). The Bowie-Dick test checks that a prevacuum machine removes air properly, chemical indicators change colour to show exposure, and biological indicators using spores are the gold standard. Always load loosely, never overload, let loads dry, and record every cycle. Follow your CSSD's own cycle settings.

Loading and safety

Pack items loosely so steam can circulate, place containers with openings facing down and never overload the chamber. Let the pressure return to zero before opening the lid, and allow loads to dry before storing. Wear heat-resistant gloves and follow your CSSD's own cycle settings and records.

Why steam under pressure

Water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. Under pressure it boils at a higher temperature, and steam at 121 °C or 134 °C kills even resistant spores. Moist heat coagulates proteins in microbes much faster than dry heat. The steam must reach every surface, so air has to be removed, which is why pre-vacuum machines pull a vacuum first and gravity displacement machines rely on steam pushing air out.

Typical cycles are 121 °C for around 15 to 30 minutes or 134 °C for 3 to 18 minutes, depending on the load and the machine.

Loading, running and monitoring

Items must be cleaned and dry before packing. Pack loosely so steam can circulate. Place heavy items at the bottom and do not stack. Run the right cycle for the load. Check the printout, the chemical indicators and, as scheduled, biological indicators and Bowie-Dick tests. Allow packs to cool and dry before handling, and store them in clean areas. Wear heat protection and follow the manufacturer's instructions.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Overloading the chamber.
  • Opening the door too soon.
  • Packing wet items.
  • Failing to record cycle details.

Check yourself

What temperature is used in a standard cycle?

121 °C or 134 °C.

Why remove air from the chamber?

Trapped air blocks steam contact.

What is the gold standard monitor?

The biological indicator.

Quick revision points

  • Steam under pressure kills spores.
  • Clean and dry items first.
  • Load loosely.
  • Use Bowie-Dick, chemical and biological indicators.
  • Record every cycle.

how-baby-s-sex-is-determined.caption: How chromosomes decide a baby's sex, and what happens when the usual pattern varies.
how-baby-s-sex-is-determined.body:
In short: Sex is determined at fertilisation by the sex chromosome carried by the sperm. This card shows the main combinations and some variations.

What the card shows

A table of chromosome combinations runs down the right of this graphic, each row showing a sperm, an egg and the result. Y sperm plus X egg gives XY, a typical male (46,XY). X sperm plus X egg gives XX, a typical female (46,XX). Other rows show variations: an XY sperm gives XXY, a male with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY); a YY sperm gives XYY (47,XYY); a sperm with no sex chromosome gives X, Turner syndrome (45,X); and an XX sperm gives XXX (47,XXX). The footer sums it up: the sperm decides, because the egg always contributes an X.

The main idea

Every egg carries an X chromosome. A sperm carries either an X or a Y. If an X sperm fertilises the egg the baby is XX, and if a Y sperm does the baby is XY. That is why the father's sperm determines the baby's sex.

About the variations

The extra rows show what happens when chromosomes do not separate properly during sperm formation. These are called sex chromosome aneuploidies, and they are not caused by anything a parent did. People with them can have a range of health needs and live full lives, with support from the right care team. The typical pairings XX and XY are the ones to learn first, and the 46 and 47 numbers show the total chromosome count.

The basics

Humans typically have 46 chromosomes, including two sex chromosomes. Eggs carry one X. Sperm carry either an X or a Y. An X sperm gives XX, typically female; a Y sperm gives XY, typically male. The SRY gene on the Y chromosome starts the development of male characteristics.

Sometimes chromosomes do not separate properly, giving combinations such as XXY (Klinefelter syndrome), X (Turner syndrome) or XYY and XXX. People with these variations can have different health needs and often live full lives with appropriate care and support.

Why theatre and clinical students should know

Understanding chromosomes helps with genetics, fertility and obstetric conditions, and it encourages respectful language with patients and families. Questions about sex and gender can arise in sensitive situations: use accurate, kind language and keep information confidential.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Saying the mother determines sex.
  • Using stigmatising words for people with chromosome variations.
  • Forgetting the SRY gene.
  • Treating variations as 'mistakes' of parents.

Check yourself

Who determines the baby's sex chromosomes?

The sperm, since eggs always carry X.

What does XXY indicate?

Klinefelter syndrome.

What is the SRY gene?

A gene on the Y chromosome that triggers male development.

Quick revision points

  • Eggs carry X; sperm carry X or Y.
  • XX typically female; XY typically male.
  • Variations occur from uneven chromosome division.
  • Use respectful, accurate language.
  • Keep patient information confidential.

perioperative-care.caption: The whole surgical journey: preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative care and the supports that run through all three.
perioperative-care.body:
In short: Perioperative care means everything before, during and after an operation. This hub card links the three phases to theatre zones, sterilisation and safety checks.

What the card shows

Six coloured boxes in a two-by-three grid sit beside me, with my hands pressed together in front of my chest. 1 Preoperative phase: assessment, consent, NPO (nothing by mouth), vitals and skin prep. 2 Intraoperative phase: WHO checklist, positioning, scrubbing, gowning and gloving. 3 Postoperative phase: recovery, vitals, pain and wound care. 4 Theatre zones: clean, sterile, protective and disposal. 5 Sterilisation: autoclave, ETO, dry heat and chemical. 6 Safety: counts, time-out and sign-in or sign-out.

The three phases

Perioperative care covers everything before, during and after surgery. The first three boxes are the phases in order, and the last three are the supports that run through all of them: the layout of the theatre, how instruments are made safe and the checks that keep the patient safe.

Why it is one idea, not three

A good operation can be spoiled by poor preparation, and good preparation can be wasted by weak recovery care. Hand-offs between phases are where mistakes creep in, so clear communication at each transfer matters most. NPO status, consent and allergies are checked on arrival, repeated at sign-in and handed over again in recovery.

How to study it

Learn the three phases first, then hang the other boxes onto them. This card is the hub, and the Intraoperative Phase, Postoperative Phase, Theatre Zones and WHO Surgical Safety Checklist cards are the spokes.

Why one continuous pathway

Preparation before surgery shapes how well the operation goes, and recovery care determines how well the patient does afterwards. Each handover, from ward to theatre, theatre to recovery and recovery to ward, is a point where information can be lost. Good communication at those points is as important as technical skill.

The phases share common themes: identity checks, allergies, consent, fasting status, infection prevention and clear documentation.

How to use this card as a student

Learn the three phases first, then hang the other topics on them. Under preoperative care: assessment, consent, fasting, medicines, skin preparation. Under intraoperative care: checklist, positioning, asepsis, counts, safety. Under postoperative care: recovery, pain, wound, fluids, discharge. The Theatre Zones, Sterilisation and Safety boxes are the foundations that support all three phases.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating each phase as someone else's job.
  • Skipping the handover details.
  • Forgetting that allergies must be checked at every stage.
  • Ignoring post-operative care in your learning.

Check yourself

Name the three phases.

Preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative.

Where do most communication failures happen?

At handovers between phases.

What are checked at every stage?

Identity, allergies and consent.

Quick revision points

  • Perioperative = before, during and after surgery.
  • Handovers need clear communication.
  • Safety checks run through all phases.
  • Zones and sterilisation support the whole pathway.
  • Everyone shares responsibility.

surgical-hand-scrub-gowning.caption: The full sequence from scrub to drying, gowning and gloving, with the golden rule.
surgical-hand-scrub-gowning.body:
In short: Scrubbing, gowning and gloving are one chain: a mistake early on carries through to the end. This card shows the whole sequence.

What the card shows

Six coloured bars run down the right of this graphic, with me pointing at them, and a green Golden Rule box underneath. 1 Preparation: remove jewellery, short nails and put on PPE. 2 Scrub: five minutes with chlorhexidine, anatomical method. 3 Rinsing: hands up, elbows down, no touching. 4 Drying: sterile towel, one hand per side. 5 Gowning: sterile gown by the closed method. 6 Gloving: closed gloving with no contamination. The Golden Rule says scrub from clean to dirty, go from fingertips to elbows and never drop your hands below the waist, because sterility is your shield.

One sequence from start to finish

This card joins three skills into one flow: scrub, then dry, then gown and glove. Each step protects the next, so a mistake early on carries through. If your hand drops below the waist or touches the tap after scrubbing, you must start again.

The towel

Dry one hand with one end of the towel and the other hand with a separate part, working from fingertips to elbow and never moving back. Drop the towel without touching the outside of the gown.

Related cards

For more on each part, see the Hand Scrub Technique card, the Sterile Gowning Technique card and the Sterile Gloving Technique card. Scrub durations and antiseptic choices vary with hospital policy.

A chain, not separate tasks

Scrub reduces the germs on the hands. Drying with a sterile towel must not undo that. Gowning is done with the hands inside the sleeves so the outside of the gown is never touched by skin. Closed gloving keeps the cuff covering the hand until the glove is on, so skin never touches the glove's outside.

If any link in the chain is broken, for example the hand touches the tap or the outside of the gown, the person must start that part again.

Practice makes sterile

These steps feel awkward at first. Practise in the skills lab with an old gown and gloves. Ask a partner to watch for errors. Work slowly and think 'clean to dirty'. When something goes wrong, say so; changing a glove or gown costs seconds, while an infection costs far more.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Drying the hands in the wrong direction.
  • Touching the outside of the gown with bare skin.
  • Rushing gloves and tearing them.
  • Continuing after contamination.

Check yourself

What is the golden rule of scrubbing?

Scrub from clean to less clean and keep hands above elbows.

Why use closed gloving?

So bare skin never touches the glove's outside.

What should you do after contamination?

Declare it and change or re-scrub.

Quick revision points

  • Scrub, dry, gown, glove in order.
  • Hands up, elbows down.
  • Closed method for gown and gloves.
  • Declare contamination immediately.
  • Follow local antiseptic and time rules.

normal-vital-signs.caption: The six vital signs and their typical adult ranges, and why trends matter.
normal-vital-signs.body:
In short: Vital signs give a quick picture of how the body is coping. This card lists six and their normal values.

What the card shows

Six rounded coloured cards run down the right of this graphic, with me holding a clipboard on the left. Temperature: 36.5 to 37.5 °C (97.7 to 99.5 °F). Pulse: 60 to 100 beats per minute. Blood pressure: 120/80 mmHg. Respiratory rate: 12 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation: 95 to 100 per cent. Pain: a 0 to 10 scale where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst pain. The footer says "Know your baseline, early detection saves lives".

Reading the numbers

These are ranges for a healthy adult at rest. A single reading means less than a trend, so what you want to see is how the numbers move over time, and whether they differ from the patient's own baseline.

Why a baseline helps

Some people always run a slow pulse or a lower blood pressure, and an athlete's heart rate can sit below 60 without any problem. Knowing the usual figure lets you spot a real change early. Pain is included as the fifth vital sign in many hospitals because it guides treatment and recovery.

What to do with abnormal readings

Report them, recheck with a good technique and record the time. Ranges differ for children, older adults and in pregnancy, and slightly between references: this card gives 36.5 to 37.5 °C for temperature, while the Body Temperature card uses 36.1 to 37.7 °C for the normal band. Follow your hospital's escalation chart.

What each sign tells you

Temperature shows infection, inflammation or heat loss. Pulse shows heart rate and rhythm. Blood pressure shows the pressure that drives blood through tissues. Respiratory rate is often the first sign that a patient is becoming unwell. Oxygen saturation shows how much haemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Pain is assessed because it affects recovery and signals complications.

Using a scoring system, such as an early warning score, helps teams decide when to escalate.

Measuring correctly

Use the right equipment and technique: the correct cuff size, a rested patient, a warm finger for the pulse oximeter, counting breaths for a full minute without telling the patient. Record the time, the site and any abnormal findings, and act on them. A single reading is less important than the trend over time compared with the patient's baseline.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Telling the patient you are counting their breaths.
  • Using the wrong blood pressure cuff.
  • Trusting a pulse oximeter on cold or painted fingers.
  • Recording but not reporting abnormal values.

Check yourself

What is a typical adult pulse range?

About 60 to 100 beats per minute.

Which vital sign often changes first in deterioration?

Respiratory rate.

Why compare with baseline?

Normal varies between people.

Quick revision points

  • Six signs: temperature, pulse, BP, respirations, SpO2, pain.
  • Trends matter more than single readings.
  • Use the correct technique and equipment.
  • Report abnormal values.
  • Know local escalation rules.

family-planning-methods-explained.caption: Six groups of family planning methods and how they compare for effectiveness and protection.
family-planning-methods-explained.body:
In short: Family planning lets people choose whether and when to have children. This card shows the main categories of method.

What the card shows

Six colour-coded boxes with icons fill the right of this graphic: 1 natural (calendar method, withdrawal, lactational amenorrhoea), 2 barrier (male condoms, female condoms, diaphragm), 3 hormonal (pills, injectables such as Depo, implants such as Jadelle), 4 IUD (Copper T 380A and hormonal Mirena), 5 permanent (vasectomy, tubal ligation) and 6 emergency (P2 within 72 hours, plus counselling). A blue strip at the bottom states the WHO idea: family planning helps people choose the number of children and spacing of births, which improves maternal and child health.

How the groups compare

Long-acting methods such as implants, IUDs and permanent methods are the most effective because they do not depend on remembering anything daily. Pills and injectables are effective when used on time. Barrier methods are less reliable but condoms are the only option here that also lowers the risk of sexually transmitted infections. Natural methods depend heavily on correct use and are the least reliable.

Why theatre students need this

Tubal ligation, vasectomy and IUD insertion or removal may all appear on the list. Counselling and informed consent matter as much as the procedure. Everyone's body, health and plans differ, so the right method is one chosen with a trained provider, not from a poster alone.

How the methods differ

Long-acting reversible methods such as implants and IUDs are among the most effective, because they do not depend on daily action. Hormonal methods such as pills and injectables work well when used on schedule. Barrier methods such as condoms prevent sperm reaching the egg, and condoms also reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections. Natural methods rely on tracking fertility and are less reliable. Permanent methods, vasectomy and tubal ligation, are intended for people who do not want more children. Emergency contraception can be used soon after unprotected sex.

Each method has benefits, side effects and medical eligibility rules.

Counselling and consent

Choosing a method is a personal decision made with accurate information, respect and privacy. A trained provider asks about health, plans and preferences, explains how to use the method and what side effects to expect, and gives follow-up information. Surgical methods require informed consent and are performed by trained staff in suitable facilities. Theatre staff should treat these patients with dignity and confidentiality.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Believing one method is best for everyone.
  • Skipping counselling.
  • Assuming condoms are unnecessary with other methods when infection risk exists.
  • Pressuring anyone into a decision.

Check yourself

Which methods are most effective?

Implants, IUDs and permanent methods.

Which method also reduces STI risk?

Condoms.

What is needed before sterilisation?

Informed consent and counselling.

Quick revision points

  • Six groups: natural, barrier, hormonal, IUD, permanent, emergency.
  • Long-acting methods are most effective.
  • Condoms protect against STIs.
  • Counselling and consent are essential.
  • Respect privacy and choice.

sterile-field-why-it-matters.caption: A patient-friendly explanation of the sterile field and the infection-prevention steps around surgery.
sterile-field-why-it-matters.body:
In short: Patients and families often wonder what makes an operating theatre 'sterile'. This card answers six simple questions.

What the card shows

Six question cards in different pastel colours run down the right of this graphic, with me standing calmly on the left. Q1 asks what a sterile field is: a clean area free of germs around the operation site. Q2 asks why it matters: it helps prevent infection and protects the patient. Q3 asks who maintains it: the scrub nurse and surgical team following strict steps. Q4 asks what sterile technique is: hand washing, gowns, gloves and sterile instruments. Q5 asks what the patient should know: the team checks and maintains it throughout. Q6 asks about your role: follow instructions and ask the team about safety.

Written for patients as well

The question format makes it friendly for families. Surgery is a big step, and understanding that a team is working to keep the area clean can reduce worry.

What patients can do

Follow the pre-operative instructions about washing and clipping hair, do not touch the surgical area or the dressings, tell staff if something looks wrong and ask questions. It is not rude to ask the team whether hands were cleaned or whether antibiotics were given if that was in your plan.

What the team does

Hands are scrubbed, sterile gowns and gloves are worn, instruments are sterilised and the field is draped, and everyone watches it for the whole operation. The goal is to prevent surgical site infection. See the Sterile Field Principles card for the student version.

What the sterile field is

The sterile field is the area around the operation site that is covered with sterile drapes and contains only sterile instruments and sterile people. Anything that enters it must be sterile. The rest of the room is clean but not sterile, and the team works carefully to keep the two separate.

The goal is to prevent surgical site infections, which can cause pain, longer stays and sometimes serious illness.

What patients can do

Follow instructions on washing, hair removal and fasting; do not shave the area yourself unless told; tell the team about any skin problems, infections or allergies; keep dressings dry and untouched; and ask questions. Families can help by washing hands, not visiting when unwell and following ward rules. Hospital teams also give antibiotics at the right time when they are needed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Shaving the surgical site at home with a razor.
  • Touching or scratching a wound dressing.
  • Not telling staff about a skin infection.
  • Visiting while ill.

Check yourself

What is a surgical site infection?

An infection of the wound or deeper tissues after surgery.

Who maintains the sterile field?

The scrubbed team.

What can patients do to reduce risk?

Follow washing and fasting instructions and keep the wound clean.

Quick revision points

  • Sterile field = sterile drapes, instruments and people.
  • Purpose: prevent surgical site infection.
  • The team maintains it throughout.
  • Patients follow preparation instructions.
  • Ask questions.

medicines-and-allergies-checklist.caption: A pre-surgery checklist of what to tell the team about medicines, allergies and past anaesthesia.
medicines-and-allergies-checklist.body:
In short: The team can only protect you from risks they know about. This card shows six things to prepare before your operation.

What the card shows

Six question cards in different pastel colours sit beside me, with my hand on my hip. Q1 asks what medicines to list, and the answer is all prescriptions, vitamins and supplements. Q2 asks about allergies: medicines, food and latex reactions. Q3 asks about past anaesthesia, including any problems or family history. Q4 asks about health conditions such as heart, lung and diabetes. Q5 asks who to tell: the surgeon, anaesthetist and nurse. Q6 asks when to update the list, which is any time something changes or you start a new medicine. The footer says every question matters, so write them down and ask your team.

Why it matters before surgery

Some medicines change bleeding risk, some interact with anaesthetic drugs and some need to be stopped or continued on a specific day. An allergy to latex, an antibiotic or an anaesthetic can be life-threatening if the team does not know.

How to prepare

Write down every medicine with its dose, including herbal products and over-the-counter tablets. Note any allergy and what happened. Mention anything that went wrong in an earlier anaesthetic, or in a relative's. Bring the list on the day and repeat it to each member of the team, because each one asks for a different reason. Do not stop any medicine on your own, as the team will tell you which ones to take. This is a general education card, not a personal medical instruction.

Why each item matters

Some medicines thin the blood, affect blood pressure, interact with anaesthetic drugs or must be continued or paused on specific days. Allergies to latex, antibiotics, adhesives or foods linked to certain drugs can cause severe reactions. A past problem with anaesthesia or a family history of one may change the plan. Long-term conditions such as diabetes, asthma or heart disease affect the plan and the risk.

Herbal products and supplements can also affect bleeding and drug action.

How to prepare

Write a list: medicine names, doses and times, including herbal and over-the-counter ones. Note allergies and what reaction you had. Write down earlier anaesthetic problems. Bring the list and any medicine boxes to the hospital. Repeat the information at each stage; it is normal to be asked many times. Ask which medicines to take on the day of surgery and never decide alone.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Forgetting herbal medicines.
  • Saying 'no allergies' when unsure.
  • Stopping heart or blood pressure tablets without advice.
  • Not mentioning family problems with anaesthesia.

Check yourself

Why include supplements?

They can affect bleeding or interact with drugs.

What should you do about medicines on the day of surgery?

Follow the team's instructions.

Who needs to know about allergies?

Everyone in the team: surgeon, anaesthetist and nurses.

Quick revision points

  • List all medicines and supplements.
  • Report allergies and reactions.
  • Mention past anaesthesia problems.
  • Do not stop medicines on your own.
  • Expect to be asked repeatedly.

theatre-etiquette.caption: Six behaviours that make a theatre safer and a student more welcome.
theatre-etiquette.body:
In short: Etiquette in theatre is about safety, respect and communication. This card turns that into six habits.

What the card shows

Six numbered coloured bars run down the right of this graphic, with me standing straight on the left. 1 Entry: change, wear a mask and cap and use clean shoes before entering. 2 Movement: minimal traffic, be quiet and face the sterile field. 3 Sterility: do not touch sterile areas and keep your hands above the waist in front. 4 Communication: speak clearly, ask before touching and declare breaks. 5 Respect: teamwork, punctuality, phone away, observe and learn. 6 Safety: follow the checklist, report concerns and maintain focus. A footer reads learn, practise, safety first.

Why etiquette is more than manners

Every rule on the card has a safety reason. Fewer people moving means less air disturbance and fewer chances of contamination. Quiet means clear communication. Phones away means attention stays on the patient.

Communication in a tense room

Speak clearly and use the person's role or name. Repeat back instructions, especially for drugs and counts. If you notice something wrong, say so politely and early. A good team culture lets the most junior person speak up without fear.

Small habits

Arrive early, introduce yourself, learn the team's names and thank people. If you do not know what to do, ask during a quiet moment. The six points here are a short version of the larger set in the Inside the Operating Theatre series, so use them together.

Why the rules exist

Moving less means less air disturbance and fewer chances of contamination. Speaking quietly and clearly helps critical information be heard. Keeping hands where they can be seen prevents accidental contamination. Phones are distractions and infection risks. Courtesy builds a team in which people feel able to speak up about danger.

Etiquette also covers punctuality, appearance and willingness to learn.

Habits of a good student

Arrive early and ready. Introduce yourself to the team. Ask permission before moving close or touching anything. Keep to your role. Observe quietly and note questions to ask later. Say thank you. Admit when you do not know something. Respect patient dignity at all times; remember that the patient cannot speak for themselves under anaesthesia.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Chatting loudly during critical moments.
  • Using a phone in theatre.
  • Wandering around the room.
  • Not introducing yourself.

Check yourself

Why limit movement in theatre?

To reduce air disturbance and contamination.

When should you ask questions?

At a safe, quiet moment, not during critical steps.

Why keep phones out?

They distract and can carry germs.

Quick revision points

  • Dress and enter correctly.
  • Move less and speak clearly.
  • Do not touch sterile items.
  • Phones away.
  • Respect every member of the team.

after-surgery-what-to-expect.caption: What patients can expect after an operation and the questions to ask before going home.
after-surgery-what-to-expect.body:
In short: Recovery is easier when you know what to expect. This card gives six questions for patients and families.

What the card shows

Six pastel question cards sit beside me on this graphic, each numbered and each with one short answer line. Q1 asks how you will feel afterwards (grogginess is common, so ask the team what to expect). Q2 covers pain and the pain plan. Q3 is about when you can eat, drink and move. Q4 is which warning signs to report and who to call. Q5 asks who helps at home. Q6 asks when the follow-up visit is. The footer says every question matters, so write them down and ask your team.

Why I built it as questions

Patients often feel too groggy or too nervous to ask anything useful in the recovery area. Turning the topic into questions gives families a ready script they can read on their phone or write on paper before the day.

What the team is actually watching

In recovery, staff check breathing, blood pressure, pulse, wound, pain and nausea at regular intervals. Eating and moving are usually restarted in steps, not all at once. Warning signs such as heavy bleeding, fever, worsening pain, or a swollen, red wound should be reported early. This is general education only. Your own surgical team's instructions always come first, and a written discharge plan with a contact number is the best safety net you can have.

What recovery looks like

Many patients feel drowsy, sore, thirsty or sick after anaesthesia. Staff watch breathing, blood pressure, pulse, temperature, pain and the wound. Pain relief, anti-sickness drugs and oxygen are given as needed. Eating and drinking restart gradually, and walking is encouraged early unless there is a reason not to.

Patients go home when they meet the unit's criteria, which usually include being awake, stable, able to drink and with controlled pain.

Questions to ask before leaving

How long will pain last and what can I take? How do I care for the wound and when is it dry or changed? When can I eat, bathe, drive or return to work? What warning signs should make me call or return? Who can help me at home? When is my follow-up appointment? Write down the answers or ask for a written copy and phone number.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving without written instructions.
  • Going home alone after anaesthesia when someone should stay.
  • Ignoring warning signs.
  • Stopping pain medicine too early or taking too much.

Check yourself

Why ask for written instructions?

People forget information when drowsy.

Name a warning sign after surgery.

Fever, spreading redness, heavy bleeding or worsening pain.

Who should be with you at home?

A responsible adult, especially the first night.

Quick revision points

  • Expect drowsiness and some pain.
  • Ask for a written plan.
  • Know the warning signs.
  • Arrange help at home.
  • Keep follow-up appointments.

safe-recovery-at-home.caption: Practical guidance for caring for yourself or a family member at home after surgery.
safe-recovery-at-home.body:
In short: Most recovery happens at home. This post sets out the basics of wound care, pain control, movement, food and warning signs.

Going home after surgery is a milestone, but the first days away from the ward are when small problems can grow if nobody notices them. This post sets out the basics that most discharge plans cover, so a patient and their family know what to look for before they leave.

Before you leave the hospital

Ask for the instructions in writing: how to care for the wound, which medicines to take and when, which activities to avoid and for how long, and a phone number to call if worried. Check that someone will be with you for the first night or two, and that you know the date of the follow-up visit. Collect any dressings or supplies you need.

Wound, pain and movement

Keep the dressing clean and dry unless told otherwise, and wash your hands before and after touching it. Take pain medicine as prescribed, because pain that is controlled lets you breathe deeply and move, which helps to prevent chest and clot problems. Gentle walking is usually encouraged, but lifting and strenuous work are not, until the surgeon says so.

Signs to report

Contact your team if you notice a fever, spreading redness, pus, a bad smell, a wound that opens, bleeding that soaks the dressing, worsening pain, a swollen painful leg, shortness of breath or persistent vomiting. In an emergency, go to the nearest hospital straight away.

Eating and rest

Eat regular, balanced meals with protein and plenty of fluids, and rest when tired. This is general education, and your surgeon's instructions always take priority.

Common sense that prevents problems

Keep the dressing clean and dry and follow instructions on when to change it. Wash hands before and after touching it. Take prescribed medicines as directed; do not skip antibiotics if prescribed and do not share medicines. Drink fluids and eat balanced meals with enough protein. Walk gently as advised, which lowers the risk of clots and chest problems. Avoid smoking and alcohol while healing.

Sleep and rest also help the body repair.

When to seek help

Contact the team or go to the nearest facility for fever, a wound that is more painful, red, swollen or leaking pus, bleeding that soaks the dressing, a hot swollen calf, breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled vomiting or confusion. In an emergency, do not wait. Keep contact numbers handy and follow the discharge plan.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Delaying care because of fear or cost.
  • Removing dressings too early.
  • Lifting heavy items against advice.
  • Smoking during recovery.

Check yourself

Why is gentle walking encouraged?

It lowers the risk of blood clots and chest problems.

Name two warning signs.

Fever and pus or spreading redness.

What should you do if worried?

Contact the team or go to the nearest facility.

Quick revision points

  • Follow the written discharge plan.
  • Keep the wound clean and dry.
  • Eat well, drink fluids, rest.
  • Walk gently and avoid heavy lifting.
  • Know when to get help.

day-of-surgery-checklist.caption: What to expect and what to do on the day of an operation.
day-of-surgery-checklist.body:
In short: Many cancellations are avoidable. This card gives six questions that help patients arrive ready.

What the card shows

Six pastel question cards line up beside me on this graphic, with my arms folded and a calm expression to set the tone. Q1 asks what happens at check-in (ID, consent, questions and an allergy check). Q2 covers what to wear (loose clothes, no jewellery, and following the instructions you were given). Q3 asks whether you can eat or drink and tells you to follow your fasting instructions. Q4 asks who stays with you and suggests a support person and contact plan. Q5 lists what the team will check: vitals, site marking and safety checks. Q6 reminds you that you can ask questions any time and should write them down.

Why this matters

Most last-minute cancellations come from small things: someone ate when they should not have, jewellery was left on, or the family could not be reached. A simple checklist the night before prevents those.

What the team is doing behind the scenes

At check-in staff confirm identity, the planned procedure, the consent form and allergies. Site marking is done when the operation involves a side or a specific place. Vital signs give a baseline for the anaesthetist. As a student I notice how calm patients become when they know the order of events, so take a moment to explain what happens next. Always follow your own hospital's written instructions.

A typical day of surgery

You will be asked to confirm your name, the planned operation, any allergies and when you last ate or drank. A nurse checks vital signs, and the surgeon or anaesthetist may see you. The site may be marked. You change into a gown, remove jewellery, dentures and contact lenses as asked, and walk or are wheeled to theatre. In theatre you meet the team, who confirm your details again before anaesthesia.

Being asked the same questions repeatedly is part of safety, not a sign of disorganisation.

Prepare the night before

Follow fasting instructions exactly. Take only the medicines the team approved. Pack comfortable clothes, your medicine list, ID, insurance details and phone numbers. Arrange transport and a support person. Do not wear makeup, nail polish or jewellery. If you are unwell with a cough, fever or infection, call the hospital because surgery may need to be delayed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Eating or drinking after being told to fast.
  • Forgetting to bring the medicine list.
  • Wearing jewellery or nail polish.
  • Not mentioning a new illness.

Check yourself

Why are you asked the same questions many times?

Repeated checks prevent errors.

Why follow fasting rules?

Food or fluid in the stomach can enter the lungs during anaesthesia.

What should you tell the team if you have a new fever?

Call before coming; surgery may need rescheduling.

Quick revision points

  • Arrive on time with ID and medicine list.
  • Follow fasting instructions.
  • Remove jewellery and nail polish.
  • Expect repeated safety checks.
  • Bring a support person.

anatomy-pop-quiz.caption: Six quick anatomy facts every health student should know, with a short explanation of each.
anatomy-pop-quiz.body:
In short: Quick recall of core facts builds confidence and speed. This card tests six basics.

What the card shows

Six quiz cards in different pastel colours are lined up beside me, each showing a question with its answer: how many bones in an adult (206), the largest organ (skin), how many heart chambers (4), the longest bone (femur), approximate blood volume (about 5 litres) and how many lobes the right lung has (3). The footer reads "Think fast • Anatomy recall • Quick revision for nurses".

Why quick recall works

These are the facts everyone is expected to know cold, and that is exactly why they are good for testing yourself. The goal is speed. Cover the answers, say yours aloud, then check. Anything you hesitate on goes onto your revision list.

A little extra on each answer

The 206 count is for adults; babies have more bones that fuse over time. Skin is the largest organ by surface area and weight. The heart has four chambers, two atria and two ventricles. The femur is the longest and strongest bone. An average adult carries roughly five litres of blood, though this varies with size. The right lung has three lobes, while the left has two to leave room for the heart. If you can add one extra fact to each answer, you are no longer just recalling, you are understanding, and that is what exam questions reward.

The six facts and a little more

The adult skeleton has 206 bones. The skin is the largest organ and acts as a barrier, temperature regulator and sensor. The heart has four chambers: right and left atria and right and left ventricles. The femur is the longest and strongest bone. The average adult has about 5 litres of blood. The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, leaving room for the heart.

These facts anchor bigger topics: bones link to orthopaedics, skin to wound healing, heart chambers to circulation and blood volume to transfusion.

Using quizzes to learn

Cover the answer, say yours aloud, then check. Write the ones you miss on a card for tomorrow. Add one extra fact to each answer, such as what the skin layers are or which side of the heart pumps to the lungs. Quizzes work best when repeated over days and when you explain answers in your own words.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Memorising numbers without understanding.
  • Mixing up left and right lung lobes.
  • Forgetting that bone count changes with age.
  • Only quizzing yourself once.

Check yourself

How many chambers does the heart have?

Four.

Which lung has two lobes?

The left.

What is the longest bone?

The femur.

Quick revision points

  • 206 bones in an adult.
  • Skin is the largest organ.
  • Heart: 4 chambers.
  • Femur: longest bone.
  • Blood volume about 5 litres; right lung 3 lobes.

sterile-field-principles.caption: Six principles for creating, maintaining and recovering a sterile field.
sterile-field-principles.body:
In short: Sterile technique follows simple rules that everyone in the room must know. This card lists six of them for students.

What the card shows

Six numbered coloured bars run down the right of this graphic, with me holding a clipboard on the left. 1 Definition: a sterile field is an area free of microbes, created around the surgical site. 2 Boundaries: only sterile touches sterile, and the table level and above is sterile. 3 Movement: face the sterile field, do not turn your back and keep your hands in sight. 4 If contaminated: declare it immediately and re-establish sterility. 5 Common breaks: reaching over a non-sterile item and contact below the waist. 6 Student tips: scrub correctly, gown and glove properly, and watch and ask. The footer says learn, practise, safety first.

The core rule

Anything below the level of the table is treated as non-sterile, because it cannot be watched. That is why instruments are never dropped over the edge and then picked up, and why a sterile drape that hangs below the table is treated as contaminated.

Declaring a break

Nobody gets in trouble for saying "that is contaminated". The danger is in hiding it, because the patient pays for it afterwards with an infection. Re-establish the field by replacing the item or the drape.

How to use this card

Say the six words aloud: definition, boundaries, movement, contamination, breaks, tips. Then connect it to the Maintaining the Sterile Field card in the Inside the Operating Theatre series.

The rules and their logic

Sterile touches sterile only: if a sterile item touches an unsterile one, it is contaminated. Only the table surface and above is considered sterile because what is below cannot be seen. A sterile gown is sterile in front from chest to waist level and on the sleeves; the back, neck, shoulders and below the waist are not. Edges of packs and the one-inch border of a drape are considered contaminated. Face the field and keep your hands in sight.

When in doubt, consider it contaminated.

If sterility is broken

Speak up straight away. Replace the item, change gloves or gown, or re-drape. Never hide a break. Remember that time and traffic also affect sterility: events such as long exposure and many people moving around raise risk. Package integrity and expiry matter before opening.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Reaching across the sterile field.
  • Turning your back on the field.
  • Dropping an instrument below the table and using it.
  • Failing to report a possible break.

Check yourself

What is sterile on a gown?

The front from chest to waist and the sleeves.

What should you do if unsure about sterility?

Treat it as contaminated.

Why not use items that fall below table level?

They cannot be watched and are considered non-sterile.

Quick revision points

  • Sterile touches sterile.
  • Table level and above only.
  • Face the field.
  • Say 'contaminated' immediately.
  • When in doubt, replace it.

inside-the-operating-theatre.caption: Who is in the operating theatre, what each person does and where you fit as a student.
inside-the-operating-theatre.body:
In short: The operating theatre team is bigger than most people think. This opening card shows the main roles and how they work together.

What the card shows

Six pastel cards beside me list who is in the operating theatre and what they do. 1 Surgeon: performs the operation and leads the plan. 2 Anaesthesia team: monitors the patient and keeps them safe and comfortable. 3 Scrub nurse: maintains the sterile field and passes instruments. 4 Circulating nurse: coordinates safety checks and documentation. 5 Safety checks: ID, consent, site marking and teamwork. 6 You are central: every question matters, so ask your team. The footer says "Every patient matters, teamwork, safety first".

How the roles fit together

The surgeon decides what to do, the anaesthesia team keeps the patient alive and pain-free, the scrub nurse works inside the sterile field and the circulating nurse works outside it, fetching, recording and checking. The patient is the sixth and most important member of the team, which is why the card says you are central.

Why I made it the opening card

Students often arrive without knowing whom to ask for what. Knowing the roles helps you ask the right person at the right time, and it shows how many people it takes to keep one operation safe. The roles may be named a little differently in your hospital, for example theatre technologist or operating department practitioner, but the idea is the same. Use this as the first page for the whole Inside the Operating Theatre series.

A closer look at each role

The surgeon leads the operation and makes surgical decisions. The anaesthetist or anaesthesia team keeps the patient asleep or comfortable, monitors vital signs and manages the airway, fluids and drugs. The scrub practitioner works in the sterile field, prepares instruments, passes them and keeps counts. The circulating practitioner works outside the sterile field, opening supplies, labelling specimens, fetching items, documenting and communicating. Assistants, theatre technologists, porters, cleaners, radiographers and others also support each case.

The patient is the centre of everything: every role exists to keep them safe.

How to behave and learn

Introduce yourself, learn names and roles, and ask who to ask for what. Ask the circulating practitioner where to stand. Watch how team members communicate: short, clear, closed-loop messages. Ask questions during quiet moments. Remember that titles differ between hospitals, but the functions are the same.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming the surgeon is the only decision maker.
  • Not knowing who to ask for help.
  • Standing in the way of the circulating practitioner.
  • Not learning team members' names.

Check yourself

Who works inside the sterile field?

The surgeon, assistants and scrub practitioner.

What does the circulating practitioner do?

Supports with supplies, counts, documentation and communication outside the sterile field.

Who is the most important team member?

The patient.

Quick revision points

  • Surgeon, anaesthesia team, scrub, circulating.
  • Each role protects the patient.
  • Learn names and roles.
  • Ask at the right moment.
  • Teamwork and communication are safety tools.

inside-the-operating-theatre-ppe-donning.caption: Putting on and taking off PPE in theatre, including the common mistakes.
inside-the-operating-theatre-ppe-donning.body:
In short: Theatre PPE protects you and the patient. This card shows the order for putting on and removing it and what to avoid.

What the card shows

The banner says "Always: don before patient, doff after, remove slowly, hand hygiene between". Donning Order lists hand hygiene, gown, cap, mask and eye protection, gloves, a fit check with no gaps and a buddy check with a mirror. Doffing Order lists gloves (peeling inside out), gown (peeling inside out), hand hygiene, removing cap and mask, eye protection, hand hygiene again, no touching the face and disposing in the correct bin. In Theatre PPE adds: scrub cap always, mask over nose and mouth and changed daily, eye protection when there is a splash risk, gloves for body fluids, double gloving for scrub, an apron when washing instruments and no PPE outside theatre.

Why doffing is the risky part

The outside of used PPE is contaminated, and people usually touch their face or clothes while removing it. Slow, deliberate movements and hand hygiene between steps are what keep you safe.

Common errors and habits

Doffing too fast, touching the face with gloves, reusing a mask, wearing PPE in the cafeteria, taking things off in the wrong order and leaving a gown on outside theatre. Learn the donning poster, check each other, fit-check masks, change PPE immediately if contaminated and put it in the correct bin, never a litter bin. Your hospital's doffing sequence may differ slightly, so follow its protocol.

Why order matters

When you put PPE on, you build layers from the cleanest to the working surface: hand hygiene, gown, mask, eye protection, then gloves over the gown cuffs. When you take PPE off, the outside is contaminated, so you remove the dirtiest items first and finish with hand hygiene. Moving slowly avoids touching your face or clothes with contaminated surfaces.

In theatre, surgical masks protect the patient from the wearer's droplets and protect the wearer from splashes; respirators are used for airborne infections according to policy.

Check and correct

Use a buddy or mirror to check fit: the mask covers nose and mouth, caps cover all hair, goggles seal, no skin gaps. Replace wet or torn PPE. Discard in the correct bin. Do not wear theatre PPE outside the theatre complex.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Pulling a mask down under the chin.
  • Touching the face during doffing.
  • Wearing PPE in the canteen.
  • Putting on gloves before hand hygiene.

Check yourself

What is removed first when doffing?

Gloves (in most protocols).

What always follows doffing?

Hand hygiene.

Why check fit?

Gaps defeat the protection.

Quick revision points

  • Don clean to working layer; doff dirty first.
  • Hand hygiene before and after.
  • Do not touch your face.
  • Check fit with a buddy.
  • Follow hospital protocol.

inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.caption: Day 1 of the word series: ASEPSIS, what it means and how you see it in practice.
inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.body:
In short: Asepsis is the foundation of theatre practice. This card explains the word, why it matters and what you will see and hear.

What the card shows

This is the first card in a four-day word series. The word is ASEPSIS, pronounced "a-sep-sis", tagged as a concept. Three boxes explain it. What It Means: the absence of harmful microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses, in other words free from infection. Why It Matters in Theatre: it prevents surgical site infection, it is the foundation of all theatre practice and it protects both patient and staff. You Will See and Hear: the surgeon saying "maintain asepsis", no-touch technique and the rule that the sterile field must stay aseptic. A speech bubble carries "Ezra's Tip": asepsis is why we scrub, gown and glove, and everything we do keeps theatre aseptic. A pink Quick Quiz asks what breaks asepsis, and the answer is touching sterile items with non-sterile hands.

Asepsis versus antisepsis

Asepsis means keeping germs out. Antisepsis means using a chemical on living tissue, such as skin prep, to lower the germs already present. Both are used together.

How to use the card

When you hear a surgeon say "maintain asepsis", picture the sterile field and the rules around it. Test yourself by naming three things you do in theatre purely to keep it aseptic, such as hand scrub, gowning and sterile draping.

From word to practice

Asepsis means the absence of harmful microorganisms. In theatre it is achieved by combining sterilised instruments, sterile drapes and gowns, hand antisepsis, clean air and strict behaviour rules. It is different from simply being 'clean': clean means visible dirt is removed, sterile means no living microorganisms.

There are two related terms: medical asepsis (reducing germ spread in general care) and surgical asepsis (sterile technique used in operations).

Use the word
