When you hear 'maintain asepsis', it means: do not break the sterile field. When a pack is wet or torn, it is not aseptic. When your hands drop below the waist, asepsis is at risk. Try listing three things you do in theatre purely to protect asepsis and say why for each.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Confusing clean with sterile.
  • Thinking a quick wipe is enough.
  • Using an instrument after dropping it.
  • Not reporting a break in technique.

Check yourself

What does asepsis mean?

Absence of harmful microorganisms.

What breaks asepsis?

Touching sterile items with non-sterile hands or surfaces.

How is it different from antisepsis?

Antisepsis reduces germs on living tissue; asepsis prevents contamination.

Quick revision points

  • Asepsis = freedom from harmful microbes.
  • Foundation of theatre practice.
  • Prevents surgical site infection.
  • Clean is not the same as sterile.
  • Report any break.

inside-the-operating-theatre-who-5-momen.caption: The five moments when hand hygiene must be done and how to do it properly.
inside-the-operating-theatre-who-5-momen.body:
In short: Clean hands prevent infection. This card explains the five moments set out by the World Health Organization and how to clean your hands correctly.

What the card shows

A banner reads "Always clean: before and after patient contact, aseptic procedure". The 5 Moments are: 1 before touching a patient, 2 before an aseptic procedure, 3 after body fluid exposure risk, 4 after touching a patient and 5 after touching the patient's surroundings. How To: hand wash for 40 to 60 seconds with soap and water, hand rub for 20 to 30 seconds with alcohol, keep nails short, remove jewellery and use the WHO poster technique. When In Theatre: before entering, after removing gloves, before handling drugs, after touching waste bins, before eating after theatre and using hand rub at the bedside.

Why moments, not routines

Hands carry germs between patients and surfaces. The five moments are the points where that transfer is most likely, so cleaning at exactly those points stops infection chains.

Common errors and habits

Washing only when hands look dirty, wearing gloves instead of cleaning hands, long or polished nails, washing for five seconds and touching your face afterwards. Carry a pocket alcohol rub, remind each other, watch the WHO video, practise with UV light to see missed spots, audit your own habits and thank those who remind you. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene: clean hands before putting them on and after taking them off.

The five moments

Before touching a patient; before a clean or aseptic procedure; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; and after touching patient surroundings. Each moment protects either the patient (before) or you and the environment (after).

Hand rub with alcohol is quicker and usually preferred when hands are not visibly soiled; soap and water are needed when hands are visibly dirty or after some infections such as C. difficile.

Doing it properly

Use enough product to cover all surfaces: palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips and wrists. Rub for the time the product requires. Keep nails short, avoid artificial nails and cover cuts. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; clean hands before wearing them and after removing them. Local rules for theatre also include scrubbing before gowning.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Washing only when hands look dirty.
  • Using gloves as a substitute.
  • Rushing the rub.
  • Touching the surroundings immediately after cleaning.

Check yourself

Name two of the five moments.

Before touching a patient and after touching a patient.

When must soap and water be used?

When hands are visibly soiled.

Do gloves replace hand hygiene?

No.

Quick revision points

  • Five moments: before patient, before aseptic task, after body fluids, after patient, after surroundings.
  • Alcohol rub is quick and effective if hands are not visibly dirty.
  • Cover all surfaces.
  • Gloves are not a substitute.
  • Short nails, no jewellery.

inside-the-operating-theatre-where-to-st.caption: Safe places for students to stand, and zones to avoid, in an operating theatre.
inside-the-operating-theatre-where-to-st.body:
In short: A crowded or badly placed observer can endanger a patient. This card shows where to stand and why.

What the card shows

The banner says "Always stand outside the sterile field, do not block the door, do not block the anaesthetist", and a small floor-plan sits in the top corner showing the anaesthetist, instrument table, surgeon, circulating nurse and door. Green Zones (safe): the back wall near the door to observe from a distance, near the circulating nurse without blocking the trolley path, and near the documentation table. Red Zones (no entry): within one metre of the sterile trolley, between the surgeon and the instrument table, behind the anaesthetic machine, near the diathermy foot pedal and in the door swing area. Movement Rules: never walk between sterile persons, ask "May

Why position matters

A crowded theatre is an unsafe theatre. Staying in the green zones keeps the sterile field, the patient's airway and the team's movement safe.

Common errors and habits

Standing behind the surgeon, leaning on a sterile trolley, blocking the circulating nurse's path, walking between the anaesthetist and the patient and crossing the sterile field. Ask the circulating nurse "Where should I stand?", move when asked without argument, take small steps and keep your voice low. Be invisible but attentive.

Why position matters

The sterile field must be protected, the anaesthetist needs access to the patient's head and equipment, and the circulating practitioner needs clear routes for supplies and emergency equipment. Standing in the wrong place can block these, distract staff or cause contamination.

The safest place for a student is usually near a wall or the circulating practitioner, at a distance from sterile areas and away from doors and busy paths.

Practical rules

Ask 'Where may I stand?' before you enter close. Keep hands behind your back or clasped in front, never in pockets. Face the sterile field when passing. Do not stand behind the anaesthetic machine, between the surgeon and the instrument table or near foot pedals. Move when asked and keep movement small. If you need to see better, ask for a step stool in a safe spot.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Standing in the door swing area.
  • Leaning against sterile or equipment surfaces.
  • Crossing between sterile persons.
  • Crowding the patient's head end.

Check yourself

Where is it usually safe to stand?

Near the wall or circulating nurse, away from sterile areas.

Why avoid the anaesthetist's area?

They need clear access to the patient and equipment.

What should you ask first?

'May I stand here?'

Quick revision points

  • Ask before entering close.
  • Stay outside the sterile field.
  • Do not block doors or access.
  • Keep hands visible and still.
  • Move when asked.

inside-the-operating-theatre-logbook-pro.caption: How to keep a useful logbook and show professionalism during attachment.
inside-the-operating-theatre-logbook-pro.body:
In short: The logbook is your proof of learning and your professional diary. This card shows what to write and how to behave.

What the card shows

The banner reads "Always write: learn, respect, confidentiality, punctuality". Logbook Daily lists date, theatre case, procedure, your role (observed or assisted), what you learned, challenges and the supervisor's signature, with a note to write the same day, not at the end of attachment, using medical terms. Professionalism lists arriving 30 minutes early, greeting everyone, no phone in theatre, no patient photos, keeping your voice low, respecting cleaners as equals, keeping confidentiality, no gossip outside and asking questions at the right time. Growth Mindset covers accepting correction, saying thank you, admitting "I don't know", asking to learn, requesting feedback, reading about cases next day and teaching a junior after you learn.

Why the logbook matters

It is the proof that you actually learned the skills your course requires, and supervisors cannot sign what you cannot remember. Writing the same day keeps details accurate.

Common errors

Leaving the logbook empty until the last week, coming late, phones ringing in theatre, arguing with staff, posting theatre photos online and sleeping while standing. Best practices are keeping a pocket notebook and pen, thanking the team, offering "Can I assist?", learning team names and reflecting daily on what went well. Professional behaviour makes the team want to teach you, which is the real benefit of attachment.

Why a logbook matters

Your logbook records skills practised, cases observed, your role, feedback and supervisor signatures. It supports your assessment and shows employers what experience you have. Write it the same day, while details are fresh, and describe what you actually did or observed, not what you wish you had done.

A good entry includes the date, specialty or procedure, your role, what you learned, a skill you practised, a question for tomorrow and a supervisor's signature. Never record patient names or identifying details.

Professional habits

Arrive early, dress correctly, stay off your phone, keep patient information private, respect cleaners and porters as colleagues, accept feedback, say thank you, admit what you do not know and follow up by reading about cases. Teams remember reliable students and teach them more.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving the logbook until the last week.
  • Writing patient names.
  • Exaggerating your role.
  • Arguing with feedback.

Check yourself

When should you write your logbook?

The same day.

What should you never write?

Patient names or identifying information.

Why get signatures daily?

They confirm the work and avoid disputes.

Quick revision points

  • Write the logbook the same day.
  • Be honest and objective.
  • Do not record patient identifiers.
  • Arrive early and stay professional.
  • Welcome feedback.

inside-the-operating-theatre-changing-ro.caption: Theatre dress code and changing room routine, and the infection-control reasons behind them.
inside-the-operating-theatre-changing-ro.body:
In short: Dress code is infection control. This card covers changing steps, cap and mask rules, and jewellery and phones.

What the card shows

A red banner reads "Always dress: correct scrubs, cap, mask, no jewellery", and the main body has three columns. Changing Steps: enter the changing room, remove outside shoes and street clothes, store them in a locker, wear correct-size hospital scrubs, tuck the top in and wear dedicated theatre shoes or clogs. Cap and Mask Rule: the cap covers all hair, the mask covers nose and mouth, change the mask daily, never leave it dangling, never wear it outside theatre and never reuse cloth caps without washing. Jewellery and Phone: remove all jewellery, no nail polish or artificial nails, phone on silent and kept in the locker, no photos without permission, hand hygiene before entering.

Why dress code is infection control

Scrubs, caps and masks are not a uniform for show. They reduce the shedding of skin cells, hair and droplets into the clean air of the theatre, and jewellery and long nails hide germs that scrubbing cannot reach.

Common errors and habits

Students are often caught with outside shoes in the theatre, long nails, a cap that does not cover all hair, a mask under the chin or a photo of a patient. Better habits are bringing an extra inner vest, checking scrubs are clean, washing or ironing caps daily and carrying a small notebook. Good hygiene and deodorant are part of professionalism, because you work close to others.

Why scrubs, caps and masks

People shed skin cells, hair and droplets constantly. Clean scrubs, hair coverings, masks and dedicated footwear reduce the amount of contamination shed into the theatre. Nail polish, artificial nails and jewellery trap germs and can tear gloves. Phones carry germs and can distract.

Dress rules also help distinguish zones: street clothes in the unrestricted zone, scrubs in the semi-restricted zone, and full attire in the restricted zone.

Good habits

Change in the changing room, store your belongings in the locker, wear clean scrubs of the right size with the top tucked in, cover all hair, wear a mask covering nose and mouth, and put on theatre shoes. Remove everything in the same order when leaving. Do not wear theatre clothes outside the complex. Clean your hands before you enter.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Wearing outside shoes into theatre.
  • Letting hair show.
  • Wearing the mask below the nose.
  • Taking phones into the restricted zone.

Check yourself

Why remove jewellery?

Germs hide under it and it can damage gloves.

Where do you store your own clothes?

In a locker in the changing room.

What must a cap cover?

All hair.

Quick revision points

  • Change, cap, mask, theatre shoes.
  • No jewellery or artificial nails.
  • Phone in locker.
  • Do not wear theatre clothes outside.
  • Clean hands before entering.

inside-the-operating-theatre-sterile-glo.caption: Closed and open gloving methods, with the common errors to avoid.
inside-the-operating-theatre-sterile-glo.body:
In short: Sterile gloving keeps the hands' protective barrier intact. This card compares closed and open methods and gives practical tips.

What the card shows

Under the banner "Always glove: no touch, skin check, size, no holes" there are three columns, with me holding a pair of gloves in the corner and my name tagged as a surgical instructor. Closed Method (hands inside gown cuffs): pick up the glove by the cuff side, place it palm down on the cuff, pull it over, unfold it with the fingers going in, repeat for the second glove and keep no skin exposed. This is the preferred method. Open Method (hands out of the cuffs): pick up the folded cuff, touch only the inside, slide the fingers in, use the gloved hand to pick up the second glove by its folded cuff and touch only the outside. Use it when not gowned. After Gloving: check the fit and holes, interlace the fingers, do not touch the face, keep hands at chest level and change a torn glove at once.

Common errors

Skin touching the outside, the wrong size, touching the outside with a bare hand, a dropped glove (discard and reglove) and blowing into a glove.

Habits that help

Know your size, such as 6.5, 7 or 7.5, check the expiry, practise it ten times and ask the circulating nurse to watch you. Dispose of used gloves properly and thank the scrub nurse who corrects you.

Closed versus open

In closed gloving, you put the glove on through the gown cuff so that your bare hand never emerges. This method is used when gowning. In open gloving, your hands are outside the cuffs, so you must handle only the inside of the glove cuff with your bare hand and use the gloved hand to pick up the second glove from the outside of the cuff. Open gloving is used for procedures without a sterile gown.

Both methods aim to ensure that skin touches only the inside of the glove.

Making it routine

Choose the right size; check the pack and expiry; use a clean, dry flat surface; and open the glove wrapper carefully. After gloving, check for holes and fit. Double gloving is commonly used in surgery to reduce the risk of exposure. If a glove is torn or contaminated, change it immediately and discard properly.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Touching the outside of the glove with bare skin.
  • Using the wrong size.
  • Continuing with a torn glove.
  • Blowing into gloves to open them.

Check yourself

Which method is used when you are gowned?

Closed gloving.

What do you do with a torn glove?

Replace it immediately.

Why double glove?

To reduce the risk of exposure if the outer glove tears.

Quick revision points

  • Closed method with gown; open method without.
  • Touch only the inside of the cuff with bare hands.
  • Check size and holes.
  • Change at once if torn.
  • Practise with feedback.

inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.caption: Day 4 of the word series: APPENDICITIS, what it is and why it is a common emergency.
inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.body:
In short: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and a frequent reason for emergency surgery. This card explains the word and what theatre staff should know.

What the card shows

Day 4 features APPENDICITIS, pronounced "a-pen-di-sy-tis", tagged as a disease. What It Means: inflammation of the appendix, a small finger-like organ off the caecum, usually because of obstruction by a faecalith or infection. Why It Matters in Theatre: it is the most common emergency laparotomy and the appendix can perforate and cause peritonitis, but if caught early an appendicectomy cures it. You Will See and Hear: pain in the right iliac fossa (RIF), tenderness at McBurney's point, and the surgeon doing a gridiron or laparoscopic appendicectomy, with the appendix sent to the lab as a specimen. Ezra's Tip says appendicitis is why you will be called at night, so learn the signs early. The Quick Quiz asks for the classic sign: pain that starts around the umbilicus, moves to the RIF and comes with loss of appetite and fever.

Why timing matters

An inflamed appendix that is removed early is a routine case. One that bursts spreads infection through the abdomen and makes recovery longer and riskier.

What the theatre team does

Prepares for emergency cases, checks the count and handles the specimen correctly. Notice how the card links to Peritoneum (Day 3), because rupture leads to peritonitis. Learning words in pairs like this helps both stick.

What happens

The appendix is a small pouch off the caecum. When it becomes blocked by hardened stool, a lymph follicle or infection, it swells and bacteria multiply, causing pain and inflammation. Left untreated, it can perforate and cause peritonitis. The classic pattern is pain that starts around the navel, moves to the lower right abdomen, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever. Diagnosis depends on examination, blood tests and imaging such as ultrasound or CT, though clinical judgement is key.

Treatment is usually appendicectomy, open or laparoscopic, with antibiotics.

For the theatre team

Emergency cases may come at night, so be ready with a general set, laparoscopic equipment if available, suction, diathermy, specimen containers and counts. Expect a possible infected field and prepare for drains and irrigation if requested. The specimen must be labelled and sent to the lab. Be aware that appendicitis can be hard to diagnose in children, older adults and pregnant women.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming every right-sided pain is appendicitis.
  • Forgetting to label the specimen.
  • Not preparing for conversion from laparoscopic to open surgery.
  • Delaying a case that is deteriorating.

Check yourself

Where does the pain finally localise?

The right lower abdomen (right iliac fossa).

What complication follows rupture?

Peritonitis.

What is the usual operation?

Appendicectomy.

Quick revision points

  • Appendicitis = inflamed appendix.
  • Pain moves from the navel to the right lower abdomen.
  • Perforation causes peritonitis.
  • Appendicectomy is the standard treatment.
  • Label and send the specimen.

inside-the-operating-theatre-touch-vs-do.caption: What students may and may not touch in theatre, and the hand rules that prevent accidents.
inside-the-operating-theatre-touch-vs-do.body:
In short: Knowing what not to touch is as important as knowing what to do. This card gives clear boundaries.

What the card shows

A banner reads "Always ask before touching anything; if in doubt, do not touch". Never Touch: sterile trolleys and instruments, sterile packs, anaesthetic machine dials, the diathermy machine, suction knobs, the patient without permission, the surgeon's instruments and drums or sutures. Can Touch With Permission: non-sterile trolley handles, doors with the elbow if taught, the documentation table, chairs, circulating equipment under supervision and waste bins. Hand Rules: if not scrubbed, keep hands behind your back or clasped in front, never in pockets and never crossed over the chest; if scrubbed, keep hands up at chest level, never below the waist and never touching your face, mask or cap.

The one-hand rule

Keeping one hand behind your back stops you from reaching for things without thinking. Add about a metre of distance from the sterile area and you remove most accidents.

Common errors and habits

Opening a sterile pack, touching a wound, touching anaesthetic drugs, adjusting the light without asking and leaning on the bed. For the first three days just observe, then start to assist. When you slip, say "Sorry, I did not know, I will learn", and ask "What can I help with?" Having clear boundaries makes the team trust you, and trust is what earns you hands-on chances later.

Why boundaries exist

Sterile items lose their sterility if touched by non-sterile hands. Machine controls can change settings that affect the patient's safety. Instruments may be sharp. Interrupting a task by touching someone else's equipment can cause errors or injuries. Having clear boundaries protects patients, staff and students.

As you progress, your supervisor will authorise you to do more, but only after training and with permission.

How to behave

Keep your hands visible: clasped in front or behind your back. Ask before touching anything. Keep a metre away from sterile trolleys. If you make a mistake, say so at once. Learn by watching, then do tasks under supervision. When invited to help, repeat the instruction back to be sure you understand.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Reaching to 'help' by adjusting equipment.
  • Touching sterile packs.
  • Leaning on trolleys.
  • Hiding a mistake.

Check yourself

What should you do before touching anything unfamiliar?

Ask permission.

Where should unscrubbed hands be?

Behind your back or clasped in front, visible.

What if you touch something sterile by accident?

Report it immediately.

Quick revision points

  • If in doubt, do not touch.
  • Ask before helping.
  • Keep hands visible and still.
  • Admit mistakes immediately.
  • Trust grows with reliability.

inside-the-operating-theatre-after-use-r.caption: How to restock the emergency trolley after use, document it and verify it is ready.
inside-the-operating-theatre-after-use-r.body:
In short: The emergency trolley is useless if it is incomplete. This card shows how to restock, document and verify it.

What the card shows

A red banner across the top says "Always restock immediately: checklist, signature, seal", and three numbered columns follow. Column 1, Immediate Action, lists replacing used drugs and airway items, checking expiry on new stock, cleaning the trolley surface and never leaving it empty. Column 2, Documentation, covers writing used items in the book with time, date and patient, signing your name, and returning empty ampoules to pharmacy. Column 3, Verify, lists a two-person check, a completed checklist, sealing the trolley, a photo of the sealed trolley and handover to the next shift. Below sit Common Errors and Best Practices boxes.

Why the trolley must never stay empty

The emergency trolley is used when seconds count. If it was used in the last emergency and not restocked, the next patient pays for it. That is why the card says "restock fast, no empty trolley".

The errors to avoid

The common mistakes are skipping the restock after an emergency, restocking with an expired item, forgetting to document, and leaving a broken seal. The best habits are having a restock kit ready, restocking within thirty minutes, using a laminated list and charging the defibrillator after every use. As a student, ask to take part in the two-person check so you learn the contents of the trolley.

Why restocking is urgent

Cardiac arrests, airway emergencies and severe reactions need immediate equipment and drugs. If the trolley was used and not restocked, the next patient will be at risk. A standard restocking process makes sure nothing is missed and the trolley is returned to a ready state.

It also shows which items are used often, so supplies can be planned.

The process

Replace used and expired items with new ones in the right place; check expiry dates; record the items and quantities used; sign; return empty ampoules where required; have a second person check against the checklist; seal the trolley with a numbered seal and record the number; and hand over at the shift change. Test the defibrillator and suction after use.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving the trolley unsealed.
  • Restocking with expired drugs.
  • Not recording what was used.
  • Delaying restock until the next shift.

Check yourself

Why use a numbered seal?

It shows if the trolley has been opened.

Who checks the restock?

A second person.

When should restocking be done?

Immediately after use.

Quick revision points

  • Restock immediately.
  • Check expiry dates.
  • Document and sign.
  • Second-person check.
  • Seal and record the number.

inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-e.caption: The emergency drugs on a theatre trolley and the checks that make them safe to use.
inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-e.body:
In short: Emergency drugs must be ready, correct and in date. This card shows common examples and the checks for dose, expiry and dilution.

What the card shows

A red banner says "Always check: dose, expiry, dilution, documentation". Common Drugs lists adrenaline 1 mg in 10 ml, atropine 0.6 mg, amiodarone 150 mg, an adrenaline infusion preparation and lignocaine 2 per cent. Expiry Log describes a red sticker for items expiring within one month, a yellow sticker for three months, a daily photo of the list, a check before each shift and removing expired items immediately. Dilution covers adrenaline 1 mg in 100 ml normal saline, atropine ready to use, amiodarone given slowly IV, labelling with date and time, and a dilution chart kept on the trolley.

The four checks

Dose is what you give, expiry is whether it still works, dilution is how it is prepared and documentation is the record that you did all three. A mistake in any one can harm the patient.

Common errors and habits

Expired adrenaline, wrong dilution, unlabelled syringes and a missing dose chart are the typical failures. Good habits are a laminated dose chart, a signed expiry book, photo evidence and a two-person double check. Concentrations and protocols differ between hospitals, so always use your own pharmacy-approved chart. As a student you are there to learn the names and the checks, not to prepare or give these drugs.

What the drugs are for

Adrenaline is used in cardiac arrest and severe allergic reactions. Atropine treats some slow heart rates. Amiodarone treats certain dangerous heart rhythms. Lignocaine is a local anaesthetic and also used for some rhythm problems. Each has strict indications, doses and routes defined by guidelines and prescribed by trained clinicians.

The trolley may also hold glucose, naloxone, hydrocortisone and other drugs depending on the hospital.

Checks for readiness

Drugs must be in date, correctly labelled, stored as directed, with dilution charts and dose references available. Expiry logs show items that will expire soon so they can be replaced. Because errors can be fatal, units use double checks and clear labelling. Students learn the names and the system, but do not prepare or give these drugs unless authorised and trained.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using unlabelled syringes.
  • Missing expiry dates.
  • Diluting from memory.
  • Giving a drug without a second check.

Check yourself

What are the four checks?

Dose, expiry, dilution and documentation.

Who prepares emergency drugs?

Trained, authorised staff.

Why keep a dilution chart?

To avoid dosing errors.

Quick revision points

  • Check dose, expiry, dilution and documentation.
  • Label every syringe.
  • Expiry log with colour stickers.
  • Use hospital-approved charts.
  • Students observe and learn.

inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-co.caption: When and how to count swabs, sharps and instruments, and what to do when the count is wrong.
inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-co.body:
In short: The surgical count is the last safety net before closing a wound. This card explains the process and your role.

What the card shows

A red banner says "Always count: before incision, before closure, before patient leaves; count with scrub and circulating". When To Count: before incision (baseline), before closure of the cavity, before skin closure and a final count before the patient leaves, covering all sharps, instruments and swabs, with an extra count if staff change and a requirement to tell the surgeon if the count is wrong. How To Count: aloud, verbal and heard, showing each item, on a whiteboard to track the tally, by scrub and circulating together, with no distractions and phones silent. Student Role: observe without interrupting, learn instrument names, say "I added" if you bring something in, help search if there is a discrepancy and never hide a dropped item.

Why we count

A retained sponge or instrument can cause infection, pain and another operation. The count is the last safety net before closing.

Common errors and habits

Counts skipped or rushed, silent counting, forgetting items added, phones ringing, miscounts through distraction and not reporting a wrong count. Learn about twenty common instruments and the types of gauze, know where the count board is, say thank you after a count and document that the count was correct or what action was taken. Count saves lives.

How a count works

At the start of the case, the scrub and circulating practitioners count every swab, sharp and instrument aloud and record the totals. Items added during the case are recorded as they are added. Before closing a cavity and before skin closure, the same items are counted again and compared with the record. A final count is performed before the patient leaves. Any discrepancy must be resolved before the case proceeds.

Counting requires focus, so reduce distractions during counts.

What students can do

Observe how counts are done, learn instrument and swab names, say 'I brought this in' if you add something, help search if a count is wrong and never hide a dropped item. Learn the whiteboard system and where counted waste goes. Treat every count as seriously as if you were responsible, because eventually you will be.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Counting silently.
  • Skipping the count in an emergency.
  • Forgetting items added during surgery.
  • Closing despite a discrepancy.

Check yourself

When are counts done?

Before incision, before closure, at skin closure and before the patient leaves.

What if a count is wrong?

Stop, search, tell the surgeon and image if needed.

Why count aloud?

So the other person can hear and verify.

Quick revision points

  • Count aloud with two people.
  • Record additions.
  • Repeat when staff change.
  • Resolve discrepancies before closing.
  • Document the outcome.

inside-the-operating-theatre-weekly-audi.caption: How regular audits and numbered seals keep an emergency trolley reliable.
inside-the-operating-theatre-weekly-audi.body:
In short: A trolley that is never audited is a trolley that will fail. This card shows weekly and monthly checks and how seals work.

What the card shows

The banner reads "Always audit: weekly, monthly, quarterly, seal integrity". Weekly Audit: count the full emergency trolley against its list, check expiry of all drugs, test the defibrillator battery, clean and dust the trolley, log the seal number and sign the audit book. Monthly Deep Check: rotate near-expiry stock, replace damaged packaging, update the dose chart, photograph the audit and train new staff. Seal System: an intact seal means the trolley is unused, a broken seal means it was used and must be restocked, the seal number goes in the book, a different colour is used each month and only a proper seal is acceptable, never tape.

Why seals work

A numbered, coloured seal shows at a glance whether the trolley has been opened, so staff do not need to open it to check. If the number does not match the book, someone knows to investigate.

Common errors and habits

The audit not signed, a broken seal that is never reported, tape used as a seal and expiry dates missed. Good habits are auditing on the same day every week, setting a calendar reminder, having two people do the audit and even rewarding the best-kept trolley. An audit is boring until the day it matters, and then it is the difference between a trolley that works and one that does not.

Why audits matter

Stock expires, packages get damaged and batteries run down. A weekly audit finds these problems before an emergency. A monthly deep check rotates stock, updates charts and trains staff. Numbered seals let staff see at a glance whether a trolley is ready or has been used, without opening it.

Audits also create a written record, which helps with inspections and learning.

Good practice

Audit on the same day each week, with two people. Compare contents with the checklist, check expiry, test the defibrillator and suction, clean the trolley, record the seal number and sign the book. Use proper numbered seals and change colours monthly. Report any missing or damaged item and replace it promptly.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using tape instead of a proper seal.
  • Not signing the audit book.
  • Missing expiry dates.
  • Ignoring a broken seal.

Check yourself

What does a broken seal mean?

The trolley has been opened and needs checking and restocking.

How often is the full audit done?

Weekly, with a deeper check monthly.

Why record seal numbers?

To detect unauthorised opening.

Quick revision points

  • Weekly audit, monthly deep check.
  • Two-person check.
  • Numbered seals, not tape.
  • Record and sign.
  • Replace stock promptly.

inside-the-operating-theatre-emergency-r.caption: What a student should and should not do during a theatre emergency.
inside-the-operating-theatre-emergency-r.body:
In short: In an emergency, a calm student who stays out of the way and follows instructions is a help. This card shows how.

What the card shows

A red banner says "Always call for help, do not panic, do not run, do not touch the emergency trolley unless trained". The first column, Do, says stay calm, stand back to a safe zone, call for help loudly, watch and learn, note the time of events, help with non-sterile tasks, fetch items if asked, clear the way for the trolley and comfort other patients outside. The second column, Do Not, says do not shout, run out, touch the emergency trolley or drugs unless told, touch the defibrillator, crowd the patient, block the anaesthetist, take photos or discuss the case outside. The third, Learn After, covers debrief, a written reflection, asking questions and talking to a mentor if you are distressed.

Why the student role is limited

In an emergency every second goes to people with training. A student who freezes in the doorway or crowds the bed becomes a hazard, so the safest help is to stay calm, keep clear and follow instructions.

How to prepare

Know the crash bell number and the locations of the emergency trolley, oxygen and suction. Learn BLS, and if you are trained you can offer: "Can I help with chest compressions?" Never use your phone or post anything online. After the event, write a reflection: what happened, what you learned and what you would do next time.

Why limits matter

Emergencies move fast and involve high-risk actions such as defibrillation and drug administration. Untrained involvement can cause harm or delay the team. Your safest and most valuable contribution is to stay calm, call for help if you are first to notice, keep clear of the patient and equipment, and follow clear instructions.

If you hold a valid BLS certificate and are asked to help, you may support with compressions or other tasks within your training.

Before and after

Learn the emergency numbers, the location of the emergency trolley, oxygen and suction, and the evacuation route. After the event, take part in the debrief, write a reflection and look after yourself. Talk to a supervisor or mentor if you feel distressed. Never photograph or share details of an emergency.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Freezing in the doorway.
  • Running or shouting.
  • Touching the defibrillator without training.
  • Discussing the case outside.

Check yourself

What is the first thing to do if you notice a collapse?

Call for help loudly.

Who handles the emergency trolley?

Trained staff.

What should you do afterwards?

Debrief and reflect.

Quick revision points

  • Stay calm and call for help.
  • Stand clear and follow instructions.
  • Do not touch emergency equipment unless trained.
  • Note times if asked.
  • Debrief and seek support.

inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.caption: Day 3 of the word series: PERITONEUM, the membrane lining the abdomen.
inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.body:
In short: The peritoneum is a thin, glistening membrane that you will see in nearly every abdominal operation. This card explains it.

What the card shows

Day 3 features PERITONEUM, pronounced "per-i-toe-nee-um", tagged as anatomy, in green, blue and yellow boxes. What It Means: the thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity, with the parietal layer lining the wall and the visceral layer covering the organs. Why It Matters in Theatre: all abdominal surgery goes through it, inflammation (peritonitis) is an emergency, and it heals quickly but can form adhesions, so it is handled gently. You Will See and Hear: the surgeon saying "open peritoneum", seeing it shiny and glistening, closing it at the end and checking the peritoneal fluid. Ezra's Tip says the peritoneum is why the abdomen is sterile inside, so learn to recognise it as shiny and thin. The Quick Quiz asks what inflammation of the peritoneum is called, and the answer is peritonitis, a surgical emergency.

A simple way to picture it

Imagine a plastic bag that lines the inside of a room and also wraps around the furniture. The lining is the parietal peritoneum and the wrapping is the visceral peritoneum, and the space between them is the peritoneal cavity.

Why it connects to other cards

It appears in the 7 Layers Closed in C-Section card and in Appendicitis, the Day 4 word. Spotting the same word across topics is how knowledge sticks.

Structure and function

The parietal peritoneum lines the inside of the abdominal wall; the visceral peritoneum covers the organs. Between them lies the peritoneal cavity, which contains a small amount of lubricating fluid so organs can slide smoothly. The peritoneum also holds blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves, and has a strong ability to absorb and respond to infection or irritation.

When it becomes inflamed, the condition is called peritonitis, a serious emergency causing severe pain, a rigid abdomen and fever.

Why it matters in surgery

Entering the abdomen means opening the peritoneum, so the field must be protected from contamination. After surgery, adhesions (scar bands) can form. Surgeons handle it gently, irrigate if contamination occurs and may close or leave it open depending on technique. Look for its shiny, thin appearance in the next abdominal case you observe.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Confusing peritoneum with muscle or fascia.
  • Rough handling.
  • Missing signs of peritonitis.
  • Forgetting irrigation fluids.

Check yourself

What lines the abdominal wall?

The parietal peritoneum.

What is peritonitis?

Inflammation of the peritoneum.

What can form after surgery?

Adhesions.

Quick revision points

  • Peritoneum: thin, shiny abdominal lining.
  • Parietal lines the wall; visceral covers organs.
  • Peritonitis is an emergency.
  • Adhesions can follow surgery.
  • Handle gently.

inside-the-operating-theatre-waste-segre.caption: How to sort waste correctly in the theatre: general, infectious, sharps and special waste.
inside-the-operating-theatre-waste-segre.body:
In short: Theatre generates large amounts of waste, and mixing it makes it dangerous and costly. This card shows the sorting rules.

What the card shows

A red banner reads "Always segregate at the point of generation: black, yellow, red sharps". The Black Bin is general waste: paper, wrappers, uncontaminated packaging and food waste, with no blood and no sharps, tied when three-quarters full, followed by hand hygiene. The Yellow Bin is infectious waste: blood-soiled gauze, gloves and masks used with the patient, suction tubing and contaminated drapes, labelled and sent for incineration. The Red Sharps section covers sharps boxes for needles and blades with no recapping, filling to the three-quarters line, closing and sealing, and also lists a red bag for highly infectious waste, anatomical waste such as placenta and tissue, specimen waste and separate chemical waste.

A note on colour codes

Colour schemes vary. This card uses black, yellow and red, while the Biomedical Waste Segregation card uses red, yellow, black and white. Learn the chart of your own hospital and follow it, because the system only works when everyone uses the same one.

Errors and habits

Sharps in a black bag, infectious waste in the black bin, overfilled bins, recapped needles, food waste in the yellow bin and general waste in the sharps box. Always segregate at the point of generation, close bins when three-quarters full, carry waste with care, wash hands afterwards and thank the cleaners.

Why sorting matters in theatre

Theatre waste includes packaging, blood-soaked swabs, tubing, sharps, tissue and chemicals. If sharps go into bags, cleaners can be injured. If infectious waste goes into general waste, others are exposed. Sorting at source protects everyone and reduces the volume that needs expensive treatment.

Colour codes vary, so follow your hospital's system, displayed near the bins.

Daily practice

Place bins close to where waste is made. Decide before you throw. Never recap needles, and place sharps directly into the container. Tie bags when three-quarters full, handle them by the neck and never compress with your hands. Keep specimen containers and tissue in the proper routes. Clean up spills and wash hands after handling waste.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Overfilled bins.
  • Recapped needles.
  • Infectious waste in general bins.
  • Food in clinical waste.

Check yourself

Where do blood-soaked swabs go?

In the infectious waste bin or bag.

When are bags tied?

At about three-quarters full.

Why sort at the point of generation?

To prevent mixing and exposure.

Quick revision points

  • Segregate at the point of generation.
  • Follow your hospital's colour code.
  • Never recap needles.
  • Do not overfill.
  • Wash hands after.

inside-the-operating-theatre-common-scru.caption: The most common scrubbing, gowning and sterile field errors, and what to do when you make one.
inside-the-operating-theatre-common-scru.body:
In short: Everyone makes mistakes when learning. This card lists the common ones and how to correct them safely.

What the card shows

This is the busiest graphic in the series, with a red banner saying "Always check: if contaminated say loudly and change immediately". Three upper columns list errors. Scrub errors: scrubbing under two minutes, touching the tap after scrubbing, long or polished nails, jewellery left on, water dripping from elbow to hand, and flicking water or shaking hands. Gown and glove errors: touching the outside of the gown, the gown touching the floor, wrong glove size, touching the face after gloving, adjusting the mask with sterile hands, continuing with a torn glove and picking a glove up from the floor. Sterile field errors: hands below the waist, turning your back to the sterile field, walking away in a sterile gown, touching a non-sterile trolley, reaching over a non-sterile area, leaning on the bed and sitting in a sterile gown.

What to do if contaminated

Stop immediately, say "I am contaminated", step back, ask the circulating nurse for a new gown and gloves, and re-scrub if needed. Do not hide the mistake: honesty saves the patient.

Student tips

Watch three cases before you scrub, ask a mentor to supervise your first time, practise in the skills lab, trim nails every Sunday night and remove jewellery before you leave home. Thank the team when they correct you, because a correction is a free lesson.

Why errors cluster

Scrubbing is rushed when students worry about time; gowning errors occur when the gown touches the floor or the hands touch the outside; sterile field errors happen when attention drifts and hands move below the waist or the body turns away from the field. Most are habits that can be changed with practice and feedback.

The key is not to avoid being corrected but to make it easy for others to correct you early.

The right response

If you realise you are contaminated, stop, say so aloud, step back and ask for a new gown or gloves or to re-scrub. Do not argue and do not hide it. After the case, ask what you could do better. Practise in the skills lab, watch experienced staff and keep nails trimmed and jewellery off.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Hiding a break in technique.
  • Rushing the scrub.
  • Touching the face after gloving.
  • Adjusting the mask with sterile gloves.

Check yourself

What do you do if you contaminate yourself?

Announce it and change or re-scrub.

Why is touching the tap after scrubbing an error?

It recontaminates the hands.

How can you improve fast?

Practise and ask for feedback.

Quick revision points

  • Declare contamination immediately.
  • Do not hide errors.
  • Watch hands, waist level and back.
  • Practise in the skills lab.
  • Accept corrections gracefully.

inside-the-operating-theatre-welcome-to-.caption: What to know on your first day of theatre attachment: layout, people and expectations.
inside-the-operating-theatre-welcome-to-.body:
In short: The first day sets the tone for the whole attachment. This card is a quick orientation to theatre layout, roles and manners.

What the card shows

A red banner reads "Always remember: you are a guest, learn, observe, respect". Theatre Layout lists the changing room and lockers, the scrub area, theatre rooms, recovery, CSSD and store, and where the toilet is. Who Is Who lists the theatre in-charge, circulating nurse, scrub nurse, anaesthetist, surgeon, cleaner and porter. First Day Do's include reporting 30 minutes early, wearing the correct scrubs, removing jewellery, silencing your phone, bringing your logbook and notebook, and asking before touching anything. Common Errors and Best Practices follow at the bottom.

Why the first day matters

First impressions in theatre are built on small things: being early, being dressed correctly and knowing who everyone is. Teams teach students who look ready to learn.

Mistakes to avoid

Coming late, wearing outside shoes, entering without a cap and mask, touching sterile trolleys and using a phone inside. Better habits are greeting everyone, smiling and introducing yourself, thanking people who teach you, writing notes daily and asking questions at the right time, which is usually between cases, not mid-incision. Walk the layout before the first case so you know where recovery, CSSD and the store are. This is the card I would give to every new attachment student.

Learn the geography

Find the changing room, scrub sinks, operating rooms, recovery, CSSD, stores, toilets and emergency exits. Know which areas are clean, semi-restricted and restricted. Watch how people move: staff, patients, clean supplies and dirty items follow set routes.

Know the names and roles of the theatre in-charge, nurses, anaesthetists, technologists, cleaners and porters.

Show you are ready to learn

Report early with your logbook and a notebook. Follow the dress code. Introduce yourself and say what you are able to do and what you want to learn. Ask questions between cases. Offer help with non-sterile tasks. Keep your phone away. Accept corrections and thank people who teach you.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Arriving late.
  • Not asking permission.
  • Wearing wrong footwear.
  • Not learning people's names.

Check yourself

What should you bring on day one?

Logbook, notebook, pen and correct attire.

When is a good time to ask questions?

Between cases or in quiet moments.

Why know the layout?

So you move safely and help effectively.

Quick revision points

  • Arrive early and dressed correctly.
  • Learn layout and roles.
  • Ask before touching.
  • Be helpful and humble.
  • Write your logbook daily.

inside-the-operating-theatre-theatre-cle.caption: Cleaning and disinfecting theatre between cases, daily and weekly.
inside-the-operating-theatre-theatre-cle.body:
In short: A clean theatre protects the next patient. This card shows the routines and your role.

What the card shows

A banner reads "Always clean: high-touch surfaces, between cases, daily terminal, weekly". Between Cases: remove linen and waste, wipe the bed with disinfectant, clean high-touch areas such as the anaesthetic machine, monitors and handles, clean suction, replace linen, mop the floor and check and restock. Daily Terminal: at the end of the list, clean thoroughly, including walls, lights and trolleys, empty and clean bins, mop with disinfectant, check stock and expiry and test the defibrillator. Students Role: do not clean sterile instruments (CSSD does that), observe technique, help remove linen with gloves, help with waste segregation, learn disinfectant contact times and ask "What can I help with?"

Why contact time matters

A disinfectant only works if it stays wet on the surface for the time on its label. Wiping and drying it straight away does little.

Common errors and habits

Cleaning without gloves, mixing dirty and clean cloths, using the same mop for theatre and toilet, not waiting contact time, spraying disinfectant on electronics and forgetting high-touch spots. Learn dilutions, use colour-coded mops, focus on high-touch areas, respect the cleaning team and thank them. Cleaning is part of surgery, and there are no shortcuts, because clean theatres save lives.

Why students should care

A clean theatre is the first layer of protection for the next patient on the list, so noticing a missed spot or a wet floor and telling someone is part of your job too.

Cleaning versus disinfecting

Cleaning removes visible soil with detergent and water; disinfecting kills many germs using a chemical and requires the surface to stay wet for the stated contact time. Both are needed because disinfectants do not work well on dirt. High-touch surfaces such as the table, equipment controls, handles and light handles need frequent attention.

Terminal cleaning at the end of the list covers walls, lights, floors and fixtures more thoroughly.

Good practice

Wear appropriate PPE, work from clean to dirty and from top to bottom, use colour-coded cloths and mops, change cloths and solutions as required, dilute disinfectants correctly, avoid spraying electronics and let surfaces air dry. Remove waste and linen properly, restock and record. Treat the cleaning team as essential colleagues.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Wiping disinfectant dry immediately.
  • Using the same mop everywhere.
  • Skipping high-touch areas.
  • Mixing chemicals.

Check yourself

Why wait for contact time?

The disinfectant needs time to kill germs.

Which direction do you clean?

Clean to dirty, top to bottom.

What are high-touch surfaces?

Surfaces often touched, such as handles and controls.

Quick revision points

  • Clean first, then disinfect.
  • Respect contact time.
  • Clean to dirty, top to bottom.
  • Use correct dilutions.
  • Thank the cleaning team.

inside-the-operating-theatre-sterile-gow.caption: Assisted sterile gowning step by step, and why assistance is needed.
inside-the-operating-theatre-sterile-gow.body:
In short: Putting on a sterile gown without contamination takes practice. This card explains the steps and the common errors.

What the card shows

The banner says "Always gown: sterile technique, hands up, do not touch outside". Preparation: hands up after scrubbing, the circulating nurse opens the gown pack, check the size and expiry, do not touch the outside of the gown and keep your hands inside the sleeves. Steps: pick up the gown at the neck, let it unfold without touching the floor, slide your arms into the sleeves, the circulating nurse pulls it from behind and ties it at the back, then wait for gloves and never touch the ties with sterile hands. After Gowning: hands stay inside the cuffs, do not cross your arms, wait for gloving, do not turn back to a non-sterile person, do not adjust the gown alone and stay in the sterile area.

Why assistance is built in

The back of the gown cannot be reached without breaking sterility, so a circulating nurse ties it. That is why the technique is called assisted gowning.

Common errors and habits

The gown touching the floor, touching the outside, arms through the wrong holes, adjusting the gown after gloving and a gown that is too small or too big. Ask the circulating nurse to assist, check a mirror if there is one, learn the sizes S, M and L and practise with an old gown. Remember to thank your circulating nurse every time. This card and the Sterile Gloving card are best learned together.

The steps in order

After scrubbing and drying, pick up the gown from the pack by the inside of the neck, step back to a clear area, hold it away from your body and let it unfold with the inside facing you. Slide your arms into the sleeves, keeping your hands inside the cuffs. The circulating practitioner pulls the gown on from the inside at the back and ties the neck and waist ties. A wrap-around gown gets its front panel passed to a sterile person or handled by a method that keeps sterility.

Only then are gloves put on, using the closed method.

Keeping the gown sterile

Do not touch the outside with bare hands, do not let the gown touch the floor, and keep hands in front between chest and waist. If the gown is too large or small, ask for a different size before you start. After gloving, do not adjust your mask or hair. Practise with an old gown and a coach.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Touching the outside of the gown.
  • Dropping the gown on the floor.
  • Putting gloves on before the back is tied.
  • Wearing the wrong size.

Check yourself

Who ties the back of the gown?

The circulating practitioner.

Why keep hands inside the cuffs?

To avoid touching the outside of the gown with bare skin.

What comes after gowning?

Closed gloving.

Quick revision points

  • Pick up from the inside neck.
  • Keep hands in the cuffs.
  • Circulating nurse ties the back.
  • Glove after gowning.
  • Do not adjust after gloving.

inside-the-operating-theatre-specimen-ha.caption: How to collect, label and hand over specimens safely and correctly.
inside-the-operating-theatre-specimen-ha.body:
In short: Specimens are the evidence on which diagnoses are made. This card gives the collection, labelling and handover steps.

What the card shows

A red banner says "Always label at the theatre table, before leaving theatre, no unlabelled specimen". Collection: do not touch the specimen with bare hands, watch the surgeon place it in the container, the circulating nurse labels it, check with the surgeon what the tissue is and where it came from. Labelling: patient name, IP number, date and time, type of specimen, site (left or right), whether it is in formalin or fresh and whether it is for histology or microbiology, then read the label aloud to confirm. Handover: biohazard bag and seal, entry in the specimen book with a signature and two-person check, transport with the form, never leave it on the floor or in a pocket, hand hygiene afterwards and never photograph a specimen.

Why labelling is so strict

A lost or mislabelled specimen can mean a wrong diagnosis, a repeat operation or missed cancer. Labelling at the table, with the surgeon present, removes guesswork.

Common errors and habits

Unlabelled specimens, labelling after leaving theatre, wrong patient names, lost specimens, no book entry, touching with bare hands and formalin spills. Watch your first five specimens, ask "What is this specimen?", learn which containers are for which tests and check formalin expiry. Always confirm with the surgeon and thank the lab staff who receive it.

Collect and confirm

The scrub practitioner passes the specimen to the circulating practitioner without touching the container rim, or places it in the container as directed. The surgeon states what it is and where it came from. Decide whether it goes in fixative or fresh, and for which test.

Label at once with patient name and number, specimen type, site, side, date and time, and any special instruction.

Handover and traceability

Read the label aloud, fill the request form, enter the specimen in the register, place it in a sealed biohazard bag and transport it promptly. The receiver signs. Never leave specimens on the floor, in a pocket or unlabelled. Wash your hands. Never photograph a specimen. If a specimen is lost, report immediately.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Labelling later from memory.
  • Putting two patients' specimens in one bag.
  • Not recording in the register.
  • Using the wrong fixative.

Check yourself

What details go on the label?

Patient name and number, specimen, site and side, date and time.

Why read the label aloud?

To check it with a second person.

What if you cannot find a specimen?

Report immediately and search.

Quick revision points

  • Label at the table.
  • Fixative or fresh: ask the surgeon.
  • Read back and double check.
  • Register and sign.
  • Treat as infectious.

inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-ha.caption: The six hand movements of a surgical scrub, then rinse and entry to theatre.
inside-the-operating-theatre-surgical-ha.body:
In short: A systematic scrub reaches every surface of the hand. This card shows six movements and what to do after scrubbing.

What the card shows

A red banner reads "Always scrub 2 to 5 minutes, nails and jewellery removed, no touch tap". Preparation: remove jewellery and watch, short nails with no polish, cap and mask on correctly, turn the tap on with the elbow and check the soap. The six steps are palm to palm, back of hands, interlace fingers, back of fingers to palms, thumbs in rotation, and fingertips in rotation, then rinse with hands up and elbows down, repeating for two to five minutes. After Scrub: hands up at chest level, do not shake or touch anything, keep hands higher than elbows, enter the theatre backwards and check there is no dripping in the gowning area.

Why this order

It follows a path through every surface of the hand, so no area is skipped. Doing it the same way every time turns it into muscle memory.

Common errors and habits

Touching the tap afterwards, letting the hands fall below the waist, flicking water, touching the face and water running back to the elbows. Practise before you go to theatre, watch a video, read the chart, use a three-minute timer, keep nails trimmed weekly and learn from the scrub nurse. Scrub times depend on the antiseptic and hospital policy, so follow yours. This card builds on the simpler Hand Scrub Technique card.

Why six movements

Palm to palm cleans the palms. Right palm over the back of the left hand cleans the backs. Interlaced fingers clean between the fingers. Back of fingers to opposing palms cleans the finger backs. Rotating the thumb in the opposite palm cleans the thumbs. Rotating fingertips in the opposite palm cleans the tips and nails. These movements are based on the WHO hand-rubbing technique and cover all common missed areas.

Repeat the sequence on each hand and continue up the forearm as your policy requires.

After the scrub

Rinse from fingers to elbows with hands up. Do not shake the hands. Enter the theatre backwards, holding hands up in front of the body at chest level, or as the unit requires. Dry with a sterile towel and proceed to gown and glove. Follow local timing and products.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Skipping thumbs and fingertips.
  • Touching the tap after scrubbing.
  • Rinsing in the wrong direction.
  • Rushing the sequence.

Check yourself

Which area is often missed?

Thumbs and fingertips.

How should you hold your hands after scrubbing?

Up and in front, above the elbows.

Why practise the sequence?

To make it automatic and complete.

Quick revision points

  • Six movements: palms, backs, between fingers, finger backs, thumbs, fingertips.
  • Rinse fingers to elbows.
  • Hands up.
  • Do not touch anything.
  • Follow local scrub times.

inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.caption: Day 2 of the word series: HAEMOSTASIS, how bleeding stops and how surgeons help it.
inside-the-operating-theatre-word-of-the.body:
In short: Haemostasis is the process of stopping bleeding. This card explains the natural process and surgical methods.

What the card shows

Day 2 of the word series features HEMOSTASIS, pronounced "hee-mo-stay-sis", tagged as physiology, in orange cards. What It Means: the process that stops bleeding, through vasoconstriction, a platelet plug, clotting and fibrin sealing the vessel. Why It Matters in Theatre: it prevents excessive blood loss, keeps the surgical field clear and visible and reduces the need for transfusion. You Will See and Hear: the surgeon saying "achieve hemostasis", using diathermy, ligatures and pressure, and checking bleeders before closure. Ezra's Tip says good hemostasis saves lives, so watch how the surgeon checks every bleeder before closing. The Quick Quiz asks you to name two methods, with pressure, diathermy and ligation as answers.

The three steps of natural hemostasis

First the vessel narrows, then platelets stick to form a plug, and finally the clotting cascade builds a fibrin mesh that seals it. Surgery adds mechanical help on top of this natural process.

Why surgeons check before closing

Bleeding that is missed can collect inside the body, cause pain, infection and shock and force a return to theatre. As a student, notice how often the team pauses to check the field and how the swabs are used to look for oozing. Try explaining hemostasis to a friend in two sentences.

The natural process

When a vessel is damaged, it narrows (vasoconstriction), platelets stick to form a plug, and clotting factors build a fibrin mesh to strengthen it. Later the clot is dissolved as the vessel heals. This is called primary and secondary haemostasis.

Things that interfere include anticoagulant drugs, low platelets, clotting disorders, hypothermia and low calcium.

Surgical haemostasis

Surgeons add pressure, clamps and ties (ligatures), diathermy, sutures, topical agents such as gelatin sponges or haemostatic powders, and bone wax. Before closing, they check the field for oozing and count swabs. The theatre team ensures that suction, diathermy, ties and haemostatic agents are ready and monitors blood loss.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Closing before checking for bleeding.
  • Ignoring hypothermia.
  • Not preparing haemostatic agents.
  • Underestimating blood loss on swabs.

Check yourself

Name two surgical haemostasis methods.

Pressure and diathermy (or ligation).

What does vasoconstriction do?

Narrows the vessel to reduce bleeding.

Why does hypothermia worsen bleeding?

Clotting slows.

Quick revision points

  • Haemostasis = stopping bleeding.
  • Vessel narrows, platelet plug, fibrin clot.
  • Surgery adds pressure, diathermy, ties.
  • Keep the patient warm.
  • Check for bleeding before closure.

inside-the-operating-theatre-safe-instru.caption: Safe passing and handling of instruments and sharps, and what students may and may not do.
inside-the-operating-theatre-safe-instru.body:
In short: Most instrument injuries are avoidable. This card sets out safe passing, sharps rules and boundaries for students.

What the card shows

The banner reads "Always pass sharp away from you, use tray, no hand-to-hand sharps". Sharps Safety: never pass a scalpel blade hand to hand, use a kidney tray, pass the handle first, do not recap, dispose of sharps immediately in a box closed at three-quarters full, wear eye protection and if a sharp falls, let it fall and pick it up with forceps. Instrument Passing: know the names (forceps, scissors, needle holder), pass the handle to the surgeon with the tip away from you, hold firmly, ask if unsure, never throw instruments and learn ten basic instruments in the first week. Student Boundaries: do not hold retractors unless taught, do not load or remove blades, do not handle diathermy, do not adjust suction without asking and keep your hands visible.

Why the tray method

Hand-to-hand sharp passing is the classic cause of sharps injuries. A neutral zone, like a tray, means nobody is ever holding the blade at the same time as another person.

Common errors and habits

Catching a falling sharp, pointing sharps at someone, loading a blade without training, touching the diathermy pedal, forgetting eye protection and passing the wrong instrument. Learn the tray technique, watch the scrub nurse, practise with blunt instruments and say "I am not trained for this" when needed. Double glove when handling sharps and thank the scrub nurse for teaching you.

Safe passing

Use a neutral zone such as a kidney dish or tray for sharps. Announce when you place a sharp. Pass instruments handle first with tips away from people. Use instruments, not fingers, to load and unload blades. Do not catch falling sharps. Discard sharps immediately in a rigid container. Wear eye protection and consider double gloving.

Know the names of basic instruments so you can respond quickly and pass the right one.

Student boundaries

Do not handle blades or diathermy, hold retractors, adjust suction or equipment unless taught and supervised. Keep your hands visible and ask first. Practise passing with blunt instruments in the skills lab. When asked to do something you have not been trained for, say so.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Hand-to-hand passing of sharps.
  • Recapping needles.
  • Catching a falling sharp.
  • Handling blades without training.

Check yourself

Where are sharps placed when passing?

In a neutral zone such as a tray.

What do you do if a sharp falls?

Let it fall and retrieve it with forceps.

Why wear eye protection?

To protect against splashes.

Quick revision points

  • Neutral zone for sharps.
  • Handle first, tip away.
  • Never recap.
  • Dispose immediately.
  • Students work within training.

inside-the-operating-theatre-needle-stic.caption: First aid, reporting and prevention after a needle-stick or sharps injury.
inside-the-operating-theatre-needle-stic.body:
In short: Acting fast after a sharps injury protects your health. This card shows the first steps and how to prevent injuries.

What the card shows

A red banner warns "Always report: do not hide, wash, do not squeeze, PEP within 72 hours". Immediate First Aid: wash with soap and water, do not squeeze, do not use bleach, let it bleed gently, cover with a plaster, do not touch with bare hands and remove gloves and wash hands. Report Now: tell your supervisor and the theatre in-charge, go to casualty, fill in the incident form, document date, time, device and source patient, get a PEP risk assessment and test the source if known. Prevention: never recap needles, dispose of sharps immediately in a box filled only three-quarters, never pass sharps hand to hand, use a tray or forceps, double glove and do not rush.

Why speed matters

Post-exposure prophylaxis works best when started early, and the card says within 72 hours. Reporting also protects you legally, so never hide an injury.

Common errors

Hiding the injury, scrubbing with bleach, squeezing the wound, working on without reporting, recapping a needle or putting sharps in the wrong bin. Best practices are knowing where casualty and the PEP service are, knowing the incident book, being vaccinated against hepatitis B, never carrying sharps in pockets and speaking up about unsafe disposal. Local protocols differ, so follow your hospital's policy.

What to do at once

Stop what you are doing safely, remove gloves, and wash the wound with soap and running water. Let it bleed gently; do not squeeze, scrub or use bleach. Cover the wound. For splashes to eyes, rinse with clean water or saline. Then report to your supervisor and go to the designated service for assessment and, if indicated, post-exposure prophylaxis, ideally as soon as possible after exposure.

Record the details: when, how, the device, the source patient and your vaccination status.

Prevention is the best protection

Vaccinate against hepatitis B, never recap, use neutral zones, dispose of sharps immediately, keep boxes below the fill line and do not carry sharps in pockets. Work calmly. Report unsafe disposal. Hospitals have local post-exposure protocols and counselling; follow them and keep follow-up appointments.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Hiding the injury.
  • Squeezing or scrubbing the wound.
  • Delaying reporting.
  • Skipping follow-up tests.

Check yourself

What do you do first after a needle-stick?

Wash with soap and water and let it bleed gently.

Why report quickly?

PEP and assessment work best early.

What vaccine protects health workers?

Hepatitis B.

Quick revision points

  • Wash, do not squeeze or scrub.
  • Report immediately.
  • Get PEP assessment.
  • Be vaccinated against hepatitis B.
  • Prevent: no recapping, neutral zone, dispose at once.

inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-d.caption: What a defibrillator does and how to check it every day.
inside-the-operating-theatre-meet-your-d.body:
In short: Defibrillators restore a normal heart rhythm in certain cardiac arrests. This card shows the daily checks and safety points.

What the card shows

The banner reads "Always check: power, battery, pads, energy delivery", and three columns follow. 1 Daily Checks: power-on self-test, battery 100 per cent charged, pad expiry and seal intact, cables undamaged. 2 Energy Test: set a 200 J test charge, check that it delivers and sounds the alarm, sign the logbook and report if it fails. 3 Safety: nothing flammable nearby, clear the bed during a shock, check adult or paediatric pads and keep the trolley plugged in. Below are common errors (dead battery, expired pads, no daily test, broken cable) and best practices (same-time daily check, photo of expiry, a sticker with the next due date, a two-person check).

What a defibrillator does

It delivers a controlled electric shock to reset certain dangerous heart rhythms, such as ventricular fibrillation. Early shock is the most important factor in survival, so a machine that does not work is worse than no machine because people trust it.

Why the daily test

A machine that was fine last week may have a flat battery today. The test confirms power, charge and delivery in one go. Test energy settings can differ by machine, so follow your own manufacturer's test procedure. As a student, observe the check, learn where the machine is and never handle it unless trained.

What it does

A defibrillator delivers an electric shock that can stop a chaotic heart rhythm such as ventricular fibrillation and allow the heart's natural pacemaker to take over. It works only for certain rhythms; for others, CPR and drugs are the treatment. Automated external defibrillators analyse the rhythm and guide the user.

Early shock and high-quality CPR together give the best chance of survival.

Daily checks and safety

Check that the device powers on, the battery is charged, the pads are in date and sealed, the cables are intact and the self-test passes. Where a test discharge is part of policy, follow the manufacturer's instructions and sign the log. During use, keep everyone clear, remove oxygen sources from the chest area as protocol requires, avoid wet surfaces and follow the machine's prompts. Only trained staff operate it; students observe.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Skipping daily checks.
  • Using expired pads.
  • Touching the patient during a shock.
  • Leaving the machine unplugged or uncharged.

Check yourself

What rhythm can a defibrillator treat?

Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

What must you do before shock?

Make sure everyone is clear.

What should be checked daily?

Power, battery, pads and cables.

Quick revision points

  • Defibrillators treat certain rhythms only.
  • Check daily and log.
  • Pads in date and sealed.
  • Keep clear during a shock.
  • Only trained staff use it.

inside-the-operating-theatre-perioperati.caption: What to document in theatre and how to write records and student logs.
inside-the-operating-theatre-perioperati.body:
In short: Documentation is part of patient safety. This card shows what to record, how to write it and how students should log their learning.

What the card shows

The banner says "Always document: time, date, signature, no blank space, no correction fluid". What To Write: patient name and IP number, diagnosis, procedure, surgeon and anaesthetist, time in and out, count correct, specimen details, implants, drains and catheters, complications and handover notes. How To Write: black pen, legible, no unclear abbreviations, 24-hour time, date as DD/MM/YYYY, cross out blank spaces, sign with name and designation, two-person check for counts and use approved forms only. Student Logs: be objective, say what you observed, your role, what you learned, skills practised, challenges and questions for the next day, and get your supervisor to sign daily.

Why documentation counts

A record that is missing, unsigned or unclear is treated as if the care never happened. It also protects the patient, the staff and the hospital in any later review.

Common errors and habits

Blank spaces, missing signatures or times, forgetting the count, using correction fluid, illegible handwriting, documenting before the procedure is done and writing a patient's name on scrap paper. Better habits are carrying a black pen, writing straight after the case and asking the circulating nurse what needs recording. Learn the forms: theatre register, recovery notes, count sheet and specimen book. Never post notes or patient names online.

The theatre record

Typical entries include patient identification, diagnosis, planned and performed procedure, team members, anaesthesia type, times, counts, specimens, implants, drains, complications and handover. Forms include the theatre register, anaesthesia chart, count sheet, implant log and recovery notes. Each must be legible, signed, dated and timed.

The written record is evidence that checks were done and care was given.

How to write well

Use black ink, clear handwriting and approved abbreviations. Use 24-hour time. Never leave blank spaces without crossing them out. Correct errors with a single line and initials. Write at the time or soon after. Students' logs should be honest, objective and free of patient identifiers.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving blank lines.
  • Using correction fluid.
  • Documenting before the task is done.
  • Using unapproved abbreviations.

Check yourself

How should an error be corrected?

With a single line and initials.

Why use 24-hour time?

To avoid confusion between day and night.

What must a student's log not contain?

Patient identifiers.

Quick revision points

  • Write legibly, sign, date and time.
  • Document counts, specimens and implants.
  • No blank spaces.
  • Single line to correct.
  • Keep confidentiality.

inside-the-operating-theatre-maintaining.caption: How to keep the sterile field sterile throughout an operation.
inside-the-operating-theatre-maintaining.body:
In short: Sterility is easy to lose and hard to regain. This card shows the rules, the boundaries and the common breaks.

What the card shows

A red banner says "Always remember: sterile to sterile only, face the sterile field, hands at chest-to-waist level". Sterile Rules: sterile touches sterile only, non-sterile touches non-sterile only, hands stay between chest and waist, never turn your back to the field, keep one metre from non-sterile areas, do not touch your face, mask or cap and if in doubt, you are contaminated. Boundaries: the front from chest to waist is sterile, sleeves from two inches above the elbow to the cuff, below the waist is not, the back is not, do not tuck hands under armpits, stay in the sterile zone and do not walk out of theatre. What Breaks Sterility: hands below the waist, turning to the sterile trolley, touching a non-sterile person, reaching over a non-sterile area, touching the mask or face, sweat dripping and a torn gown or glove.

The golden habit

If you think you may be contaminated, say it out loud: "I am contaminated, change gown and glove." Nobody is blamed for speaking up.

Errors and habits

Hands in pockets, crossing arms under the armpits, touching bed rails and leaning on the trolley are the usual mistakes. Keep your hands clasped at chest height, check the path before moving, give others a wide berth and say "excuse me, sterile" when you need to pass.

The boundaries

On a sterile gown, the front from chest to waist level and the sleeves from about two inches above the elbow to the cuff are considered sterile; the back, shoulders, neck and below-the-waist are not. A sterile table is sterile only on top; edges and anything below the table are not. A one-inch border of drapes and the outside of pack wrappers should be treated as non-sterile.

Because sterility cannot be seen, trust and honesty matter.

Behaviours that protect it

Keep your hands in the sterile zone and visible; face the field; pass back-to-back or face-to-face with another sterile person as taught; do not reach over non-sterile surfaces; keep a metre from non-sterile areas; do not sit or lean on tables; and keep talking to a minimum. If sterility is in doubt, say so and correct it at once.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Turning your back to the field.
  • Reaching over a non-sterile area.
  • Allowing the table edge to count as sterile.
  • Hiding a possible break.

Check yourself

Which part of the gown is sterile?

Front from chest to waist and the sleeves.

What do you do if unsure?

Treat it as contaminated and fix it.

Is the edge of a sterile table sterile?

No.

Quick revision points

  • Sterile to sterile only.
  • Face the field.
  • Keep hands between chest and waist.
  • Treat doubt as contamination.
  • Speak up immediately.

layers-of-the-scalp-scalp-mnemonic.caption: The five layers of the scalp, the SCALP mnemonic and why the layers matter in injury and surgery.
layers-of-the-scalp-scalp-mnemonic.body:
In short: The scalp has five layers that are easy to remember with one word. Each layer explains something about scalp wounds, bleeding and infection.

What the card shows

A purple card lists the five layers of the scalp under the heading "Remember: SCALP": skin, connective tissue (dense), aponeurosis (the galea), loose areolar tissue and pericranium. A short box explains why the layers matter.

Why the layers matter

The dense connective tissue layer holds the walls of scalp vessels open, so scalp wounds can bleed freely.
