The loose areolar layer allows the galea to move over the skull, and it is also the layer through which infection can spread. Learning the order gives you a map of what a scalp wound passes through.

The five layers one by one

S - Skin: thick and hair-bearing, with many oil glands (a common site for sebaceous cysts). C - Connective tissue: dense, fatty tissue rich in blood vessels; its fibrous septa hold vessels open, so scalp cuts bleed heavily. A - Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica): a tough sheet linking the frontalis and occipitalis muscles. L - Loose areolar tissue: a loose layer that lets the first three layers slide over the skull; infection and blood can spread here. P - Pericranium: the periosteum covering the skull bones.

The first three layers move together and are sometimes called the 'scalp proper'.

Why it matters clinically

Scalp lacerations bleed profusely but usually stop with firm pressure and suturing. A wound that cuts the galea needs careful repair to avoid gaping. Infection in the loose layer can travel through emissary veins into the skull, which is why it is called the 'danger area'. In theatre, neurosurgeons incise through these layers for craniotomy, and the scalp is closed in layers. Local anaesthetic with adrenaline is often injected to reduce bleeding.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Forgetting that the loose layer is the 'danger area'.
  • Underestimating scalp bleeding.
  • Mixing up galea and pericranium.
  • Not closing the galea in layered repair.

Check yourself

What does SCALP stand for?

Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

Why do scalp wounds bleed heavily?

Vessels in the dense layer are held open by connective tissue.

Which layer is the danger area?

The loose areolar tissue layer.

Quick revision points

  • SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.
  • Dense layer holds vessels open: heavy bleeding.
  • Loose layer: spread of infection.
  • The first three layers move together.
  • Close in layers after surgery.

word-of-the-day-haemostasis.caption: Haemostasis: the stopping of bleeding, naturally and in surgery.
word-of-the-day-haemostasis.body:
In short: Haemostasis is the process that stops bleeding. It is one of the first terms every theatre student must master.

What the card shows

A word-of-the-day card gives the pronunciation, the meaning and two memory hooks: haemo means blood and stasis means standing still.

In theatre

Surgeons and the team achieve haemostasis with pressure, clamps, ties, diathermy or topical agents. A bleeding vessel that is not controlled can quickly change the course of an operation, which is why swabs, suction and good lighting matter.

The word and its parts

Haemo- means blood and -stasis means standing still or stopping. In physiology, haemostasis has three steps: the vessel narrows, platelets form a plug and the clotting cascade builds fibrin to seal the break. In surgery, the term also describes the surgeon's efforts to stop bleeding by pressure, clamps, ligatures, diathermy, sutures and topical agents.

Compare it with 'haemorrhage' (bleeding) and 'haematoma' (collection of blood).

In theatre

The surgeon may say 'achieve haemostasis' before closing or 'check for bleeders'. The team keeps suction, swabs, diathermy and haemostatic products ready, counts swabs and watches blood loss. Patients with low platelets, clotting disorders, certain medicines or hypothermia are at higher risk of bleeding. Always report unusual bleeding or oozing early.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Closing without checking for bleeding.
  • Ignoring slow oozing.
  • Forgetting that cold slows clotting.
  • Not counting blood-soaked swabs.

Check yourself

What does 'stasis' mean?

Standing still or stopping.

Name two ways surgeons achieve haemostasis.

Diathermy and ligation or pressure.

What word means a collection of blood?

Haematoma.

Quick revision points

  • Haemostasis: stopping bleeding.
  • Haemo = blood; stasis = stopping.
  • Methods: pressure, clamps, ties, diathermy, topical agents.
  • Check before closure.
  • Keep the patient warm.

word-of-the-day-asepsis.caption: Asepsis: preventing contamination, and how it differs from antisepsis.
word-of-the-day-asepsis.body:
In short: Asepsis means keeping harmful microorganisms away. It is the principle behind everything in theatre from scrubbing to draping.

What the card shows

A green word-of-the-day card defines asepsis and notes how it differs from antisepsis. The memory hook reads: A means without, sepsis means infection.

Asepsis versus antisepsis

Asepsis is about preventing contamination in the first place, through hand scrub, sterile gowns and gloves and a protected sterile field. Antisepsis is the use of a chemical on living tissue, such as skin preparation, to reduce the number of germs. Both are needed in theatre.

The word and the idea

A- means without and sepsis refers to infection or putrefaction, so asepsis means 'without infection-causing germs'. It is achieved by sterilisation of instruments, sterile barriers, hand antisepsis and good behaviour in the field.

Antisepsis is the use of chemical agents on living tissue, such as alcohol, chlorhexidine or iodine, to reduce germs on the skin. Disinfection uses chemicals on objects. Sterilisation destroys all microbial life.

Putting it into practice

Aseptic technique includes scrubbing, gowning, gloving, draping, handling instruments without contamination and keeping traffic low. Mistakes include touching sterile items with unsterile hands, using wet or damaged packs and dropping items. If asepsis is broken, correct it immediately. Learn how to explain the difference between asepsis, antisepsis, disinfection and sterilisation in your own words.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using antisepsis and asepsis interchangeably.
  • Believing disinfected means sterile.
  • Using wet packs.
  • Letting the field be crowded.

Check yourself

What does asepsis prevent?

Contamination and infection.

What is antisepsis?

Reducing germs on living tissue with a chemical.

Is disinfection the same as sterilisation?

No; sterilisation destroys all microbial life.

Quick revision points

  • Asepsis: prevent contamination.
  • Antisepsis: reduce germs on living tissue.
  • Disinfection kills many germs on objects.
  • Sterilisation kills all microbes.
  • Break in asepsis: correct immediately.

team-shout-out-cssd-and-cleaning-staff.caption: A thank-you to the people who clean, pack, sterilise and turn over theatres.
team-shout-out-cssd-and-cleaning-staff.body:
In short: Behind every safe operation is a team nobody sees. This card says thank you to CSSD and cleaning staff.

What the card shows

A blue shout-out card thanks the CSSD and cleaning teams, with three short reasons they deserve it: clean trays, fast turnover and quiet hard work.

Why it matters

Safe surgery starts long before the first incision. Instruments that were properly cleaned, packed and sterilised, and a room that was properly cleaned between cases, protect every patient. The people who do this work are rarely seen, so a thank-you is well deserved.

What they do

The central sterile services department (CSSD) receives used instruments, cleans them, inspects, packs, sterilises, stores and issues them. Cleaners turn over rooms between cases, clean high-touch surfaces, manage waste and keep the theatre ready. Porters move patients and equipment. These steps happen quietly but each one protects a patient.

Mistakes in cleaning or sterilising can cause infection, so their attention to detail matters.

How to support them

Return instruments promptly and safely, remove gross soil as per policy, keep sharps contained, report damaged instruments, segregate waste and speak politely. A simple thank-you and a clear handover message go a long way. If you are a student, spend time in CSSD to learn how it works.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating CSSD as a 'backroom'.
  • Returning instruments with sharps hidden in linen.
  • Dumping waste in the wrong bin.
  • Never saying thank you.

Check yourself

What does CSSD stand for?

Central sterile services department.

Why is cleaning before sterilising important?

Dirt shelters microbes.

How can staff help CSSD?

By returning instruments safely and promptly.

Quick revision points

  • CSSD and cleaners protect every patient.
  • Return instruments safely.
  • Segregate waste correctly.
  • Report damaged instruments.
  • Say thank you.

new-on-the-site-join-the-list.caption: How to join the email list and what you get when you subscribe.
new-on-the-site-join-the-list.body:
In short: The subscribe page lets you receive new posts and study materials by email. This card explains how to join and what to expect.

What the card shows

A gold announcement card invites people to join the email list for new posts and study materials. It explains that free notes download straight from Drive and paid materials are ordered with M-Pesa, and a QR code opens the subscribe page.

How to join

Scan the QR code or visit the subscribe page, enter your email and choose what you want to hear about. You can unsubscribe any time.

What you get

Subscribers receive updates when new blog posts, study materials and content are published. You can choose the topics you care about, such as theatre technology, study tips, anatomy mnemonics or career updates. Free notes download directly from Drive; paid materials are ordered with M-Pesa through the materials page, and you can request materials that are not listed.

Your email is used only for this list and you can unsubscribe at any time.

How to join

Open the subscribe page, enter your email and optionally your name and interests, and confirm. Check your spam folder if the first message does not arrive. You can scan the QR code on the card to open the page quickly on your phone. If you ever want a different frequency or to stop, use the unsubscribe link in the email or contact me.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using a typo in the email address.
  • Not checking spam.
  • Expecting daily emails when updates are periodic.
  • Sharing a work address you may lose.

Check yourself

How can you open the subscribe page quickly?

Scan the QR code or visit the subscribe page.

Can you unsubscribe?

Yes, at any time.

How are paid materials ordered?

By M-Pesa through the materials page.

Quick revision points

  • Join through the subscribe page.
  • Choose your interests.
  • Free notes download from Drive.
  • Paid materials use M-Pesa.
  • Unsubscribe any time.

basic-general-surgery-set-example.caption: An example of what a basic general surgery instrument set may contain, grouped by function.
basic-general-surgery-set-example.body:
In short: A basic set can look like a pile of metal until you group it by job. This card lists an example and shows how to learn it.

What the card shows

A teal card lists an example tray for a basic general set: scalpel handle and blade, dissecting forceps, Mayo and Metzenbaum scissors, artery forceps, Allis tissue forceps, a needle holder, towel clips and sponge-holding forceps. A tip box reminds you that sets differ between hospitals.

Learn it by function

Group the items by what they do: cutting (scalpel, scissors), grasping (forceps), clamping (artery forceps), holding drapes (towel clips), holding swabs (sponge-holding forceps) and suturing (needle holder). It is easier to remember a tray as six jobs than as nine names. See the full article on how to learn instrument names fast.

Six jobs, nine instruments

Cutting: scalpel handle with blade, Mayo scissors (tough tissue), Metzenbaum scissors (delicate tissue). Grasping: dissecting forceps (toothed or plain). Clamping: artery forceps to control bleeding. Holding tissue: Allis forceps. Holding drapes: towel clips. Holding swabs: sponge-holding forceps. Suturing: needle holder. Retractors, suction tips and bowls are usually added by procedure.

The exact contents and names vary between hospitals, countries and surgeons.

How to learn a tray

Lay out a set and name each instrument by sight and touch. Sort them by job. Learn how to hold and pass each safely. After a case, check the count and return the set in the order used by the CSSD. Compare your hospital's tray list with this example and note differences. Ask the scrub practitioner why each item is included.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming all hospitals use the same set.
  • Using instruments for the wrong job.
  • Not counting instruments.
  • Memorising names without handling them.

Check yourself

Which instrument holds the needle?

The needle holder.

What do artery forceps do?

Clamp vessels to control bleeding.

What are towel clips used for?

Holding drapes in place.

Quick revision points

  • Group instruments by function.
  • Know the use of each.
  • Sets differ by hospital.
  • Count before and after.
  • Practise handling and passing.

theatre-abbreviations-quick-list.caption: Seven abbreviations used daily in theatre and what each stands for.
theatre-abbreviations-quick-list.body:
In short: Abbreviations save time and cause confusion if you do not know them. This card lists seven common ones.

What the card shows

A cream card lists seven common abbreviations: OT for operating theatre, CSSD for sterile services, PACU for the recovery unit, GA for general anaesthesia, LA for local anaesthesia, SSI for surgical site infection and PPE for personal protective equipment.

Learn more

There are many more, and some differ between hospitals. Read the longer list in common theatre and hospital abbreviations explained, and ask when you are not sure.

Seven essentials

OT: operating theatre. CSSD: central sterile services department, where instruments are cleaned and sterilised. PACU: post-anaesthesia care unit, the recovery area. GA: general anaesthesia. LA: local anaesthesia. SSI: surgical site infection. PPE: personal protective equipment.

Other frequent ones include NPO (nothing by mouth), IV, ECG, BP, SpO2, ASA (anaesthesia risk class), WHO checklist and DVT.

Using abbreviations safely

In documentation, use only approved abbreviations, because some are ambiguous (for example, 'MS' can mean morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate). When unsure, write the full term. Keep a notebook of abbreviations you meet and check their meaning with your supervisor. Local lists differ, so learn your hospital's approved list.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using unapproved abbreviations in records.
  • Assuming everyone uses the same meanings.
  • Writing abbreviations that can be misread.
  • Not asking when unsure.

Check yourself

What does PACU stand for?

Post-anaesthesia care unit.

What does SSI mean?

Surgical site infection.

Where is CSSD?

The central sterile services department.

Quick revision points

  • OT, CSSD, PACU, GA, LA, SSI, PPE.
  • Use approved abbreviations only.
  • If unsure, write it out.
  • Keep a personal glossary.
  • Learn your hospital's list.
